objectives.statement: Describe the arrangement, separation and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases, and explain how a change of temperature relates to a change in the average random motion of particles.

Explain the effect of particle spacing and the forces between particles on the properties of the three states, and explain Brownian motion as the result of a visible particle being struck unevenly by many fast, invisible fluid particles.

prerequisites.statement: Read a temperature from a thermometer or a labelled scale, and know that a higher reading means a hotter object.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson builds a particle explanation for temperature, so you need to already trust what a temperature reading means before you ask why it changes.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise solids, liquids and gases from everyday observable properties (a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, a gas fills whatever space is available).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The particle model in this lesson explains these familiar everyday properties; you need the properties in mind before the explanation can make sense of them.

diagnostic_items.question: Thermometer A reads 18 °C and thermometer B, placed in a different cup of water, reads 42 °C. Which cup of water is hotter, and by how many degrees?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The water in cup B is hotter, by $42-18=24$ degrees.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Cup A, because its number was mentioned first.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is not yet treating the thermometer reading itself as the thing that decides which object is hotter.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Cannot tell without knowing the room temperature.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not yet trust that comparing two temperature readings directly is enough on its own.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that a temperature reading is read as a direct, comparable number before it is linked to particle motion.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise reading two thermometers side by side and stating which is higher and by how much, before trying to explain why.

theory_blocks.title: Three states, one model
theory_blocks.body:
Solids, liquids and gases look completely different from the outside: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and settles into the bottom of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill whatever space it is given.

All three behaviours come from one single idea, the [[blue:**kinetic particle model**]]: every material is made of tiny particles that are always moving,

and what changes between the three states is how closely packed those particles are, how strongly they pull on each other, and how far each one can move before it collides with another.

In a solid, particles are packed closely in a regular pattern and held by strong forces; each one vibrates about a fixed position but cannot move away from its neighbours, which is why a solid keeps a fixed shape and volume.

In a liquid, particles are still close together and still attract each other, but the forces are weaker and the arrangement is irregular, so particles can slide past one another;

this lets a liquid flow and take the shape of its container while still keeping roughly the same volume.

In a gas, particles are far apart, moving fast in straight lines between collisions, and the forces between them are so weak they are usually ignored; a gas has no fixed shape or volume and expands to fill the space available.

assets.caption: The same particles, drawn the same size in all three panels. Solid: touching in a regular lattice, each one only vibrating about a fixed position (gold arrows). Liquid: still touching most of its neighbours but irregularly arranged with small gaps, so particles can slide past each other (red arrows). Gas: far apart, moving fast in straight lines between collisions.
assets.purpose: Show that the three states share one particle model and differ only in spacing, arrangement and freedom of movement, using a consistent particle size so no state is drawn with 'bigger' or 'smaller' particles.

theory_blocks.title: Temperature is linked to average particle motion
theory_blocks.body:
Every particle in a solid, liquid or gas is moving: vibrating in a solid, sliding and vibrating in a liquid, or travelling freely between collisions in a gas.

Not all particles in a sample move at exactly the same speed at the same instant, but a useful summary is the **average** amount of random motion of all the particles together.

Raising the temperature of a substance increases the average random motion of its particles: in a solid this means more vigorous vibration about the same fixed positions, and in a liquid or a gas it means faster average movement between collisions.

Lowering the temperature has the opposite effect, slowing the average motion down. This is why temperature can be used as evidence for what is happening to particles that are themselves far too small to see directly: a measurable,

everyday quantity (temperature) stands in for an invisible one (average particle motion).

theory_blocks.title: Reading a particle diagram correctly
theory_blocks.body:
When you read or draw a particle diagram, check three things in order: **(1) spacing** — are the particles touching and close-packed, or spread out with gaps between them?

**(2) arrangement** — is it a regular repeating pattern, or irregular? **(3) motion** — are the arrows (if drawn) short vibrations about a fixed point, or longer paths between collisions?

A diagram only counts as showing a solid if it has close, regular spacing **and** vibration-only motion; a diagram with close, irregular spacing and sliding motion is a liquid;

a diagram with widely separated particles and long free paths is a gas. All three states should be drawn with particles of the same size,

because it is the same kind of particle throughout a change of state — only the spacing, arrangement and motion change, never the particle itself.

theory_blocks.title: A visible speck is not a single particle of the fluid
theory_blocks.body:
When smoke in air, or pollen grains in water, are viewed under a microscope, the visible specks jitter and zigzag constantly in random directions.

This observation, called **Brownian motion**, is strong evidence for the particle model, but only if the speck itself is correctly identified: [[blue:it is a comparatively large, visible object (a smoke particle or a pollen grain)]], not [[red:a single molecule of the surrounding air or water]].

The air or water particles themselves are far too small to see, even with this microscope.

The speck moves erratically because it is bombarded, from all sides and at random moments, by enormous numbers of these fast-moving, invisible fluid particles.

At any instant, slightly more particles may strike one side than another, giving the speck a small, random push;

because which side gets the larger number of impacts changes from moment to moment, the speck's path zigzags rather than travelling in one steady direction.

The zigzag therefore reveals the constant, random motion of the invisible fluid particles, not a motion of the speck's own choosing.

assets.caption: Left: the microscopic cause — a large visible speck struck from random directions by many fast, invisible fluid particles (arrows show the direction of each impact). Right: the resulting observed effect — the speck's irregular zigzag path, with no single impact drawn, because individual fluid particles cannot be seen.
assets.purpose: Make the paired micro/observable Brownian-motion relationship explicit: random invisible collisions (cause, left) produce the visible zigzag path (effect, right), without ever showing the invisible particles as directly observed.

keywords.definition: The model that all matter is made of constantly moving particles, with spacing, arrangement and freedom of movement determining the state of matter.
The continuous, irregular movement of a visible particle suspended in a fluid, caused by random collisions with the fluid's invisible particles.
The average amount of motion energy of all the particles in a sample, taken together; linked directly to temperature.
The back-and-forth motion of a particle about a fixed position, characteristic of particles in a solid.
Particle motion with no preferred direction, changing constantly due to collisions.

worked_examples.statement: **Identifying the states.** Three particle diagrams are described: (A) particles close together in a regular grid, vibrating only; (B) particles close together, irregularly arranged, sliding past each other; (C) particles widely spaced, moving freely in straight lines between occasional collisions. Identify the state shown in each diagram.
knowns: diagram A: close, regular, vibration only
diagram C: widely spaced, free movement
unknowns: the state shown by each diagram
reasoning: Check spacing first: A and B are close-packed, C is widely spaced, which already marks C as a gas.
Between A and B, check the arrangement and motion: A is regular with vibration only (a solid); B is irregular with sliding motion (a liquid).
worked_examples.solution: A is a solid, B is a liquid, C is a gas.
worked_examples.interpretation: Each state is identified from spacing, arrangement and motion together, not from any one of the three alone: C could not be mistaken for a solid just because its particles also move, since its spacing is the giveaway.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling diagram B a gas because the particles are moving, without checking that they are still close together, unlike in a real gas.

worked_examples.statement: **Warming a solid.** A solid block is heated from $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $70\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ without melting. Describe what happens to its particles at the particle level.
unknowns: what changes, and what stays the same, for the particles
reasoning: The block stays solid, so the particles keep the same close, regular arrangement and the same fixed average positions throughout.
Temperature is linked to average particle motion, so a temperature rise with no change of state means the particles vibrate more vigorously about those same fixed positions.
worked_examples.solution: The particles do not move apart or change their regular arrangement; they vibrate about the same fixed positions, but more vigorously than before, because their average random kinetic energy has increased.
worked_examples.interpretation: This separates two things that are easy to run together: a rise in temperature (more vigorous vibration) and a change of state (particles breaking free of fixed positions), which has not happened here.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the particles 'spread out' or 'move faster from place to place', which describes melting, not simply warming a solid that stays solid.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining a zigzag.** A single smoke particle is watched under a microscope in still air. Over ten seconds, it changes direction abruptly many times, tracing an irregular zigzag path, even though nothing visible is pushing it. Explain this observation using the particle model, and state what it is evidence for.
knowns: a visible smoke particle changes direction abruptly and often
no visible force is pushing it in any one direction
unknowns: why the direction changes so often and so abruptly
what the observation is evidence for
reasoning: The smoke particle is far larger than the air particles around it, so it is being struck constantly by huge numbers of invisible, fast-moving air particles from every direction.

At any instant, slightly more impacts may land on one side than the opposite side, giving the smoke particle a small random push in that direction; a moment later, a different side may receive more impacts.
Because the stronger side keeps changing at random, the smoke particle's path keeps changing direction at random too.
worked_examples.solution:
The zigzag happens because unevenly timed collisions from randomly moving, invisible air particles push the visible smoke particle first one way, then another.

It is evidence that air is made of particles that are themselves in constant, random motion, even though those particles cannot be seen directly.
worked_examples.interpretation: The explanation never requires the air particles to be seen: their existence and random motion are inferred from an effect they produce on something that can be seen.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the smoke particle itself as 'a molecule of air', which removes the very thing the observation is evidence for (the invisible particles doing the striking).

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two samples.** Sample X is a gas at $15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and sample Y is the same mass of the same gas at $45\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in separate identical sealed containers of the same volume. (a) State which sample has particles with the greater average random kinetic energy, and why. (b) State one thing about the particles' spacing or arrangement that is the same in both samples.
knowns: both in identical sealed containers of equal volume
unknowns: which sample has greater average kinetic energy
what stays the same between them
reasoning: Temperature is linked to the average random kinetic energy of the particles: a higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy.

Both samples are a gas in a container of the same volume, so the overall spacing between particles (set mainly by the fixed container volume and the fixed amount of gas) is unaffected by the temperature difference alone.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Sample Y, at $45\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, has the greater average random kinetic energy, because its higher temperature means its particles move with greater average random motion.

(b) Both samples are a gas filling the same fixed container volume, so their particles are, on average, equally far apart; only how fast they move differs, not how much space they occupy.
worked_examples.interpretation: This question separates 'how fast the particles move on average' (which depends on temperature) from 'how far apart they are' (which here depends on the fixed container volume, not the temperature).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the hotter gas must also be more spread out, when in fact both samples are confined to the same fixed volume.

guided_exercises.statement: A particle diagram shows particles spread far apart, each moving freely in a straight line until it collides with another or with the container wall. (a) Name the state of matter shown. (b) The same substance is then cooled until it becomes a liquid. Describe two changes to the particles that happen as a result.
hints: Check the spacing and the type of motion (free movement between collisions, or vibration, or sliding) against the three-state summary.
Cooling reduces average particle motion; think about what happens to the gaps between particles as the substance condenses into a liquid.
A liquid still allows particles to move past one another, unlike a solid.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) A gas, because the particles are widely spaced with free movement between collisions. (b) On cooling to a liquid, the particles move much closer together (their average spacing decreases greatly) and their average speed decreases, though they can still slide past one another rather than being fixed in place.
common_errors: Describing the liquid particles as 'stopping' rather than slowing down and becoming closer together, which would wrongly describe a solid instead.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Check the spacing and the type of motion (free movement between collisions, or vibration, or sliding) against the three-state summary.

**Step 2 — Method:** Cooling reduces average particle motion; think about what happens to the gaps between particles as the substance condenses into a liquid.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** (a) A gas, because the particles are widely spaced with free movement between collisions. (b) On cooling to a liquid, the particles move much closer together (their average spacing decreases greatly) and their average speed decreases, though they can still slide past one another rather than being fixed in place.

**Step 4 — Check:** A liquid still allows particles to move past one another, unlike a solid.

guided_exercises.statement: A pollen grain suspended in water is watched under a microscope and seen to move in a continuous, irregular zigzag. A student claims this shows that water molecules are visible under this microscope. Explain why the student's claim is incorrect, and give the correct explanation for the pollen grain's motion.
hints: Ask what object is actually being seen moving: is it the pollen grain, or something smaller?
Water molecules are far too small to see even with a microscope capable of resolving a pollen grain.
The motion needs a cause that acts on the pollen grain from outside it, repeatedly and unevenly.
guided_exercises.answer: The claim is incorrect because the object seen moving is the pollen grain itself, which is far larger than a water molecule and is clearly visible; the water molecules causing its motion remain invisible throughout. The pollen grain zigzags because it is struck, from random directions at random moments, by huge numbers of fast-moving, invisible water molecules, which give it small random pushes that keep changing direction.
common_errors: Concluding that because something is seen moving erratically in water, that something must itself be a water molecule.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Ask what object is actually being seen moving: is it the pollen grain, or something smaller?

**Step 2 — Method:** Water molecules are far too small to see even with a microscope capable of resolving a pollen grain.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The claim is incorrect because the object seen moving is the pollen grain itself, which is far larger than a water molecule and is clearly visible; the water molecules causing its motion remain invisible throughout. The pollen grain zigzags because it is struck, from random directions at random moments, by huge numbers of fast-moving, invisible water molecules, which give it small random pushes that keep changing direction.

**Step 4 — Check:** The motion needs a cause that acts on the pollen grain from outside it, repeatedly and unevenly.

exercises.statement: State, for a liquid, (a) how closely its particles are spaced compared with a gas of the same substance, and (b) whether its particles can move past one another or only vibrate about fixed positions.
exercises.answer: (a) A liquid's particles are much more closely spaced than the same substance's particles as a gas. (b) A liquid's particles can move past one another; they are not fixed in place as in a solid.
exercises.full_solution: Both answers follow directly from the three-state summary: close, irregular spacing with sliding motion is what distinguishes a liquid from both a solid (fixed positions) and a gas (widely spaced, free movement).

exercises.statement: A solid is heated and its temperature rises steadily, with no change of state. Explain, in terms of particles, why the solid keeps its shape throughout this heating even though its particles are gaining energy.
exercises.answer: The particles vibrate more vigorously as they gain energy, but they remain held in the same fixed, regular positions by the strong forces between them, so the overall shape of the solid is unchanged.
exercises.full_solution: Keeping its shape depends on the particles staying in fixed positions, which is unaffected by how vigorously they vibrate about those positions; only breaking free of the fixed positions (melting) would change the shape.

exercises.statement: Explain why a visible speck undergoing Brownian motion changes direction far more often than, say, a football rolling across a field and gradually slowing down.
exercises.answer: The speck is struck from random, constantly changing directions by huge numbers of invisible fluid particles, so the side receiving the larger push keeps changing moment to moment, giving a zigzag path. The football, by contrast, is slowed by a comparatively steady resistive force (friction and air resistance) acting in roughly one direction throughout, so its path curves smoothly rather than zigzagging.
exercises.full_solution: The key contrast is the number and randomness of the pushes: many random, unevenly timed impacts versus one broadly steady resistive force.

exercises.statement: A large metal tank of water at $30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and a small metal cup of water at $70\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are placed side by side. A student argues that the cup 'has more heat' because it has the higher temperature. Using the distinction between temperature and the energy stored in an object, explain whether the student is necessarily correct.
exercises.answer: The student is not necessarily correct. Temperature measures the average random kinetic energy of the particles, not the total energy stored. The large tank contains vastly more water (many more particles) than the small cup, so even though each of its particles has, on average, less kinetic energy than a particle in the cup, the enormous number of particles in the tank can mean it stores far more total thermal energy overall.
exercises.full_solution: Without knowing the mass of water in each container, the higher-temperature cup cannot be assumed to store more total energy; temperature and total stored energy are related but distinct quantities.

exam_questions.statement: The diagram for a substance in state P shows particles in a close, regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions; the diagram for the same substance in state Q shows particles in a close, irregular arrangement, able to slide past one another. (a) Name states P and Q. (b) Describe one change in particle behaviour, other than spacing, that happens when the substance changes from state P to state Q.
exam_questions.answer: (a) P is a solid and Q is a liquid. (b) In state P the particles only vibrate about fixed positions, whereas in state Q they are free to move past one another (no longer fixed to one position), while still remaining close together.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) P is a solid and Q is a liquid. (b) In state P the particles only vibrate about fixed positions, whereas in state Q they are free to move past one another (no longer fixed to one position), while still remaining close together.
mark_scheme: Identifies state P as a solid.
Identifies state Q as a liquid.
States that particles are fixed to vibrate in place in P.
States that particles can move past one another (are no longer fixed in position) in Q.
common_errors: Naming P and Q the right way round but then describing the change backwards, as if particles became more fixed on melting.

exam_questions.statement: A student observes smoke particles in air through a microscope and sees each particle moving in a continuous, irregular zigzag path. (a) Name this observation. (b) Explain, in terms of the particles involved, why the smoke particles move in this way. (c) State why the observation is evidence for the existence of air particles, even though those particles cannot be seen.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Brownian motion. (b) The smoke particles are much larger than the surrounding air particles, which are too small to see; the smoke particles are bombarded unevenly, from random directions at random moments, by huge numbers of these fast, invisible air particles, and each uneven bombardment gives a small random push that changes the smoke particle's direction. (c) Because the smoke particles' erratic motion has no other visible cause, their motion can only be explained by assuming something invisible is striking them randomly and constantly; this is indirect evidence that air is made of constantly, randomly moving particles.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Brownian motion. (b) The smoke particles are much larger than the surrounding air particles, which are too small to see; the smoke particles are bombarded unevenly, from random directions at random moments, by huge numbers of these fast, invisible air particles, and each uneven bombardment gives a small random push that changes the smoke particle's direction. (c) Because the smoke particles' erratic motion has no other visible cause, their motion can only be explained by assuming something invisible is striking them randomly and constantly; this is indirect evidence that air is made of constantly, randomly moving particles.
mark_scheme: Names the observation as Brownian motion.
States that the smoke particle is much larger than the air particles causing its motion.
Explains the zigzag as the result of random, unevenly timed collisions from many invisible particles.
States that the motion has no other visible cause.
Concludes this is evidence that air particles exist and move randomly, even though unseen.
common_errors: Naming the observation correctly but then describing the smoke particle as being one of the air particles in part (b).

challenge_questions.statement: A student watches smoke in air through a microscope and records the jittering of the specks. She then changes one thing at a time. (a) She finds a much larger smoke speck in the same sample: its jittering is noticeably smaller and slower. Explain why, using the particle model. (b) She gently cools the whole cell of smoky air. Predict what happens to the jittering and explain your prediction. (c) A classmate concludes from these observations that 'the air molecules must stop moving when the air is cold enough to stop the speck jittering'. Explain what is wrong with this conclusion.
hints: Each push on the speck comes from the imbalance between the impacts on one side and those on the other, and a bigger speck is hit by many more particles at once.
A bigger speck also has a much greater mass, so think about what the same size of push does to it.
Lowering the temperature changes the average random motion of the air particles. Does a smaller, slower jitter mean no motion at all?
challenge_questions.answer: (a) A larger speck is struck by many more air particles at any instant, so the imbalance between the impacts on one side and the other is a much smaller fraction of the total; on top of that, a larger speck has a much greater mass, so the same small net push produces a much smaller change in its motion. Both effects make its jittering smaller and slower. (b) Cooling the air lowers the average random motion of the air particles, so they strike the speck less often and less forcefully. The net pushes are smaller, so the jittering becomes slower and smaller in scale, but it does not stop. (c) The conclusion goes beyond the evidence. The jittering becoming too small to see does not mean the air particles have stopped: they are still moving randomly, just more slowly on average, and the speck is simply no longer being pushed hard enough for the movement to be visible under that microscope. Brownian motion shows that the invisible particles are moving; it cannot be used to show that they have stopped.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) A larger speck is struck by many more air particles at any instant, so the imbalance between the impacts on one side and the other is a much smaller fraction of the total; on top of that, a larger speck has a much greater mass, so the same small net push produces a much smaller change in its motion. Both effects make its jittering smaller and slower. (b) Cooling the air lowers the average random motion of the air particles, so they strike the speck less often and less forcefully. The net pushes are smaller, so the jittering becomes slower and smaller in scale, but it does not stop. (c) The conclusion goes beyond the evidence. The jittering becoming too small to see does not mean the air particles have stopped: they are still moving randomly, just more slowly on average, and the speck is simply no longer being pushed hard enough for the movement to be visible under that microscope. Brownian motion shows that the invisible particles are moving; it cannot be used to show that they have stopped.
common_errors: Saying the large speck jitters less because the air particles cannot reach it, rather than because the impacts on it are more evenly balanced and it is heavier.
Claiming that cooling stops the jittering completely, when it only makes it slower and smaller.
Treating the visible speck as one air particle, so that cooling is thought to slow 'the particle' down directly rather than slowing the invisible particles that push it.

mcq.stem: Pollen grains suspended in water are watched under a microscope and seen to jitter and change direction constantly. What is the best explanation for this motion?

options.text: The pollen grains are themselves water molecules moving randomly.
options.why_wrong: confuses the large, visible pollen grain with the much smaller, invisible water molecules that actually strike it.

options.text: The pollen grains are pulled by a weak current that changes direction every few seconds.
options.why_wrong: invents an external current with no evidence, when the random collisions explanation already accounts for the motion.

options.text: The pollen grains repel each other and bounce apart.
options.why_wrong: describes an interaction between pollen grains, not the cause of a single grain's own erratic path.

options.text: The pollen grains are struck unevenly, from random directions, by huge numbers of invisible, fast-moving water molecules.

mcq.explanation: This is the standard particle-model explanation of Brownian motion: an unevenly, randomly bombarded large particle is pushed first one way, then another, by invisible fluid particles.

mcq.stem: A solid is cooled, but it does not change state. What happens to its particles?

options.text: They vibrate less vigorously about the same fixed positions.
They stop vibrating completely.
options.why_wrong: goes too far: particles never become perfectly still, even when strongly cooled, as long as the substance remains above absolute zero.

options.text: They move further apart from their fixed positions.
options.why_wrong: describes melting or expansion, not simply cooling a solid that stays solid.

options.text: They change from vibrating to sliding past one another.
options.why_wrong: describes becoming a liquid, which has not happened here.

mcq.explanation: Cooling reduces the average random kinetic energy of the particles, so a solid's particles vibrate less vigorously about the same fixed positions, without changing state.

mcq.stem: Which row correctly matches a state of matter to its particle spacing and motion?

options.text: Gas — close together, vibrating only.
options.why_wrong: swaps gas with solid: close spacing and vibration-only motion describes a solid, not a gas.

options.text: Solid — close together, regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
Liquid — widely spaced, moving freely between occasional collisions.
options.why_wrong: swaps liquid with gas: wide spacing and free movement describes a gas, not a liquid.

options.text: Solid — close together, irregular arrangement, sliding past each other.
options.why_wrong: swaps solid with liquid: an irregular arrangement with sliding motion describes a liquid, not a solid.

mcq.explanation: Only option D matches state to spacing, arrangement and motion correctly: a solid has close, regular, vibration-only particles.

mcq.stem: Object X has a higher temperature than object Y. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Object X stores more total thermal energy than object Y.
options.why_wrong: confuses temperature with total stored energy; a small object at a high temperature can store less total energy than a large object at a lower temperature.

options.text: Object X and object Y must be made of the same substance.
options.why_wrong: is not required at all; temperature can be compared between any two objects, whatever they are made of.

options.text: The particles in X have, on average, greater random kinetic energy than the particles in Y.
The particles in X are, on average, more closely spaced than the particles in Y.
options.why_wrong: confuses temperature (linked to average particle motion) with spacing, which depends on the state of matter and the amount of substance, not on temperature alone.

mcq.explanation: Temperature is, by definition in this model, linked directly to the average random kinetic energy of the particles; it does not by itself determine total stored energy, spacing, or what substance is involved.

flashcards.front: What three things should you check to identify a state of matter from a particle diagram?
flashcards.back: Spacing (close or widely spread), arrangement (regular or irregular) and motion (vibration only, sliding, or free movement between collisions).

flashcards.front: What is Brownian motion?
flashcards.back: The continuous, irregular zigzag movement of a visible particle (such as a smoke particle or pollen grain) suspended in a fluid, caused by random, uneven collisions with the fluid's invisible particles.

flashcards.front: True or false: the specks you see jittering in a Brownian motion demonstration are individual molecules of the fluid.
flashcards.back: False. The specks are much larger visible objects (e.g. smoke particles or pollen grains); the fluid's own particles are too small to see and are what strike the specks.

flashcards.front: How does temperature differ from the total thermal energy stored in an object?
flashcards.back: Temperature is linked to the average random kinetic energy of the particles; total stored thermal energy also depends on how much substance is present, so a large object at a lower temperature can store more total energy than a small object at a higher temperature.

flashcards.front: Why does raising the temperature of a solid that stays solid not change its shape?
flashcards.back: The particles vibrate more vigorously, but they remain held in the same fixed, regular positions by the forces between them, so the overall shape is unaffected.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The specks you see moving and jittering under a microscope in a smoke cell or in pollen-in-water are individual molecules of the air or water.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The specks are the only thing actually visible through the microscope, so it is natural to assume that what you see must be the particles the lesson is talking about.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes the moving speck itself as 'a molecule' or 'a particle of the gas/liquid', rather than as a much larger object suspended in a fluid of invisible particles.
misconceptions.correct_model: The visible speck (a smoke particle or a grain of pollen) is far larger than the surrounding gas or liquid particles, which are themselves too small to see even with this microscope. The speck moves because it is struck, from random directions and at random moments, by huge numbers of these fast but invisible particles.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the two scales side by side: a few dozen tiny arrows (invisible fluid particles) hitting one much larger dot (the visible speck) from different directions at different times, and ask what happens to the speck's path as a result.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Particles in a solid do not move at all; only liquid and gas particles move.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A solid looks completely still from the outside, so it is tempting to assume nothing is happening at the particle level either.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws solid particles with no motion arrows, or says 'solid particles are frozen in place'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they do not travel through the material, but they are never perfectly still. Raising the temperature increases how vigorously they vibrate, without yet letting them escape their positions.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two solid diagrams at different temperatures with the particles in the same fixed positions but drawn with longer or shorter vibration arrows, and ask what stays fixed and what changes.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Temperature measures the total amount of thermal energy stored in an object.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both temperature and thermal energy increase together when something is heated, so it is easy to treat them as the same quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says a large, lukewarm object must have 'less heat' than a small, hot object without comparing their total energy, or claims two objects at the same temperature must store the same total energy.
misconceptions.correct_model: Temperature is a measure of the average random kinetic energy of the particles in an object, not the total energy stored. A large block of water at 40 °C contains far more total thermal energy than a small cup of water at 90 °C, even though the cup has the higher temperature.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a swimming pool at 25 °C with a kettle of water at 90 °C, and ask which one could melt more ice before cooling to 0 °C: the pool, despite its lower temperature, can transfer far more energy because it contains so much more water.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing the visible speck in a Brownian motion demonstration as a single molecule of the surrounding fluid.
common_mistakes.why: The speck is the only thing actually visible, so it is easy to assume it must be the particle the lesson is describing.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name two separate things: the large, visible speck, and the much smaller, invisible fluid particles that strike it; never merge them into one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a higher temperature as automatically meaning more total energy stored.
common_mistakes.why: Temperature and total thermal energy both increase together on heating a single object, so they feel like the same quantity.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask how much substance is present as well as what the temperature is, before comparing two different objects' total stored energy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming solid particles are completely still.
common_mistakes.why: A solid object looks motionless from the outside.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that every particle in every state is always moving at the particle level; a solid's particles vibrate about fixed positions rather than being still.

exam_notes: Always name the three things a particle diagram must show to identify a state: spacing, arrangement and type of motion, not spacing alone.
When asked to explain Brownian motion, name both objects involved (the visible speck and the invisible fluid particles striking it) and describe the collisions as random and uneven.
Keep temperature (average particle kinetic energy) and total thermal energy (which also depends on the amount of substance) clearly separate in any answer that compares two different objects.

summary.big_idea: One particle model explains solids, liquids and gases through spacing, arrangement and motion, and temperature is the measurable stand-in for the invisible average motion of those particles.
key_points: Solids: close, regular spacing, vibration about fixed positions only.
Liquids: close, irregular spacing, particles slide past one another.
Gases: widely spaced particles, moving freely between collisions.
A higher temperature means greater average random particle motion, not necessarily more total stored energy.
Brownian motion is evidence for invisible, randomly moving fluid particles, seen indirectly through their effect on a much larger visible speck.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Every state of matter is explained by the same particles arranged, spaced and moving differently; temperature tracks their average motion, and Brownian motion is the visible fingerprint of their invisible randomness.

epistemic_overrides.note: Simplified/ideal model used for GCSE level

02_Gas_pressure_and_thermal_expansion.js.title: Gas pressure and thermal expansion
02_Gas_pressure_and_thermal_expansion.js.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe qualitatively, in terms of particles, the effect on the pressure of a fixed mass of gas of a change of temperature at constant volume and of a change of volume at constant temperature (Core); and, as Supplement, describe the pressure of a gas in terms of the forces exerted by particles colliding with surfaces, creating a force per unit area.
Describe the thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases at constant pressure, and apply this to explain everyday design features such as expansion gaps and thermometers.

prerequisites.statement: Describe the arrangement, spacing and motion of particles in a gas, and state that a higher temperature means greater average random particle motion.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Gas pressure and expansion are both explained by what gas and solid particles are doing on average; without the previous lesson's particle model, 'pressure' and 'expansion' would just be memorised words.

diagnostic_items.question: Two sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 10 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. (a) In which flask do the gas particles have the greater average speed? (b) Describe how the particles of a gas are arranged inside a flask and how they move.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: (a) Flask Y, because a higher temperature means greater average random motion of the particles. (b) The particles are far apart with no regular arrangement, and they move quickly in random directions, travelling in straight lines between collisions with each other and with the walls of the flask.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Flask X, because a cold gas is squashed up more, so its particles bump into each other more often.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is reading average speed off the spacing of the particles instead of off the temperature.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Both the same, because it is the same gas in both flasks.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats average particle speed as a fixed property of the substance, so temperature is not yet connected to particle motion at all.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles in flask Y are bigger, because the gas has been heated.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is confusing an increase in particle motion and spacing with an increase in the size of the particles themselves.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the two ideas from lesson 1 that this lesson is built on: that gas particles are far apart and move randomly at speed, and that a higher temperature means a greater average random speed. Without both, 'pressure' and 'expansion' can only be memorised.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Go back to the particle diagram and the temperature block of lesson 1, and practise saying in one sentence what changes about the particles when a substance is made hotter, before explaining anything about pressure.

theory_blocks.title: Two fixed conditions, two different outcomes
theory_blocks.body:
Predicting what happens to a fixed mass of gas on heating depends on which quantity is held fixed.

**Fixed volume (a rigid, sealed container):** heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster. Faster particles hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure increases, while the volume cannot change.

**Fixed temperature, decreasing volume (compressing a gas):** squeezing the same number of particles into a smaller space means each particle has less distance to travel before hitting a wall, so collisions with the walls happen more often in a given time, even though each particle's average speed has not changed. More frequent collisions mean higher pressure.

In both cases the underlying reasoning is the same — more frequent and/or harder collisions raise the pressure — but the cause is different: a speed increase in the first case, a frequency increase from reduced space in the second.

theory_blocks.title: Expansion is particles spreading apart, not growing
theory_blocks.body:
When a solid, liquid or gas is heated at constant pressure, it generally expands: its overall size or volume increases.

This happens because the particles vibrate (in a solid) or move (in a liquid or gas) more vigorously as the temperature rises, and on average settle slightly further apart from their neighbours.

The particles themselves do not change size at all; only the average spacing between them increases.

Gases typically expand far more than liquids for the same temperature rise, and liquids typically expand more than solids, because gas particles have almost no attractive forces between them,

so extra motion translates almost entirely into extra spacing, while a solid's strong, rigid bonds resist the particles moving much further apart.

assets.caption: Top: a rigid sealed vessel cannot change volume, so heating the same five particles makes them move faster (blue arrows) and hit the walls harder and more often; the red arrows inside the vessel are the outward force the gas exerts on each wall, which is what the higher pressure means. Bottom: in a cylinder with a free piston the pressure stays the same, so heating pushes the piston outward instead (red arrow); the green dashed line marks where the piston was when cold.
assets.purpose: Contrast the two fixed-condition cases (fixed volume vs fixed pressure) in one figure, so a learner can see directly why the same heating produces a pressure rise in one case and a volume rise in the other.

theory_blocks.title: Expansion in everyday design
theory_blocks.body:
Because solids expand (though only slightly) on heating, objects that are rigidly fixed at both ends can buckle or crack if no allowance is made for their expansion.

Railway tracks and road bridges are built with small expansion gaps so that the metal or concrete can lengthen on a hot day without pushing against the next section.

A **bimetallic strip**, made of two different metals bonded together, bends when heated because the two metals expand by different amounts for the same temperature rise;

this bending is used in some thermostats and fire alarms to make or break an electrical contact automatically.

A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because a liquid (commonly mercury or coloured alcohol) expands far more than the glass tube around it for the same temperature rise,

so a small temperature change produces a visible, measurable rise up a narrow tube.

theory_blocks.title: Pressure is the result of countless tiny impacts
theory_blocks.body:
Gas particles move freely in straight lines until they collide with something, including the walls of whatever container holds them. Each individual collision gives the wall a tiny push, far too small to notice on its own.

But a gas contains an enormous number of particles, all colliding with the walls many times every second, and it is the combined effect of all these countless tiny pushes,

spread over the whole wall area, that is felt as a steady, continuous force: [[blue:**gas pressure**]].

Anything that increases how hard, or how often, particles strike the walls increases the pressure; anything that reduces either of those reduces it.

This single idea is enough to predict what happens to pressure when either the temperature or the volume of a fixed mass of gas is changed.

keywords.definition: The force per unit area exerted on a surface by the combined collisions of gas particles with it.
A sample of gas where no particles are added or removed, so changes in pressure, volume or temperature can be compared fairly.
The increase in size of a solid, liquid or gas caused by increased average particle spacing on heating, at constant pressure.
A strip made of two different metals bonded together that bends when heated, because the two metals expand by different amounts.
A deliberate small gap left in a structure to allow for thermal expansion without the structure pushing against itself.

worked_examples.statement: **A sealed can.** A rigid, sealed metal can containing air is placed in warm sunlight and its temperature rises. The can does not change shape or size. State what happens to the pressure of the air inside, and explain why.
knowns: the can is rigid and sealed (fixed volume)
reasoning: The can's volume is fixed, so the air particles cannot spread into a larger space.
Higher temperature means the air particles move faster on average, so they hit the can's walls harder and more often.
worked_examples.solution: The pressure of the air inside increases, because the faster-moving particles collide with the walls more forcefully and more frequently, while the volume stays the same.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the fixed-volume case: with nowhere to expand into, extra particle speed can only show up as extra pressure.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the can will expand or that the air's volume increases, when the can is explicitly described as rigid.

worked_examples.statement: **Compressing a syringe.** A sealed syringe contains air at room temperature. The plunger is pushed in, reducing the volume of air trapped inside to about half its original value, while the temperature stays the same. Explain what happens to the pressure of the trapped air.
knowns: volume is reduced to about half
reasoning: At constant temperature, the particles' average speed does not change.

Squeezing the same number of particles into about half the space means each particle has, on average, a shorter distance to travel before hitting a wall, so it collides with a wall more often in a given time.
More frequent collisions, at the same average force per collision, increase the total pressure.
worked_examples.solution: The pressure of the trapped air increases, because the same number of particles now collide with the (smaller) walls more frequently, even though their average speed has not changed.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the fixed-temperature case: the increase in pressure here comes entirely from more frequent collisions due to less space, not from faster particles.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the pressure increase by saying the particles 'speed up' when the volume is reduced, when in fact the temperature (and so the average speed) has not changed.

worked_examples.statement: **Two containers, two outcomes.** Container P is a flexible balloon; container R is a rigid, sealed metal box. Equal amounts of the same gas, at the same starting temperature, are warmed by the same amount in each container. Explain why the two containers respond differently, even though the gas and the temperature rise are identical.
knowns: same gas, same temperature rise in both
reasoning: In both containers, the gas particles gain the same extra average kinetic energy from the same temperature rise.

Container P can change shape, so it allows its volume to increase instead of building up pressure; its flexible skin can stretch to balance the particles' extra push, keeping the pressure roughly constant.
Container R cannot change shape, so the particles' extra push cannot be absorbed by a volume increase; it shows up entirely as a pressure increase instead.
worked_examples.solution:
Container P (the balloon) expands, roughly keeping its internal pressure constant, while container R (the rigid box) keeps the same volume but experiences a pressure increase.

The difference comes entirely from what each container allows to change, not from any difference in the gas or the heating.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same physical cause (faster particles after heating) can show up as a volume change or a pressure change, depending only on which quantity the container's design allows to change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the rigid box must also expand slightly 'because it got hotter too', confusing thermal expansion of the solid box itself (a separate, much smaller effect) with the much larger effect on the gas pressure inside it.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing a material for a bridge joint.** A road bridge is built from a long steel span. Engineers leave a narrow gap, filled with a flexible joint, between the end of the span and the concrete support. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why this gap is necessary. (b) Suggest what might happen to the bridge on a very hot day if no such gap had been left.
knowns: the bridge span is a solid metal (steel)
a narrow gap with a flexible joint is left at the end
unknowns: what would happen without it on a hot day
reasoning: On a hot day the steel's temperature rises, so its particles vibrate more vigorously and settle slightly further apart on average, making the whole span slightly longer.
If the span has nowhere to lengthen into, the expanding steel would push hard against the fixed concrete support instead.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) The gap is necessary because the steel span expands (becomes slightly longer) on a hot day as its particles' average spacing increases;

without somewhere for this extra length to go, the span would be forced against the support. (b) Without the gap, the expanding span could push against the support with very large force, which could crack the concrete or buckle the steel span itself.
worked_examples.interpretation: This connects the particle-level explanation of expansion directly to a real design decision: the gap exists specifically to absorb the small length increase caused by thermal expansion.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the expansion as the steel 'getting softer' in the heat, rather than as its particles settling slightly further apart while the steel itself remains solid.

guided_exercises.statement: A rigid gas cylinder is cooled from room temperature to a much lower temperature, without changing its volume. State and explain what happens to the pressure of the gas inside.
hints: Cooling reduces the average particle speed; think about what that does to the force and frequency of wall collisions.
The cylinder is rigid, so volume cannot change to absorb the effect.
State the direction of the pressure change clearly, not just that 'something changes'.
guided_exercises.answer: The pressure decreases, because the cooled gas particles move more slowly on average, so they strike the rigid walls less forcefully and less often, while the volume stays fixed.
common_errors: Saying the gas 'shrinks' or its volume decreases, when the cylinder is explicitly rigid and cannot change volume.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Cooling reduces the average particle speed; think about what that does to the force and frequency of wall collisions.

**Step 2 — Method:** The cylinder is rigid, so volume cannot change to absorb the effect.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The pressure decreases, because the cooled gas particles move more slowly on average, so they strike the rigid walls less forcefully and less often, while the volume stays fixed.

**Step 4 — Check:** State the direction of the pressure change clearly, not just that 'something changes'.

guided_exercises.statement: A glass bottle is filled completely with water and sealed tightly with no air gap, then placed in a freezer. Water expands slightly as it freezes. Predict what is likely to happen to the bottle, and explain your prediction using the idea of expansion needing somewhere to go.
hints: The bottle is rigid and has no air gap to absorb any change in volume.
Freezing water expands rather than contracts, unlike most other substances.
Think about what happens when something trying to expand has nowhere to expand into.
guided_exercises.answer: The bottle is likely to crack or shatter, because the water expands slightly as it turns to ice, but the rigid, completely full, sealed bottle leaves no space for that expansion to happen into, so the expanding ice pushes outward on the glass with large force.
common_errors: Assuming water behaves like most substances and contracts on freezing, so predicting nothing happens to the bottle.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** The bottle is rigid and has no air gap to absorb any change in volume.

**Step 2 — Method:** Freezing water expands rather than contracts, unlike most other substances.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The bottle is likely to crack or shatter, because the water expands slightly as it turns to ice, but the rigid, completely full, sealed bottle leaves no space for that expansion to happen into, so the expanding ice pushes outward on the glass with large force.

**Step 4 — Check:** Think about what happens when something trying to expand has nowhere to expand into.

exercises.statement: A fixed mass of gas is held at constant volume while its temperature is increased. State what happens to (a) the average speed of its particles and (b) the pressure it exerts on its container.
exercises.answer: (a) The average speed of the particles increases. (b) The pressure increases.
exercises.full_solution: Both follow from the same cause: a higher temperature means greater average particle kinetic energy (and so greater average speed), which produces harder and more frequent collisions with the fixed container walls, raising the pressure.

exercises.statement: A student says, 'When you pump up a bicycle tyre, you are squeezing the air molecules into a smaller size.' Explain what is wrong with this statement and give the correct description of what happens to the air molecules.
exercises.answer: The statement is incorrect: pumping air into a tyre does not change the size of any individual air molecule. It increases the number of molecules (and, once the tyre is nearly full, reduces the average spacing between them), which increases how often molecules collide with the tyre's inner wall, raising the pressure.
exercises.full_solution: The key correction is that 'squeezing' changes spacing and collision frequency, never the size of the molecules themselves.

exercises.statement: A metal lid on a glass jar is often easier to remove after running hot water over the lid for a few seconds. Suggest, in terms of particle spacing, why this works.
exercises.answer: The metal lid is heated more quickly than the glass jar beneath it and expands slightly, with its particles settling a little further apart on average, which slightly increases the internal diameter of the lid. This small expansion can be enough to loosen a lid that was gripping the jar tightly.
exercises.full_solution: The explanation relies on the metal lid expanding more, and more quickly, than the glass, since the two materials are heated under the same running water but respond differently.

exercises.statement: An aerosol can carries a warning not to store it near a flame or in direct hot sunlight, even though the can is not being used. Using what you know about gas pressure in a fixed volume, explain why this warning makes sense, and suggest what could happen if it is ignored.
exercises.answer: An aerosol can is a rigid, sealed container holding gas (and often liquid propellant) at a fixed volume. Heating it raises the temperature of the gas inside, increasing the average particle speed and so the pressure, while the can's volume cannot change to relieve that pressure. If the pressure rises enough, it could exceed what the can is designed to withstand, causing the can to burst or explode.
exercises.full_solution: An aerosol can is a rigid, sealed container holding gas (and often liquid propellant) at a fixed volume. Heating it raises the temperature of the gas inside, increasing the average particle speed and so the pressure, while the can's volume cannot change to relieve that pressure. If the pressure rises enough, it could exceed what the can is designed to withstand, causing the can to burst or explode.

exam_questions.statement: A rigid cylinder of fixed volume contains a fixed mass of gas. The gas is heated from $15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $55\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. (a) State what happens to the pressure of the gas. (b) Explain your answer in terms of the motion of the gas particles and their collisions with the cylinder wall.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The pressure increases. (b) Heating increases the average kinetic energy, and so the average speed, of the gas particles. Faster particles collide with the fixed cylinder wall more forcefully and more frequently, and since the volume cannot change, this increased force and frequency of collision is felt as an increase in pressure.
exam_questions.full_solution: The explanation must link temperature to particle speed, and particle speed to the force and frequency of wall collisions, to earn full marks.
mark_scheme: States that the pressure increases.
States that the average particle speed (or kinetic energy) increases with temperature.
States that faster particles collide with the wall more forcefully.
States that faster particles collide with the wall more frequently, and links this to the pressure increase.
common_errors: Stating correctly that pressure increases but giving no particle-level reasoning, which loses most of the marks even with the right final answer.

exam_questions.statement: A bimetallic strip is made from a strip of brass bonded tightly to a strip of iron. When heated, brass expands more than iron for the same temperature rise. (a) Predict, with a reason, which way the strip bends when heated: towards the brass side or towards the iron side. (b) Describe, in terms of particle spacing, why brass and iron can expand by different amounts for the same temperature rise. (c) Suggest one practical use for a bimetallic strip.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The strip bends towards the iron side, because the brass on the outer edge of the curve has expanded (and so lengthened) more than the iron on the inner edge, which forces the strip to curve with the shorter iron side on the inside of the bend. (b) Different materials have different strengths of bonding and different arrangements of particles, so the same temperature rise produces a different increase in average particle spacing in each material; brass's particles spread apart more than iron's for the same temperature rise. (c) A practical use is in a thermostat, where the bending strip makes or breaks an electrical contact as the temperature changes, switching a heater or an alarm on or off.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The strip bends towards the iron side, because the brass on the outer edge of the curve has expanded (and so lengthened) more than the iron on the inner edge, which forces the strip to curve with the shorter iron side on the inside of the bend. (b) Different materials have different strengths of bonding and different arrangements of particles, so the same temperature rise produces a different increase in average particle spacing in each material; brass's particles spread apart more than iron's for the same temperature rise. (c) A practical use is in a thermostat, where the bending strip makes or breaks an electrical contact as the temperature changes, switching a heater or an alarm on or off.
mark_scheme: States the strip bends towards the iron (the less-expanding metal).
Gives the correct reason: brass lengthens more, forcing the strip to curve with iron on the inside.
States that different materials' particles spread apart by different amounts for the same temperature rise.
Gives a scientifically sound reason this can differ between materials (e.g. different bonding/forces between particles).
Names a valid practical use, such as a thermostat or fire alarm.
common_errors: Bending the strip the wrong way by forgetting that the material which expands more ends up on the outside, not the inside, of the curve.

challenge_questions.statement: A liquid-in-glass thermometer is taken from a cool room and lowered into a beaker of hot water. A student watching the stem closely sees the liquid level dip very slightly for a moment before climbing steadily to its final reading. (a) Explain, in terms of thermal expansion, both the brief dip and the rise that follows. (b) Thermometer A and thermometer B have identical bulbs holding the same liquid, but the bore (the narrow tube) of A has half the diameter of the bore of B. Decide which thermometer's liquid moves further along the stem for the same temperature rise, and explain by how much.
hints: The glass bulb and the liquid sealed inside it do not reach the hot water's temperature at the same moment. Which one is touching the hot water?
For the same temperature rise, liquids expand considerably more than solids such as glass. Which effect wins once both have warmed up?

In part (b) the extra volume of liquid pushed into the stem is the same for both thermometers. Length of liquid column = volume ÷ cross-sectional area, and for a circular bore $A=\dfrac{\pi d^{2}}{4}$.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The glass bulb is in direct contact with the hot water, so the glass warms first and expands, which makes the inside of the bulb slightly bigger. The liquid has not warmed yet, so the same volume of liquid now sits in a slightly larger bulb and the level in the stem falls a little. A moment later the liquid itself warms up, and because a liquid expands much more than glass for the same temperature rise, the liquid's expansion overtakes the bulb's and pushes the liquid up the stem to its final reading. (b) Thermometer A's liquid moves further. The same temperature rise pushes the same extra volume of liquid into the stem in both thermometers, and the length of that column is the extra volume divided by the cross-sectional area of the bore. Since $A=\dfrac{\pi d^{2}}{4}$, halving the diameter divides the area by $4$, so the same extra volume gives a column $4$ times longer. Thermometer A is therefore four times as sensitive as thermometer B.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The glass bulb is in direct contact with the hot water, so the glass warms first and expands, which makes the inside of the bulb slightly bigger. The liquid has not warmed yet, so the same volume of liquid now sits in a slightly larger bulb and the level in the stem falls a little. A moment later the liquid itself warms up, and because a liquid expands much more than glass for the same temperature rise, the liquid's expansion overtakes the bulb's and pushes the liquid up the stem to its final reading. (b) Thermometer A's liquid moves further. The same temperature rise pushes the same extra volume of liquid into the stem in both thermometers, and the length of that column is the extra volume divided by the cross-sectional area of the bore. Since $A=\dfrac{\pi d^{2}}{4}$, halving the diameter divides the area by $4$, so the same extra volume gives a column $4$ times longer. Thermometer A is therefore four times as sensitive as thermometer B.
common_errors: Explaining the dip by saying the liquid contracts, when nothing has cooled the liquid; it is the bulb around it that has got bigger.
Arguing that the narrower tube holds less liquid and is therefore less sensitive, instead of seeing that the same extra volume spread over a smaller cross-section gives a longer column.
Halving the diameter and assuming the column is only twice as long, forgetting that area depends on the square of the diameter.

mcq.stem: A rigid, sealed metal cylinder containing air is left in a hot car on a sunny day. What happens inside the cylinder?

options.text: The volume of the trapped air increases, because heat makes gases expand.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the cylinder is explicitly rigid and sealed, so its volume cannot change regardless of temperature.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the cylinder is sealed.
options.why_wrong: confuses being sealed (no gas can enter or leave) with being unaffected by temperature, which is not the same thing.

options.text: The pressure decreases, because warm air is lighter than cold air.
options.why_wrong: applies a convection idea about density to a sealed, rigid container where no bulk movement of gas in or out is possible.

options.text: The pressure of the trapped air increases, because the faster-moving particles collide with the fixed walls more forcefully and more often.

mcq.explanation: With the volume fixed, heating can only increase the pressure, as faster particles strike the walls harder and more often.

mcq.stem: A metal rod gets very slightly longer when heated. What is the correct particle-level explanation?

options.text: The particles vibrate more vigorously and settle, on average, slightly further apart from their neighbours.
Each metal particle expands to a larger size.
options.why_wrong: describes particles themselves growing, which does not happen; only their average spacing changes.

options.text: New particles are created inside the rod as it heats up.
options.why_wrong: invents particles appearing from nowhere, which has no basis in the particle model.

options.text: The particles move from the cooler end of the rod to the hotter end.
options.why_wrong: describes a bulk flow of particles along the rod, which is not what causes thermal expansion of a solid.

mcq.explanation: Thermal expansion comes from more vigorous vibration increasing the average spacing between particles, not from the particles themselves changing size or number.

mcq.stem: A sealed syringe of gas is compressed to half its original volume at constant temperature. What happens to the size of the individual gas molecules, and what happens to the pressure?

options.text: The molecules get smaller and the pressure increases.
options.why_wrong: wrongly shrinks the molecules themselves; only their spacing changes, not their size.

options.text: The molecules stay the same size and the pressure increases.
The molecules stay the same size and the pressure stays the same.
options.why_wrong: ignores that squeezing the same number of molecules into less space must increase how often they strike the walls, which raises the pressure.

options.text: The molecules get smaller and the pressure stays the same.
options.why_wrong: wrongly shrinks the molecules and also misses the pressure increase caused by more frequent wall collisions.

mcq.explanation: Compression changes the spacing between molecules, not their size; squeezing the same molecules into less space makes them collide with the walls more often, raising the pressure.

mcq.stem: Why do engineers leave small expansion gaps in long concrete road sections?

options.text: To let rainwater drain away between sections.
options.why_wrong: describes a drainage function, not the thermal-expansion reason the gaps are specifically designed for.

options.text: Because concrete shrinks when heated, so a gap stops sections overlapping.
options.why_wrong: gets the direction of the effect backwards; concrete, like most solids, expands rather than shrinks on heating.

options.text: To allow the concrete to lengthen slightly on hot days without pushing against the next section and cracking.
To reduce the total amount of concrete needed and save cost.
options.why_wrong: proposes a cost-saving motive, not the structural reason tied to thermal expansion that the lesson covers.

mcq.explanation: Concrete, like other solids, expands slightly on heating; the gap gives this expansion somewhere to go, preventing the sections from being forced against each other.

flashcards.front: What causes gas pressure, at the particle level?
flashcards.back: The combined effect of enormous numbers of gas particles colliding with the walls of their container every second; each tiny impact adds to a steady overall force on the walls.

flashcards.front: Heating a fixed mass of gas can raise its pressure or its volume. What decides which one happens?
flashcards.back: Whether the container can change shape. A rigid, sealed container keeps the volume fixed, so heating raises the pressure instead; a container that can expand (like a balloon or a free piston) keeps the pressure roughly constant and the volume rises instead.

flashcards.front: True or false: when a solid expands on heating, its individual particles grow larger.
flashcards.back: False. The particles stay the same size; they vibrate more and, on average, settle slightly further apart from their neighbours.

flashcards.front: Why does a bimetallic strip bend when heated?
flashcards.back: It is made of two different metals bonded together that expand by different amounts for the same temperature rise, so the strip curves towards the metal that expanded less.

flashcards.front: At constant temperature, what happens to a gas's pressure if its volume is reduced?
flashcards.back: The pressure increases, because the same number of particles collide with the (smaller) container walls more frequently.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Heating a gas always increases its volume, even inside a sealed, rigid container.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Most everyday examples of heating (a balloon, an oven, a warm room) involve something visibly growing or expanding, so 'heating = growing' feels like a safe general rule.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a rigid, sealed gas container will expand or burst from volume increase rather than pressure increase when heated.
misconceptions.correct_model: What happens when a gas is heated depends on what is held fixed. In a rigid, sealed container, the volume cannot change, so heating increases the pressure instead; only a container that can change shape (like a balloon, or a cylinder with a free piston) can expand at roughly constant pressure.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a sealed rigid bottle and a flexible balloon, both warmed gently, side by side, and ask what is free to change in each case before predicting the outcome.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a solid or liquid expands on heating, its individual particles get bigger.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The material visibly takes up more space, so it is tempting to imagine each particle swelling to fill that extra space.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes expansion as particles 'growing' or 'swelling' rather than as particles moving slightly further apart on average.
misconceptions.correct_model: The particles themselves do not change size. On heating, particles vibrate more vigorously and, on average, settle slightly further apart from their neighbours; it is this small increase in average spacing, repeated over billions of particles, that makes the whole material expand.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw a small block of a regular particle grid before and after heating with the same dot size but slightly larger gaps, and ask what has changed: the particles or the spacing between them.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Compressing a gas into a smaller volume squeezes each individual gas molecule into a smaller size.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The gas as a whole visibly takes up less room, so it seems natural to assume each molecule is also being squeezed smaller.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes compression as molecules 'getting smaller' or 'being squashed' rather than as the same-sized molecules being pushed closer together.
misconceptions.correct_model: Compressing a gas reduces the average spacing between molecules and increases how often they collide with the container walls and with each other; it does not change the size of any individual molecule, which stays the same throughout.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly: does squeezing a bag of marbles into a smaller box change the size of any marble? Then map 'marble' onto 'gas molecule' and 'box' onto 'container'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming heating a gas always makes its volume increase.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday examples (balloons, ovens) usually show visible growth, making 'heat = expand' feel universal.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always check first whether the container is rigid (fixed volume, so pressure changes) or free to change shape (fixed pressure, so volume changes).

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing thermal expansion as particles growing bigger.
common_mistakes.why: The whole object visibly takes up more space, so it is tempting to picture each particle doing the same.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Say explicitly that the particles' size never changes; only the average spacing between them increases.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining a pressure increase from compression as the particles moving faster.
common_mistakes.why: Both heating and compressing a gas can raise its pressure, so the two causes are easy to mix up.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the temperature has actually changed: if it has not, the pressure increase must come from more frequent collisions due to less space, not from faster particles.

exam_notes: Before predicting what happens to a gas on heating, state clearly which quantity is held fixed: volume (pressure changes) or pressure (volume changes).
A full explanation of a pressure change must mention both particle speed (or spacing) and the resulting change in force and/or frequency of wall collisions, not just the final pressure change alone.
Thermal expansion answers should refer to a change in average particle spacing, never to particles themselves changing size.

summary.big_idea: Gas pressure comes from particle collisions with container walls, and whether heating a gas raises its pressure or its volume depends entirely on which one the container allows to change; solids, liquids and gases all expand on heating because their particles spread slightly further apart, never because the particles themselves grow.
key_points: Gas pressure is the combined effect of countless particle collisions with the container walls.
At fixed volume, heating raises pressure because particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.
At fixed temperature, reducing volume raises pressure because particles hit the (smaller) walls more often, not because they move faster.
Thermal expansion is particles settling further apart on average, not particles growing in size.
Expansion gaps, bimetallic strips and liquid-in-glass thermometers are everyday applications of thermal expansion.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Decide what is held fixed (volume or pressure) before predicting the effect of heating a gas, and remember expansion always means particles spreading apart, never particles getting bigger.

03_Melting_boiling_and_evaporation.json.title: Melting, boiling and evaporation
03_Melting_boiling_and_evaporation.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Recall that, at standard atmospheric pressure, water melts at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; describe melting, boiling, condensation and solidification (freezing) in terms of particles; explain why the temperature stays constant during a change of state, because the energy supplied or given out changes the particle arrangement instead; and describe evaporation as the escape of the more energetic particles from the surface of a liquid, knowing that evaporation causes cooling of the liquid left behind. (Specific heat capacity and $Q=mc\Delta T$, which some items in this lesson also practise, are extension material and are not required by the core syllabus.)
Distinguish boiling from evaporation, and predict the effect of temperature, exposed surface area and air movement on the rate of evaporation.
