prerequisites.statement: Describe particle motion in solids, liquids and gases, and state that a higher temperature means greater average random particle motion.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Explaining what happens during melting, boiling and evaporation means describing a change in particle arrangement and motion; without the particle model, a heating curve is just a shape to memorise.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that energy can be transferred to a substance by heating, and that this is usually described using the idea of energy input over time.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The flat sections of a heating or cooling curve only make sense if the energy going in or out is tracked separately from the temperature, so this idea needs to already be familiar.

diagnostic_items.question: (a) Describe how the particles of a solid are arranged and how they move. (b) A beaker of water is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C, without boiling. State what happens to the average random motion of its particles.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: (a) The particles of a solid are close together in a regular arrangement, held by strong forces, and each one vibrates about a fixed position without moving away from its neighbours. (b) The average random motion of the particles increases: on average they move faster.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles of a solid are completely still, which is why a solid keeps its shape.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has turned 'fixed positions' into 'no motion', so there is nothing left to change when the solid is heated.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Heating makes the water particles themselves get bigger.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner explains heating by a change in particle size rather than by a change in particle motion and spacing.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Nothing happens to the motion until the water reaches 100 °C and boils.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner ties particle motion to changes of state only, and has not connected it to temperature in general.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the particle picture of a solid and the link between temperature and average random particle motion from lesson 1. Melting, boiling and evaporation are all described as changes in particle arrangement and motion, so neither idea can be missing here.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit the three-state particle diagram and the temperature block of lesson 1, and practise describing each state in one sentence covering both arrangement and motion, before starting on changes of state.

theory_blocks.title: A heating curve has flat steps
theory_blocks.body:
If a block of ice is heated steadily and its temperature is recorded against time, the graph is not a single straight rising line.

Instead, the temperature rises, then stays completely flat for a while, then rises again, then stays flat again, before rising once more.

The two flat sections happen exactly at [[blue:$0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$]] (while the ice is melting into water) and at [[orange:$100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$]] (while the water is boiling into steam), at standard atmospheric pressure.

Outside those two flat sections, the temperature of the ice, the liquid water, or the steam rises steadily as it is heated.

assets.caption: Heating $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of ice steadily from $-20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until it has all turned to steam, at standard atmospheric pressure. The curve is flat only during melting (at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) and boiling (at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). The liquid water warms at about half the rate of the ice, because water needs about twice as much energy per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise; the boiling plateau is drawn much shorter than it really is, because boiling the water away takes far longer than melting the ice.
assets.purpose: Show the characteristic shape of a water heating curve, with the two flat sections at the correct reference temperatures and each labelled beside the plateau it describes, and with the rising sections drawn at the correct relative steepness (ice steeper than liquid water).

theory_blocks.title: A flat section does not mean no energy is entering
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to read a flat section of the heating curve as 'nothing happening', but the heater is still supplying energy at exactly the same steady rate throughout.

What changes is where that energy goes. Away from a flat section, energy input increases the particles' average random kinetic energy, so the temperature rises.

During a flat section, the substance is changing state (melting or boiling), and [[blue:every joule of energy supplied is instead used to loosen or break the forces holding particles in their solid or liquid arrangement, rearranging them into a more free liquid or gas structure]].

Because none of this energy is going into average kinetic energy at that moment, the temperature does not rise until the change of state is complete, even though heating has not stopped.

theory_blocks.title: Condensation and freezing: the same changes in reverse
theory_blocks.body:
Melting and boiling are only half the story. Run each change backwards and you have **condensation** and **solidification**, which is usually just called **freezing**.

In [[blue:**condensation**]], gas particles moving freely in all directions transfer energy to their surroundings, so their average speed falls.

Once they are slow enough, the attractive forces between them are strong enough to hold them together whenever they come close, pulling them into the much closer, irregular arrangement of a liquid.

Energy is given out to the surroundings while this happens, and, exactly as in boiling, the temperature stays constant until all of the gas has condensed.

In [[blue:**freezing**]], the particles of the liquid lose energy in the same way and slow down further, until they can no longer slide past one another.

The forces between them then hold them in the regular, close-packed arrangement of a solid, in which each particle only vibrates about a fixed position. Again energy is given out and the temperature stays constant until all of the liquid has frozen.

For a pure substance these reverse changes happen at the same temperatures as the forward ones: at standard atmospheric pressure, water condenses at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and freezes at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the very temperatures at which it boils and melts.

That is why a cooling curve has flat sections in the same places as a heating curve.

The four terms belong together as two pairs, one of each pair taking energy in and the other giving it out:

| Change of state | Direction | Energy |
|---|---|---|
| melting | solid → liquid | taken in |
| freezing (solidification) | liquid → solid | given out |
| boiling | liquid → gas | taken in |
| condensation | gas → liquid | given out |

Evaporation is also a liquid → gas change that takes energy in, but, unlike boiling, it happens only at the surface and at any temperature; the next blocks deal with it. Changes straight between solid and gas are not required by the syllabus.

assets.caption: Cooling steam steadily from $110\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ down to $-10\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at standard atmospheric pressure. The curve is flat while the steam condenses (at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) and while the water freezes (at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Energy is being given out to the surroundings throughout, including during the two flat sections; segment lengths are schematic, not drawn to a real energy scale.
assets.purpose: Show that a cooling curve has flat sections at exactly the same two temperatures as the heating curve earlier in the lesson, so condensation and freezing are seen as melting and boiling in reverse.

theory_blocks.title: Evaporation: the fastest particles escape
theory_blocks.body:
Within any liquid, not every particle moves at exactly the same speed: there is a spread of speeds around the average, with some particles moving much faster than average and some much slower, at any given instant.

Near the surface, a particle moving fast enough, in roughly the right direction, can overcome the attractive forces pulling it back into the liquid and escape into the air above as a gas.

This is **evaporation**, and it can happen at any temperature, because there are always at least a few unusually fast particles near the surface, even when the average speed (and so the temperature) is fairly low.

Because it is specifically the higher-energy particles that escape, the particles left behind in the liquid have, on average, slightly less energy than before: the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid has fallen.

Since temperature is linked to average kinetic energy, this means the remaining liquid is slightly cooler.

This is **evaporative cooling**, and it is why sweat cooling on skin, or a wet surface in a breeze, feels cold: the liquid that evaporates carries away more than its fair share of energy, cooling what remains.

assets.caption: Particles near the liquid surface move at a range of speeds (short arrows). Only the fastest, best-aimed particle (red, longer arrow) has enough energy to escape through the surface into the air; the particles left behind have, on average, slightly less energy than before, so the liquid cools slightly.
assets.purpose: Make explicit that evaporation removes high-energy particles selectively, directly supporting the evaporative-cooling explanation and pre-empting the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Raising temperature takes energy: specific heat capacity
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension (beyond this course).** Specific heat capacity and $Q=mc\Delta T$ are not required by the Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences (GCSE) syllabus, which only asks you to describe melting and boiling in terms of energy input without a change in temperature. Nothing in this block or the next one will be examined; they are here because they answer the natural follow-up question, *how much* energy a temperature change actually costs.

Away from a change of state, the energy needed to raise a substance's temperature depends on three things: how much substance there is, what it is made of, and how big a temperature change is wanted.

This is captured by the substance's **specific heat capacity**, $c$: the energy needed to raise the temperature of $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of that substance by $1\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$,

measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius ($\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,^{\circ}C^{-1}}$, usually written $\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$).

Water has an unusually large specific heat capacity, about $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$: it takes $4200\,\mathrm{J}$ to raise the temperature of just $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water by $1\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Most metals have a much smaller specific heat capacity — aluminium is about $900\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$ and copper is about $390\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$ — so the same energy input produces a much bigger temperature rise in a metal than in an equal mass of water.

This is exactly the quantitative version of the energy-input idea from the previous block: specific heat capacity tells you how much of that steady energy input is needed, away from a plateau, for each degree of temperature rise.

theory_blocks.title: Using $Q = mc\Delta T$
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension (beyond this course).** Like the block before it, this one is not examinable on this course.

The energy $Q$ (in joules) needed to change the temperature of a mass $m$ (in kilograms) of a substance with specific heat capacity $c$ (in $\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) by a temperature change $\Delta T$ (in $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) is:
$$Q = mc\Delta T$$
This equation only applies away from a change of state: if the substance is melting or boiling during the heating, this equation does not describe that part of the process,

because that energy changes the particles' arrangement rather than their temperature.

To use it: (1) identify $m$, $c$ and $\Delta T$ from the question, converting any mass given in grams to kilograms; (2) substitute directly if $Q$ is unknown;

(3) if $m$ or $\Delta T$ is unknown instead, rearrange first — $m=\dfrac{Q}{c\Delta T}$ or $\Delta T=\dfrac{Q}{mc}$ — then substitute.

Always check a rearranged answer by substituting it back into $Q=mc\Delta T$ and confirming it reproduces the original value of $Q$.

theory_blocks.title: Boiling and evaporation are not the same process
theory_blocks.body:
Both boiling and evaporation turn a liquid into a gas, but they are different processes. **Boiling** happens throughout the whole liquid, not just at its surface, producing bubbles of vapour that form and rise from within the liquid;

it happens only at one specific temperature for a given substance at a given pressure (for water, $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at standard atmospheric pressure), and the temperature stays at that value,

as the flat section of the heating curve shows, until all the liquid has boiled away.

**Evaporation** happens only at the liquid's exposed surface, and it can happen at any temperature, not just the boiling point: a puddle dries up on a cool day, and washing on a line dries without ever reaching $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Evaporation is also usually much slower than boiling and does not produce bubbles within the liquid.

theory_blocks.title: Three factors that speed up evaporation, tested fairly
theory_blocks.body:
Three factors increase the rate of evaporation from a liquid's surface: **higher temperature** (more particles near the surface have enough energy to escape at any instant),

**larger exposed surface area** (more particles are positioned at the surface where escape is possible),

and **air movement across the surface** (moving air sweeps away escaped particles before they can collide with the surface and be recaptured, keeping the air just above the surface less crowded with vapour).

To test any one of these factors fairly, the other two — along with the mass or volume of liquid used — must be kept the same between the compared setups, changing only the factor being tested.

For example, comparing how fast two equal volumes of water dry from two equal-sized dishes, one left still and one placed in front of a fan, with both dishes at the same starting temperature, isolates air movement as the only variable being tested.

keywords.definition: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** The energy needed to raise the temperature of $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of a substance by $1\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, measured in $\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$.
A change between solid, liquid and gas (such as melting, boiling, condensing or freezing) during which temperature stays constant while energy changes particle arrangement.
A change from liquid to gas that happens throughout the liquid, producing bubbles, only at a substance's specific boiling point.
A change from liquid to gas that happens only at the liquid's exposed surface, at any temperature, as the highest-energy surface particles escape.
The fall in temperature of a liquid caused by the selective escape of its highest-energy particles during evaporation.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading a heating curve.** A pure solid is heated steadily. Its temperature rises from $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $65\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, stays at $65\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for four minutes, then rises again. Explain each section.
knowns: The temperature is constant at $65\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for four minutes.
unknowns: What happens in each section of the heating curve.
reasoning: A rising temperature means the particles' average kinetic energy is increasing.
A flat section during continued heating marks a change of state: energy separates particles rather than raising temperature.
worked_examples.solution: Below $65\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the solid warms. At $65\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ it melts at constant temperature while solid and liquid coexist. After all the solid has melted, the liquid warms and its temperature rises again.
worked_examples.interpretation: A flat heating-curve section does not mean heating has stopped; it shows that supplied energy is producing a change of state.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying that particles stop gaining energy on the flat section; their potential energy increases even though temperature is constant.

worked_examples.statement: **Evaporation or boiling?** Water in an open dish slowly disappears at $22\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, while water in a heated beaker forms bubbles throughout at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Compare the two processes.
knowns: The dish is below water's boiling point.
The beaker is at water's boiling point and bubbles form throughout.
unknowns: Which process occurs in each case and why.
reasoning: Evaporation occurs at the surface and can happen at any temperature.
Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at a fixed temperature when vapour bubbles can form.
worked_examples.solution: The dish loses water by evaporation: higher-energy surface molecules escape, so it can occur at $22\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The beaker is boiling: vapour bubbles form throughout the liquid at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Evaporation and boiling both form a gas, but they differ in location, temperature conditions and bubble formation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling every liquid-to-gas change boiling; slow surface loss below the boiling point is evaporation.

worked_examples.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** **Same mass, same energy, different materials.** Equal $1.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ samples of water ($c=4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) and aluminium ($c=900\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) each absorb $63\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy, with no change of state. Calculate the temperature rise of each, and explain why they differ so much.
reasoning: Use $\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{mc}$ for each material, keeping $Q$ and $m$ the same and changing only $c$.
Compare the sizes of the two specific heat capacities before calculating, to predict which sample should warm up more.
worked_examples.solution: Water: $\Delta T = \dfrac{63\,000}{1.5\times 4200} = 10\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Aluminium: $\Delta T = \dfrac{63\,000}{1.5\times 900} \approx 46.7\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
The aluminium warms up roughly $4.7\times$ more than the water for exactly the same energy input and mass,

because its specific heat capacity is about $4.7\times$ smaller: a smaller specific heat capacity means each joule of energy produces a bigger temperature rise.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Expecting the two temperature rises to be similar because the mass and energy input are the same, without accounting for how differently specific heat capacity scales the result.

worked_examples.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** **Finding an unknown mass.** A block of copper (specific heat capacity $390\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) is heated with $23\,400\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy and its temperature rises by $40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, with no change of state. Calculate the mass of the copper block.
reasoning: $m$ is unknown, so rearrange $Q=mc\Delta T$ to $m=\dfrac{Q}{c\Delta T}$ before substituting.
Substitute the known values into the rearranged equation.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substitution: $1.5 \times 390 \times 40 = 23\,400\,\mathrm{J}$, which matches the given energy.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Rearranging incorrectly to $m = Q \times c \times \Delta T$, multiplying all three instead of dividing by the product of $c$ and $\Delta T$.

guided_exercises.statement: A beaker of ice is heated steadily. For the first two minutes its temperature rises; for the next three minutes its temperature stays at exactly $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; then it starts rising again. Explain what is happening to the ice during the three-minute flat section, and why the temperature does not rise during that time even though heating continues.
hints: A flat section of a heating curve always corresponds to a change of state; identify which one is happening at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Ask where the energy supplied during the flat section is going, if it is not increasing the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Link your answer to what is happening to the forces holding the solid's particles in fixed positions.
guided_exercises.answer: During the three-minute flat section, the ice is melting into water. The energy supplied continues at the same steady rate, but instead of increasing the particles' average kinetic energy, it is used to loosen the strong forces holding the solid's particles in fixed positions, changing their arrangement into the looser, irregular arrangement of a liquid. Because none of this energy raises the average kinetic energy while melting is in progress, the temperature stays constant at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all the ice has melted.
common_errors: Saying the heater must have been switched off or turned down during the flat section, instead of explaining where the continuing energy input actually goes.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** A flat section of a heating curve always corresponds to a change of state; identify which one is happening at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

**Step 2 — Method:** Ask where the energy supplied during the flat section is going, if it is not increasing the average kinetic energy of the particles.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** During the three-minute flat section, the ice is melting into water. The energy supplied continues at the same steady rate, but instead of increasing the particles' average kinetic energy, it is used to loosen the strong forces holding the solid's particles in fixed positions, changing their arrangement into the looser, irregular arrangement of a liquid. Because none of this energy raises the average kinetic energy while melting is in progress, the temperature stays constant at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all the ice has melted.

**Step 4 — Check:** Link your answer to what is happening to the forces holding the solid's particles in fixed positions.

guided_exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** A $0.80\,\mathrm{kg}$ aluminium pan (specific heat capacity $900\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) absorbs $21\,600\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy from a hob, with no change of state. Calculate the pan's temperature rise.
hints: Decide which quantity is unknown ($\Delta T$) and rearrange $Q=mc\Delta T$ before substituting.
Keep the units consistent: mass in kilograms, specific heat capacity in $\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$, energy in joules.
Check your answer by substituting it back into $Q=mc\Delta T$ and confirming it reproduces $21\,600\,\mathrm{J}$.
common_errors: Dividing $Q$ by $c$ alone and forgetting the mass, which gives $21\,600 \div 900 = 24\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, or multiplying by $m$ instead of dividing by it.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide which quantity is unknown ($\Delta T$) and rearrange $Q=mc\Delta T$ before substituting.

**Step 2 — Method:** Keep the units consistent: mass in kilograms, specific heat capacity in $\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$, energy in joules.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\Delta T = \dfrac{21\,600}{0.80\times 900} = \dfrac{21\,600}{720} = 30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Check: $0.80\times 900\times 30 = 21\,600\,\mathrm{J}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by substituting it back into $Q=mc\Delta T$ and confirming it reproduces $21\,600\,\mathrm{J}$.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** Calculate the energy needed to heat $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water from $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, without yet boiling it. Take the specific heat capacity of water as $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$.
exercises.answer: $Q = 1.0 \times 4200 \times 75 = 315\,000\,\mathrm{J} = 315\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
exercises.full_solution: $\Delta T = 100-25 = 75\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; substituting directly into $Q=mc\Delta T$ gives $315\,000\,\mathrm{J}$. This energy only accounts for warming the water up to $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; it does not include the further energy needed to actually boil it away, which is a separate quantity not covered by this equation.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** A $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ block of copper (specific heat capacity $390\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$) absorbs $46\,800\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy, with no change of state. Calculate its temperature rise.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $3.0\times 390\times 40 = 46\,800\,\mathrm{J}$, which matches the given energy.

exercises.statement: Two identical wet cloths, A and B, start at the same temperature and hold the same amount of water. Cloth A is left folded up in a bowl; cloth B is spread out flat on a washing line in a gentle breeze. State which cloth dries faster, and identify every variable that must be controlled for this to be a fair comparison of the effect of surface area and air movement together.
exercises.answer: Cloth B dries faster, because spreading it out increases its exposed surface area and the breeze removes evaporated water vapour from just above its surface, both of which speed up evaporation; cloth A, folded up, has far less exposed surface and no air movement across it. For a fair comparison, the two cloths must start at the same temperature, be in surroundings at the same air temperature, hold the same mass of water, and be made of the same material, so that only surface area and air exposure differ between them.
exercises.full_solution: This combines two of the three evaporation-rate factors (surface area, air movement) in one scenario, while the controlled variables (temperature, water mass, material) ensure the comparison isolates those two effects.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** Coastal towns often have milder weather than inland towns at the same latitude: the sea nearby heats up and cools down more slowly than the land. For example, if $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater near the surface absorbs $8400\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy from a day's sunshine, calculate its temperature rise (take its specific heat capacity as approximately that of water, $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$), and use this to explain why a large body of water changes temperature only slowly.
exercises.answer: $\Delta T = \dfrac{8400}{0.50\times 4200} = \dfrac{8400}{2100} = 4.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Water's large specific heat capacity means a given amount of absorbed energy produces only a modest temperature rise; a large mass of seawater absorbing a day's sunshine therefore warms by only a small amount, and correspondingly releases only a small amount of energy (and cools only slightly) overnight, which keeps coastal temperatures milder and steadier than inland temperatures over a similar area of land.
exercises.full_solution: Land has a much smaller effective specific heat capacity than water, so the same solar energy input produces a much larger temperature swing on land than on the sea, which is the physical reason coastal climates are milder.

exercises.statement: Steam from a kettle reaches a cold window, and a film of liquid water appears on the glass. (a) Name the change of state that has taken place. (b) Describe, in terms of particles, what has happened to the water particles. (c) State whether energy is taken in from the window or given out to it during this change.
exercises.answer: (a) Condensation. (b) The water particles in the steam transfer energy to the cold glass, so they slow down; once they are slow enough, the attractive forces between them hold them together whenever they come close, pulling them into the much closer, irregular arrangement of a liquid. (c) Energy is given out to the window, which is why the glass warms slightly where the steam condenses.
exercises.full_solution: Condensation is boiling in reverse, so every part of the description is the reverse of the boiling description: particles lose energy instead of gaining it, slow down instead of speeding up, and are pulled together by the forces between them instead of escaping from them.

Take the specific heat capacity of water as $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$. (a) Calculate the energy needed for this temperature rise. exam_questions.statement:
A sample of a pure liquid X is cooled steadily and its temperature is recorded.

| Time (min) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature ($^{\circ}$C) | 60 | 38 | 25 | 25 | 25 | 15 |

(a) State the freezing point of X. (b) The sample is losing energy to its surroundings at a steady rate throughout. Explain why its temperature does not fall between $4$ and $8$ minutes. (c) Describe how the arrangement and motion of the particles of X change during that time.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The freezing point of X is $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the temperature of the flat section. (b) Energy is still being transferred out of the sample throughout the flat section. During those minutes X is freezing, and the energy given out comes from the particles being pulled into a fixed arrangement by the forces between them, not from a fall in their average kinetic energy. Because the average kinetic energy does not change, the temperature stays at $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all of X has frozen. (c) The particles change from being close together in an irregular arrangement, sliding past one another, to being held in a regular, close-packed arrangement in which each particle only vibrates about a fixed position.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The freezing point of X is $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the temperature of the flat section. (b) Energy is still being transferred out of the sample throughout the flat section. During those minutes X is freezing, and the energy given out comes from the particles being pulled into a fixed arrangement by the forces between them, not from a fall in their average kinetic energy. Because the average kinetic energy does not change, the temperature stays at $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all of X has frozen. (c) The particles change from being close together in an irregular arrangement, sliding past one another, to being held in a regular, close-packed arrangement in which each particle only vibrates about a fixed position.
mark_scheme: States the freezing point as $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
States that energy continues to be transferred out of the sample during the flat section.
States that X is freezing (changing from liquid to solid) during the flat section.

Explains that the energy given out comes from the change of particle arrangement, so the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change and the temperature stays constant until the change is complete.
Describes the liquid arrangement and motion: particles close together but irregularly arranged, sliding past one another.
Describes the solid arrangement and motion: particles in a regular, close-packed arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
common_errors: Saying that the sample stops losing energy during the flat section, when the question states that energy is lost at a steady rate throughout.
Describing only the arrangement in part (c) and forgetting to say how the particles move in each state.

exam_questions.statement: A student takes $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of crushed ice from a freezer at $-20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and heats it at a steady rate, recording the temperature every minute. The temperature rises to $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ after $2.0$ minutes, stays at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until $18$ minutes, then rises steadily again, reaching $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ after $38$ minutes, where it becomes steady once more. (a) Name the change of state taking place between 2.0 minutes and 18 minutes. (b) Explain why the temperature does not change during that time, even though the heater keeps supplying energy at the same steady rate. (c) The student repeats the experiment with the same mass of ice but a more powerful heater. State and explain the effect this has on the temperature of the first flat section.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Melting (the ice turning into liquid water). (b) The heater is still transferring energy to the ice at the same rate, but while the ice is melting that energy is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in their fixed solid positions and rearrange them into a liquid, not to make the particles move faster. The average kinetic energy of the particles therefore does not increase, so the temperature stays at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all the ice has melted. (c) The flat section is still at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The melting temperature is a fixed property of the substance at a given pressure; a more powerful heater supplies the energy needed for melting in less time, so the flat section is shorter, but it is not at a higher temperature.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Melting (the ice turning into liquid water). (b) The heater is still transferring energy to the ice at the same rate, but while the ice is melting that energy is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in their fixed solid positions and rearrange them into a liquid, not to make the particles move faster. The average kinetic energy of the particles therefore does not increase, so the temperature stays at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all the ice has melted. (c) The flat section is still at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The melting temperature is a fixed property of the substance at a given pressure; a more powerful heater supplies the energy needed for melting in less time, so the flat section is shorter, but it is not at a higher temperature.
mark_scheme: (a) Melting (accept fusion; accept 'ice changing to water').
(b) States that energy is still being supplied to the ice at the same steady rate.
(b) States that this energy is used to overcome or weaken the forces between the particles and change their arrangement from solid to liquid.
(b) States that the average kinetic energy of the particles does not increase, so the temperature does not rise until all the ice has melted.
(c) States that the flat section is still at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
(c) Explains that the melting temperature is fixed for the substance at that pressure, and the more powerful heater only makes the flat section shorter.
common_errors: Saying that the heater must have been turned down or switched off during the flat section, instead of explaining where the energy supplied actually goes.
Saying that a more powerful heater melts the ice at a higher temperature, confusing how fast the plateau is passed with the temperature at which it occurs.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Describe two differences between boiling and evaporation. (b) A few drops of ethanol are placed on the back of a student's hand and the hand soon feels cold. Explain, in terms of particles, why the evaporating ethanol cools the hand.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Any two of: boiling takes place throughout the liquid, producing bubbles of vapour inside it, while evaporation takes place only at the exposed surface; boiling happens only at one fixed temperature (the boiling point) for a given pressure, while evaporation happens at any temperature; boiling is fast, while evaporation is usually much slower. (b) The particles in the ethanol do not all have the same energy. Only the more energetic particles at the surface have enough energy to escape from the liquid, so they are the ones that evaporate. The particles left behind therefore have a lower average kinetic energy, which means the remaining ethanol is at a lower temperature, and thermal energy is transferred from the warmer hand to the cooler ethanol, so the hand feels cold.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Any two of: boiling takes place throughout the liquid, producing bubbles of vapour inside it, while evaporation takes place only at the exposed surface; boiling happens only at one fixed temperature (the boiling point) for a given pressure, while evaporation happens at any temperature; boiling is fast, while evaporation is usually much slower. (b) The particles in the ethanol do not all have the same energy. Only the more energetic particles at the surface have enough energy to escape from the liquid, so they are the ones that evaporate. The particles left behind therefore have a lower average kinetic energy, which means the remaining ethanol is at a lower temperature, and thermal energy is transferred from the warmer hand to the cooler ethanol, so the hand feels cold.
mark_scheme: (a) Boiling takes place throughout the liquid (bubbles form inside it), whereas evaporation takes place only at the surface of the liquid.
(a) Boiling happens only at the boiling point (a fixed temperature at a given pressure), whereas evaporation happens at any temperature (accept: boiling is fast, evaporation is slow).
(b) States that only the more energetic particles at the surface escape from the liquid.
(b) States that the average kinetic energy of the particles remaining in the liquid therefore decreases.
(b) Links lower average kinetic energy to a lower temperature, so thermal energy is transferred from the hand to the ethanol and the hand feels cold.
common_errors: Writing that evaporation happens 'below $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and boiling above it', instead of saying that boiling occurs only at the boiling point while evaporation occurs at any temperature.
Saying that 'the cold evaporation takes heat away' without mentioning that it is the more energetic particles that escape, which is the mark-earning step.

challenge_questions.statement: Two identical open beakers are put into the same freezer at the same time. Beaker A holds $100\,\mathrm{g}$ of water and beaker B holds $200\,\mathrm{g}$ of water, both starting at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The temperature of each is recorded until both have completely frozen, and each cooling curve turns out to have a flat section. (a) State and explain which beaker reaches $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ first. (b) State the temperature of each flat section and explain why the two are the same. (c) Explain which beaker's flat section lasts longer. (d) A student concludes that the flat section shows the freezer has stopped removing energy from the water. Explain what is wrong with this, and say what is happening to the water particles during that time.
hints: The freezer removes energy from each beaker at roughly the same steady rate, because the beakers are identical and in the same freezer.
In (b), ask yourself whether the temperature at which a pure substance freezes depends on how much of it there is.
In (c), think about how much water has to be turned into ice in each beaker, and how long it takes to remove the energy needed for that at a steady rate.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Beaker A reaches $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ first. With the same cooling conditions, energy is removed from each beaker at roughly the same rate, but A contains only half as much water, so less energy has to be removed to cool it through the same $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ drop, and it gets there sooner. (b) Both flat sections are at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the freezing point of water at standard atmospheric pressure. The freezing temperature of a pure substance is a property of the substance, not of how much of it there is, so doubling the mass does not change it. (c) Beaker B's flat section lasts longer: twice as much water has to be frozen, so twice as much energy has to be removed at that temperature, and at the same rate of removal this takes about twice as long. (d) The freezer has not stopped removing energy; it goes on removing it at the same steady rate throughout. During the flat section the water is freezing, and the energy removed is given out as the particles are pulled into the fixed, regular arrangement of ice by the forces between them, instead of coming from a fall in their average kinetic energy. Since the average kinetic energy is what the temperature measures, the temperature stays at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ until all of the water has frozen.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The whole question turns on one idea applied four times: the freezer removes energy at a steady rate, so 'how long' always means 'how much energy has to be removed'. (a) Half the mass, half the energy to remove for the same temperature drop, so A arrives at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ first. (b) The plateau temperature is set by the substance and the pressure, not the amount, so both sit at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. (c) Twice the mass to freeze means twice the energy to remove at that temperature, so B's plateau is about twice as long. (d) The plateau is not a pause in energy transfer but a change in where the energy comes from: the particle arrangement rather than the particle speeds.
common_errors: Expecting the larger beaker to freeze at a lower temperature, by confusing how much water there is with the temperature at which it freezes.
Reading the flat section as a pause in the cooling, when energy is being removed at the same rate throughout.
Saying that during the flat section the particles slow down, which would mean the temperature was still falling.

mcq.stem: A heating curve for a pure substance is flat for several minutes at its melting point, even though a heater is still supplying energy at a steady rate throughout. What is happening during this flat section?

options.text: The heater has automatically switched itself off.
options.why_wrong: contradicts the question, which states the heater is still supplying energy at a steady rate throughout.

options.text: The substance has stopped absorbing any energy at all.
options.why_wrong: confuses the temperature staying constant with the energy input stopping, when the question states heating continues.

options.text: The particles have stopped moving completely.
options.why_wrong: describes particles becoming motionless, which never happens and is unrelated to a change of state.

options.text: The energy supplied is being used to change the particles' arrangement, not to raise their average kinetic energy.

mcq.explanation: During a change of state, energy input continues but is used entirely to change particle arrangement (overcoming the forces holding them in place), not to raise their average kinetic energy, so the temperature stays constant.

mcq.stem: A puddle of water slowly disappears on a mild, dry day, even though the air temperature is nowhere near $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Which statement correctly explains this?

options.text: Evaporation can happen at any temperature, as some surface particles always have enough energy to escape.
The puddle is boiling slowly at a lower temperature than usual.
options.why_wrong: misapplies boiling, which only happens at a substance's specific boiling point, to a process happening well below that temperature.

options.text: The water must actually be above $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in direct sunlight.
options.why_wrong: assumes a temperature with no supporting evidence, when evaporation does not require reaching the boiling point at all.

options.text: The puddle is not really disappearing, only becoming invisible while remaining liquid.
options.why_wrong: denies the observation altogether instead of explaining it.

mcq.explanation: Evaporation happens at the liquid's surface at any temperature, because some particles there always have enough energy, at that instant, to escape, regardless of how low the average temperature is.

mcq.stem: Which pair of factors, if both increased while everything else is kept the same, would both increase the rate of evaporation from a liquid's surface?

options.text: Lower temperature and smaller exposed surface area.
options.why_wrong: both changes listed would decrease, not increase, the rate of evaporation.

options.text: Higher temperature and air movement across the surface.
Higher temperature and a sealed, airtight container.
options.why_wrong: a sealed container traps evaporated vapour above the surface, which slows net evaporation rather than increasing it, unlike moving air.

options.text: Smaller exposed surface area and still air.
options.why_wrong: both changes listed would decrease, not increase, the rate of evaporation.

mcq.explanation: Higher temperature gives more surface particles enough energy to escape, and air movement sweeps away vapour that has already escaped, both increasing the net evaporation rate.

mcq.stem: A warm liquid evaporates slightly and cools down. Which statement best explains why evaporation cools the remaining liquid?

options.text: Evaporation removes the lowest-energy particles first, leaving higher-energy ones behind.
options.why_wrong: gets the direction backwards: it is the highest-energy particles that escape, not the lowest-energy ones.

options.text: All the particles lose the same amount of energy together as some escape.
options.why_wrong: assumes every particle is equally affected, when only the escaping high-energy particles are removed; the rest are unaffected individually.

options.text: The particles that escape are, on average, the highest-energy ones, so the particles left behind have a lower average energy.
Evaporation always removes exactly half of the liquid's total energy, regardless of how much evaporates.
options.why_wrong: invents a fixed fraction with no physical basis; the cooling effect depends on how much liquid evaporates, not a fixed half.

mcq.explanation: Only the highest-energy particles near the surface have enough energy to escape; removing them selectively lowers the average energy, and so the temperature, of the liquid left behind.

mcq.stem: Liquid water in a freezer has been cooling steadily, but its temperature has now stopped falling even though the freezer is still running. Which statement describes what is happening to the water particles?

options.text: They have stopped moving altogether, which is why the temperature has stopped falling.
options.why_wrong: particles never stop moving; in ice they still vibrate about fixed positions.

options.text: They are gaining energy from the freezer at the same rate as they lose it, so the temperature cannot change.
options.why_wrong: a freezer removes energy from what is inside it; it does not supply energy to the water.

options.text: They are shrinking as the water turns into ice, so there is less to cool.
options.why_wrong: particles do not change size during a change of state; only their arrangement and motion change.

options.text: The forces between them are pulling them into a fixed, regular arrangement, and energy is given out while this happens.

mcq.explanation: The water is freezing. Energy is still being removed from it, but it comes from the particles settling into the fixed, regular arrangement of a solid rather than from a fall in their average kinetic energy, so the temperature stays at the freezing point until all the water has frozen.

flashcards.front: At standard atmospheric pressure, at what temperature does water melt and at what temperature does it boil?
flashcards.back: Water melts at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, both at standard atmospheric pressure.

flashcards.front: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** What equation relates energy, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change, and when does it apply?
flashcards.back: $Q = mc\Delta T$, which applies only away from a change of state (not while the substance is melting or boiling).

flashcards.front: True or false: a flat section of a heating curve means the heater has stopped supplying energy.
flashcards.back: False. Energy keeps entering at the same rate; it is being used to change the particles' arrangement (melting or boiling) rather than to raise their average kinetic energy.

flashcards.front: How does evaporation differ from boiling?
flashcards.back: Evaporation happens only at the liquid's surface, at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid, producing bubbles, and only at the substance's specific boiling point.

flashcards.front: Why does sweat evaporating from skin feel cooling?
flashcards.back: The particles that evaporate are, on average, the highest-energy ones; removing them lowers the average energy, and so the temperature, of the sweat and skin left behind.

flashcards.front: Describe, in terms of particles, what happens during condensation and during freezing.
flashcards.back: In condensation, gas particles lose energy and slow down until the attractive forces between them hold them together in the closer, irregular arrangement of a liquid. In freezing, liquid particles lose more energy, slow down further and can no longer slide past each other, so the forces hold them in the regular, close-packed arrangement of a solid. Energy is given out in both, and the temperature stays constant until the change is complete.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A flat section on a heating curve means no energy is entering the substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Because temperature is the quantity usually read off a graph, a flat line (no change in temperature) is easily read as 'nothing is happening'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says heating has 'stopped' or 'paused' during a plateau, or that the heater must have been turned off.
misconceptions.correct_model: Energy keeps entering the substance at a steady rate throughout a plateau; it is being used entirely to change the particles' arrangement (breaking or loosening the forces holding them in a solid or a liquid), not to increase their average kinetic energy, so the temperature does not rise until the change of state is complete.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly where the energy is going during the flat section if it is not raising the temperature, and connect the answer to what is changing about the particles' arrangement at that moment.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Evaporation only happens at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the boiling point.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Boiling and evaporation are both ways liquid turns to gas, and boiling is the more dramatic, more familiar one, so it is easy to assume both need the same high temperature.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says a puddle cannot be drying up unless the temperature is near $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, or treats 'evaporating' and 'boiling' as interchangeable words.
misconceptions.correct_model: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature, because even at a low average temperature, some particles near the surface happen to have enough energy to escape at that moment. Boiling, in contrast, happens throughout the liquid, not just at the surface, and only at the substance's specific boiling point.
misconceptions.remediation: Point to a drying puddle at ordinary outdoor temperature as evidence that evaporation does not require anywhere near the boiling point, then contrast this with a kettle visibly bubbling throughout the water only once it reaches $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: All the particles in a liquid have the same amount of energy, so they all escape (or stay) together.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Temperature is often taught as a single number for the whole substance, which can make it sound as if every particle shares exactly that one value of energy.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner cannot explain why only some particles evaporate at a given moment, or assumes evaporation would make the whole liquid disappear instantly once any particle gains enough energy.
misconceptions.correct_model: Temperature describes the average kinetic energy of all the particles, but individual particles have a spread of energies around that average at any instant. Evaporation happens because only the particles with unusually high energy, near the liquid's surface and moving in the right direction, manage to escape; the rest remain in the liquid.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the particles in a liquid to runners in a race with a wide range of speeds: only the fastest few reach the finish line (escape the surface) in a given short time, even though most runners are much slower.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a flat section of a heating curve as a sign that heating has stopped.
common_mistakes.why: Temperature is the quantity being graphed, so a flat temperature line looks like 'nothing is changing'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask explicitly where the continuing energy input is going: into particle arrangement (during a plateau) or into average kinetic energy (everywhere else).

common_mistakes.mistake: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** Applying $Q=mc\Delta T$ across a change of state, for example treating melting ice as if its energy requirement were just $mc\Delta T$ with $\Delta T=0$.
common_mistakes.why: The equation looks like it should cover any energy/temperature situation, so it is easy to apply it everywhere on a heating curve.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check first whether a change of state is happening; $Q=mc\Delta T$ only applies to the rising sections of the curve, never to a plateau.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming evaporation needs a temperature close to the boiling point.
common_mistakes.why: Boiling is the more dramatic and memorable way a liquid turns to gas, so it is easy to assume it sets the minimum temperature needed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that evaporation only needs a few unusually fast surface particles, which exist at any temperature, however low the average energy is.

exam_notes: Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus): always state explicitly whether a change of state is happening before deciding whether $Q=mc\Delta T$ applies.
An explanation of a heating-curve plateau must say where the energy is going (into particle arrangement), not just that the temperature 'stays the same'.

When distinguishing boiling from evaporation, mention both where each happens (throughout the liquid, or only at the surface) and the temperature condition for each (a fixed boiling point, or any temperature).

summary.big_idea: A heating or cooling curve is flat only while energy is going into, or coming out of, a substance to change its particle arrangement during a change of state, which is why the temperature holds steady at the melting and boiling points; melting and boiling take energy in, while condensation and freezing give it out; and evaporation, unlike boiling, happens at the surface at any temperature because it is always the fastest particles that escape, cooling what remains.
key_points: Water melts at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and boils at $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at standard atmospheric pressure; a heating curve is flat at exactly these temperatures.
During a plateau, energy keeps entering but changes particle arrangement, not temperature.

Condensation and freezing are the reverse changes: particles lose energy, slow down, and the forces between them pull them into a liquid, then into a fixed solid arrangement, with energy given out while the temperature stays constant.
Boiling happens throughout a liquid at one fixed temperature; evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature.
Evaporation selectively removes the highest-energy particles, lowering the average energy, and so the temperature, of the liquid left behind.
formulas: Q = mc\Delta T \quad \text{(extension only: not required by 0654)}
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A flat section of a heating or cooling curve means energy is changing particle arrangement, not temperature; condensation and freezing are melting and boiling run backwards, with energy given out instead of taken in; and evaporation cools a liquid because it is always the fastest particles that escape first.

04_Conduction_through_materials.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Identify thermal conductors and insulators from everyday examples and simple comparative experiments.
Explain conduction in terms of particles passing on vibration energy to their neighbours, and explain why metals are especially good conductors because of mobile (delocalised) electrons.

prerequisites.statement: Describe particles in a solid as vibrating about fixed positions, with more vigorous vibration at a higher temperature.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Conduction is explained entirely as vibration energy being handed from particle to particle, so the previous lesson's picture of a vibrating solid is the starting point for this one.

diagnostic_items.question: (a) A metal spoon is lying on a table at room temperature. Describe what its particles are doing. (b) One end of the spoon is then put into hot water. State what happens to the motion of the particles at that end.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: (a) The particles are close together in a regular arrangement and each one vibrates about a fixed position, without moving away from its neighbours. (b) The particles at that end vibrate more vigorously, with more energy, but still about the same fixed positions.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles of a solid do not move at all; that is why the spoon keeps its shape.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has turned 'fixed positions' into 'no motion', which leaves conduction with nothing to pass along.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The hot particles travel along the spoon from the hot end to the cold end.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner expects energy to be carried by particles moving through the solid, which is convection rather than conduction and is exactly the idea this lesson has to correct.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles at the hot end get bigger, so the spoon feels hotter.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is explaining heating by a change in particle size rather than by a change in how vigorously the particles vibrate.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the picture of a solid as particles vibrating about fixed positions, more vigorously when hotter. Conduction is described entirely as that vibration being passed on, so this must be secure first.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Go back to the solid panel of the three-state particle diagram in lesson 1 and practise describing it in one sentence that covers both the fixed arrangement and the vibration, then say what heating changes and what it does not.

theory_blocks.title: Conductors and insulators, by comparison
theory_blocks.body:
If identical metal, wood and plastic rods are heated at one end and a thermometer or a dab of wax is placed at the same distance along each rod, the metal rod registers a temperature rise (or melts the wax) far sooner than the wood or plastic rods.

This is a fair comparison because the rods are the same shape, the same length, and heated with the same temperature difference: only the material is different, so the material alone explains the difference in how quickly energy reaches the far end.

A material that transfers thermal energy quickly from a warmer region to a cooler region, like most metals, is called a [[blue:**thermal conductor**]].

A material that transfers thermal energy only slowly, like wood, plastic, glass, air and most other non-metals, is called a **thermal insulator**.

'Insulator' does not mean 'blocks transfer completely': it means the transfer happens much more slowly than through a conductor.

theory_blocks.title: A good conductor doesn't store extra heat, and a good insulator doesn't block transfer completely
theory_blocks.body:
Being a good thermal conductor is about how quickly a material transfers energy, not about how much energy it stores. A metal spoon left in the same room as a wooden spoon for hours reaches exactly the same temperature as the wooden spoon;

[[blue:it has no extra 'stored heat' or 'stored cold']]. When you touch the metal spoon, it feels colder than the wooden spoon only because [[orange:it conducts energy away from your warmer hand much faster]],

giving a stronger, quicker sensation of energy leaving your skin.

Similarly, calling a material an insulator does not mean it stops thermal energy transfer completely: it only transfers energy much more slowly than a conductor would.

A well-insulated drink still cools down eventually; the insulation simply makes that process take far longer.

theory_blocks.title: Conduction: energy passed along, particles stay put
theory_blocks.body:
At the end of a solid that is heated, the particles gain extra vibration energy and vibrate more vigorously about their fixed positions.

Because each particle is held close to its neighbours by strong forces, this extra, more vigorous vibration is passed on: a particle that is vibrating more strongly collides more forcefully with its neighbours, making them vibrate more too.

This process repeats from particle to particle along the material, gradually passing vibration energy from the hot end towards the cold end.

Crucially, no particle actually travels along the material: each one stays close to its own fixed position throughout.

What moves along the solid is vibration energy, handed from particle to particle, not the particles themselves and not any flow of material.

assets.caption: Top: in a non-metal, vibration energy is passed only from particle to particle, so it weakens noticeably further from the hot end in the same time. Bottom: in a metal, the same particle-to-particle vibration happens, but mobile (delocalised) electrons also drift quickly through the lattice, carrying energy along much faster, which is why metals are much better conductors.

theory_blocks.title: Metals conduct faster because of mobile electrons
theory_blocks.body:
Metals are unusual among solids: some of their electrons are not held tightly to one particular atom and are free to drift through the whole structure.

These are called **delocalised** (or mobile, or 'free') **electrons**. At the hot end of a metal, these electrons gain extra kinetic energy and, because they can move freely through the metal,

they drift rapidly towards the cooler end, carrying that extra energy with them and transferring it to particles they encounter along the way.

This gives metals two mechanisms for conduction working together: the particle-to-particle vibration mechanism that every solid has, and the much faster electron-drift mechanism that only metals have.

Because the electron mechanism is so much faster at carrying energy along, metals conduct thermal energy far better than non-metals, which rely on the particle-to-particle mechanism alone.

keywords.definition: A material that transfers thermal energy quickly from a warmer region to a cooler region.
A material that transfers thermal energy only slowly, not completely blocking transfer.
The transfer of thermal energy through a material by particles passing on vibration energy to their neighbours, without the particles themselves travelling.
A mobile electron in a metal, not held to one particular atom, free to drift through the structure and carry thermal energy quickly.
The vibration of particles about their fixed positions in a solid, which passes energy to neighbouring particles during conduction.

worked_examples.statement: **Why metal feels colder.** A metal door handle and a wooden door, both in the same cold room overnight, are touched by the same person at the same moment. Explain why the metal handle feels colder, even though both are at the same temperature.
knowns: metal handle and wooden door are at the same (cold) temperature
both have been in the same room overnight
reasoning: Both objects are at the same starting temperature, so neither is actually colder than the other.
Metal is a much better thermal conductor than wood, so it transfers thermal energy away from the warmer hand much faster than the wood does.
worked_examples.solution: The metal handle feels colder because it conducts thermal energy away from the hand much faster than the wooden door, giving a stronger sensation of energy leaving the skin, even though both objects started at exactly the same temperature.
worked_examples.interpretation: This separates 'feels colder' (a rate-of-transfer effect) from 'is colder' (an actual temperature difference), which this scenario shows are not the same thing.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that the metal must actually be at a lower temperature than the wood, when the question states they are at the same temperature.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two rods.** Identical copper and glass rods are both heated at one end with the same temperature difference maintained between the ends. After the same amount of time, wax placed at the far end of the copper rod has melted, but wax at the same position on the glass rod has not. Explain this difference in terms of particles.
knowns: copper's wax melts; glass's wax does not, in the same time
unknowns: why copper transfers energy to the far end faster
reasoning: Both rods conduct energy by passing vibration from particle to particle along the solid, since both are solids.
Copper is a metal, so it also has mobile delocalised electrons that drift quickly from the hot end, carrying extra energy with them; glass does not have this second mechanism.
worked_examples.solution: The copper rod's wax melts first because copper, as a metal, conducts energy both by particle-to-particle vibration and by fast-drifting delocalised electrons, while glass, a non-metal, relies on the much slower particle-to-particle mechanism alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the standard conductor/insulator contrast explained specifically through the extra electron mechanism that only metals have.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the difference only as 'copper conducts better', without saying why, which misses the electron-based reasoning this lesson specifically teaches.

worked_examples.statement: **Designing a saucepan.** A saucepan has a metal base and body, but its handle is made of a moulded plastic. Explain, in terms of conduction, why this combination of materials is a sensible design.
unknowns: why this material choice makes sense
reasoning: The base needs to transfer thermal energy quickly from the hob to the food, which requires a good conductor: a metal.
The handle needs to transfer as little thermal energy as possible to the hand holding it, which requires a poor conductor (a good insulator): a plastic.
worked_examples.solution:
The metal base is a good conductor, so it quickly transfers energy from the hob to the food being cooked.

The plastic handle is a poor conductor (a good insulator), so it transfers only a little thermal energy to the hand, keeping the handle safe to hold even while the base is very hot.
worked_examples.interpretation: This shows that 'good design' in this case means deliberately choosing a good conductor where fast transfer is wanted, and a good insulator where slow transfer is wanted, in the same object.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the whole pan should be made of the best possible conductor, without recognising that the handle specifically needs the opposite property.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining an experiment.** In an experiment, four rods of equal length and thickness — aluminium, iron, glass and wood — are set up with one end of each in the same beaker of boiling water, and a small blob of wax holding a pin onto the other end of each rod. (a) Predict the order in which the pins are likely to fall, from first to last. (b) Explain, in terms of particles and (for the metals) electrons, why the two metal rods are expected to lose their pins well before the glass and wood rods.
knowns: four identical-length, identical-thickness rods: aluminium, iron, glass, wood
all heated at one end by the same boiling water
a wax-held pin at the far end of each
reasoning: The pin falls once enough energy has reached the far end to melt the wax there, so the fastest conductor should lose its pin first.

Aluminium and iron are metals, so they conduct via both particle-to-particle vibration and fast-drifting delocalised electrons; glass and wood are non-metals, relying on particle-to-particle vibration alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a classic comparative conduction experiment: the order the pins fall is the observable evidence, and the electron mechanism is the particle-level explanation for why metals win that comparison.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the result only as 'metals conduct better' without naming the electron mechanism that the Supplement-level explanation specifically requires.

guided_exercises.statement: A student wraps one mug of hot tea in a woollen scarf and leaves another identical mug of hot tea, at the same starting temperature, unwrapped, both in the same room. After twenty minutes, the wrapped mug's tea is noticeably warmer than the unwrapped mug's tea. Explain this result, and state whether the wrapped mug's tea will stay hot forever.
hints: Identify which material (wool or the air around the unwrapped mug) is acting as the insulator in this comparison.
Remember that being a good insulator means slowing transfer down, not stopping it.
Think about what will eventually happen to both mugs if left for long enough, such as overnight.
guided_exercises.answer: The wrapped mug's tea stays warmer for longer because wool is a good thermal insulator, slowing the rate at which thermal energy transfers from the hot tea to the cooler surroundings, compared with the unwrapped mug. However, the wrapped mug's tea will not stay hot forever: insulation only slows the transfer down, it does not stop it, so given enough time, both mugs will eventually cool to room temperature.
common_errors: Concluding that the wrapped mug's tea will never cool down at all, treating the insulator as if it blocked transfer completely.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which material (wool or the air around the unwrapped mug) is acting as the insulator in this comparison.

**Step 2 — Method:** Remember that being a good insulator means slowing transfer down, not stopping it.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The wrapped mug's tea stays warmer for longer because wool is a good thermal insulator, slowing the rate at which thermal energy transfers from the hot tea to the cooler surroundings, compared with the unwrapped mug. However, the wrapped mug's tea will not stay hot forever: insulation only slows the transfer down, it does not stop it, so given enough time, both mugs will eventually cool to room temperature.

**Step 4 — Check:** Think about what will eventually happen to both mugs if left for long enough, such as overnight.

guided_exercises.statement: Explain, using the idea of vibration being passed from particle to particle, why a long metal poker left with one end in a fire takes a noticeable amount of time before its other end, held in your hand, becomes warm, even though metal is a good conductor.
hints: Conduction passes vibration energy from one particle to the next, not instantly along the whole length at once.
Think about how many particle-to-particle handovers are needed to cross the whole length of a long poker.
'Good conductor' means faster than other materials, not instantaneous.
guided_exercises.answer: Even in a good conductor, energy must still be passed from particle to particle (and carried along by drifting electrons) step by step along the whole length of the poker; this takes a measurable amount of time, especially over a long length, even though metal does this much faster than a poor conductor would.
common_errors: Assuming a good conductor transfers energy instantly over any distance, rather than simply faster than a poor conductor over the same distance.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Conduction passes vibration energy from one particle to the next, not instantly along the whole length at once.

**Step 2 — Method:** Think about how many particle-to-particle handovers are needed to cross the whole length of a long poker.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Even in a good conductor, energy must still be passed from particle to particle (and carried along by drifting electrons) step by step along the whole length of the poker; this takes a measurable amount of time, especially over a long length, even though metal does this much faster than a poor conductor would.

**Step 4 — Check:** 'Good conductor' means faster than other materials, not instantaneous.

exercises.statement: Classify each of the following as a good thermal conductor or a good thermal insulator: (a) copper, (b) foam packaging, (c) iron, (d) wool.
exercises.answer: (a) Copper — conductor. (b) Foam packaging — insulator. (c) Iron — conductor. (d) Wool — insulator.
exercises.full_solution: Metals (copper, iron) are good conductors; most non-metals, especially those with trapped air pockets like foam and wool, are good insulators.

exercises.statement: A student claims that a thermos flask 'stops heat getting in or out completely', which is why a hot drink inside stays hot. Explain what is scientifically inaccurate about this claim, using the idea of conduction.
exercises.answer: The claim is inaccurate because no insulator stops thermal energy transfer completely; a thermos flask's good insulation only slows the rate of conduction (and the other transfer mechanisms) dramatically, so the hot drink stays hot for much longer than in an uninsulated container, but it will still gradually cool down if left long enough.
exercises.full_solution: The claim is inaccurate because no insulator stops thermal energy transfer completely; a thermos flask's good insulation only slows the rate of conduction (and the other transfer mechanisms) dramatically, so the hot drink stays hot for much longer than in an uninsulated container, but it will still gradually cool down if left long enough.

exercises.statement: Explain, in terms of delocalised electrons, why silver (a metal) is an even better thermal conductor than most other metals.
exercises.answer: Silver has delocalised electrons that are especially free to drift through its structure, carrying thermal energy from the hot end to the cold end particularly quickly; since this electron-drift mechanism is what gives metals their advantage over non-metals, a metal whose electrons drift unusually freely conducts especially well compared with other metals too.
exercises.full_solution: Silver has delocalised electrons that are especially free to drift through its structure, carrying thermal energy from the hot end to the cold end particularly quickly; since this electron-drift mechanism is what gives metals their advantage over non-metals, a metal whose electrons drift unusually freely conducts especially well compared with other metals too.

exercises.statement: Double-glazed windows have two sheets of glass with a thin layer of trapped air (a poor conductor) sandwiched between them, instead of one thick sheet of glass. Using the idea of conduction, explain why this design reduces thermal energy loss from a warm room through the window, compared with a single thick sheet of glass of the same total thickness.
exercises.answer: The trapped air layer between the two glass sheets is a much poorer thermal conductor than glass itself, so inserting it significantly slows the overall rate at which thermal energy can be conducted through the window from the warm room to the cold outside, more than an equal thickness of glass alone would, reducing thermal energy loss.
