exam_questions.statement: A camping mug is made with a metal inner cup and a thick plastic outer sleeve. (a) State which part is the better thermal conductor. (b) Explain, in terms of particles, how thermal energy passes along the metal inner cup from the hot drink to its outer surface. (c) Suggest why a plastic sleeve, rather than a bare metal handle, is a sensible design choice.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The metal inner cup is the better thermal conductor. (b) Particles at the hot inner surface of the metal vibrate more vigorously and pass this extra vibration energy on to their neighbouring particles through collisions; this repeats from particle to particle, with additional fast-drifting delocalised electrons also carrying energy, gradually passing energy outward to the cup's outer surface, while each particle stays close to its own fixed position. (c) The plastic sleeve, being a poor conductor (a good insulator), transfers much less thermal energy to the hand holding it than bare metal would, making the mug safer and more comfortable to hold while still hot inside.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The metal inner cup is the better thermal conductor. (b) Particles at the hot inner surface of the metal vibrate more vigorously and pass this extra vibration energy on to their neighbouring particles through collisions; this repeats from particle to particle, with additional fast-drifting delocalised electrons also carrying energy, gradually passing energy outward to the cup's outer surface, while each particle stays close to its own fixed position. (c) The plastic sleeve, being a poor conductor (a good insulator), transfers much less thermal energy to the hand holding it than bare metal would, making the mug safer and more comfortable to hold while still hot inside.
mark_scheme: States the metal inner cup is the better conductor.
Describes vibration energy being passed from particle to particle via collisions.
States that delocalised/mobile electrons also carry energy quickly through the metal.
Explains that the plastic sleeve reduces the rate of energy transfer to the hand, making it safer/more comfortable to hold.
common_errors: Describing the metal particles themselves as moving from the inside to the outside surface of the cup, rather than staying in place and passing on vibration energy.

exam_questions.statement: In an experiment, a student compares the time taken for a wax-held pin to fall from the far end of a copper rod and from the far end of a glass rod, both of identical length and thickness, heated at one end by the same boiling water. (a) State two variables that must be kept the same for this to be a fair comparison, other than the material of the rods. (b) Predict which rod loses its pin first, with a reason. (c) Explain this prediction fully in terms of the particles and electrons involved.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Any two of: the length of the rods, the thickness (cross-sectional area) of the rods, the temperature of the water used to heat them, and the position of the wax/pin along each rod. (b) The copper rod loses its pin first, because copper is a much better thermal conductor than glass. (c) Copper, as a metal, has mobile delocalised electrons that drift rapidly from the hot end, carrying energy quickly along the rod, in addition to the particle-to-particle vibration mechanism that both rods share; glass, a non-metal, relies only on the slower particle-to-particle mechanism, so energy reaches its far end, and melts its wax, much more slowly.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Any two of: the length of the rods, the thickness (cross-sectional area) of the rods, the temperature of the water used to heat them, and the position of the wax/pin along each rod. (b) The copper rod loses its pin first, because copper is a much better thermal conductor than glass. (c) Copper, as a metal, has mobile delocalised electrons that drift rapidly from the hot end, carrying energy quickly along the rod, in addition to the particle-to-particle vibration mechanism that both rods share; glass, a non-metal, relies only on the slower particle-to-particle mechanism, so energy reaches its far end, and melts its wax, much more slowly.
mark_scheme: States two valid controlled variables (length, thickness, water temperature, or pin/wax position).
Correctly predicts the copper rod loses its pin first.
States that copper has mobile/delocalised electrons that drift quickly, carrying energy along.
States that glass lacks this mechanism and relies on particle-to-particle vibration alone.
Links the faster energy transfer in copper to the pin falling sooner.
common_errors: Naming only one controlled variable in part (a) when two are required, or naming the material itself (which is the variable being tested, not controlled).

challenge_questions.statement: A student investigates insulation. Two identical cans of hot water are wrapped in the same woollen jumper: around can A the jumper is left loose and fluffy, while around can B it is squashed flat and taped tightly to the can. Both cans are left in the same room. Can A stays hot for noticeably longer. (a) Explain, in terms of what the wool is actually holding, why the loose wrapping insulates better. (b) Explain why air is a poor thermal conductor, in terms of particles. (c) The student repeats the test with both jumpers soaked in water. Both cans now cool much faster than before. Explain why. (d) A classmate says the experiment proves that wool only works on hot objects. Suggest a test that would settle this, and predict its result.
hints: Ask what fills the spaces inside a loose, fluffy jumper, and what happens to those spaces when it is squashed flat.
Compare the spacing of the particles in a gas with their spacing in a solid, and think about how conduction passes energy on from particle to particle.
In (c), think about what has replaced the thing that was doing the insulating.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The wool fibres themselves are only part of the insulation; most of the job is done by the air trapped in small pockets between the fibres, and air is a very poor conductor. Squashing the jumper flat forces most of that air out, so energy has to pass mainly through the fibres, which conduct better than air does, and can B cools faster. (b) In a gas the particles are far apart, so each one travels a relatively long way before it collides with another and passes energy on; there are also far fewer particles in a given volume than in a solid. Energy is therefore handed on much more slowly than in a solid, where particles are touching and vibrate against their neighbours continuously. (c) Water has taken the place of the trapped air. Water is a far better thermal conductor than air, so energy now passes out through the soaked wool much more easily and both cans cool quickly; this is why wet clothing stops keeping you warm. (d) Repeat the experiment with two cans of iced water instead of hot water, everything else kept the same, and record how long each takes to warm up to room temperature. The loosely wrapped can should stay cold longer: insulation slows energy transfer in whichever direction it is going, so it works just as well at keeping a cold object cold.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The key idea running through the whole question is that a good insulator is usually a way of trapping still air. (a) Loose wool = many small air pockets; compressed wool = fibres touching, with the air squeezed out. (b) Conduction needs particles close enough to pass vibration energy on; in a gas they are far apart and sparse, so transfer is slow. The pockets must also be small, so that the trapped air cannot set up convection currents of its own. (c) Replacing trapped air with water replaces a poor conductor with a much better one. (d) The direction of transfer never changes the physics: insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer between the object and its surroundings, whichever way the energy is flowing.
common_errors: Saying the thick jumper 'blocks the heat completely', when insulation only slows the rate of transfer; the water still cools in the end.
Crediting the wool fibres alone and never mentioning the trapped air, which makes part (c) impossible to explain.
Claiming that insulation keeps cold things cold by 'keeping the cold in', instead of by slowing energy transfer from the warm surroundings into the cold water.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes what happens to the particles of a solid during conduction?

options.text: Each particle stays close to its own fixed position and passes on vibration energy to its neighbours.
The particles travel from the hot end of the solid to the cold end.
options.why_wrong: describes a bulk flow of particles, which does not happen in conduction through a solid.

options.text: The particles near the cold end move to fill gaps left by particles near the hot end.
options.why_wrong: invents particle movement and gaps that are not part of the conduction mechanism in a solid.

options.text: The particles swap places with each other along the length of the solid.
options.why_wrong: describes a kind of mixing or diffusion, not the vibration-handover mechanism of conduction.

mcq.explanation: Conduction passes vibration energy from particle to particle through collisions; no particle actually travels along the solid.

mcq.stem: A camping cooler box is described as 'a good insulator'. What does this correctly mean?

options.text: It stops all thermal energy transfer into or out of the box completely.
options.why_wrong: overstates what an insulator does; no insulator stops transfer entirely, it only slows it down.

options.text: It transfers thermal energy much more slowly than a typical conductor would.
It actively removes thermal energy from inside the box.
options.why_wrong: describes active cooling, which an insulator does not do; it only slows the natural transfer of energy.

options.text: It keeps its contents at a fixed temperature forever.
options.why_wrong: confuses slow transfer with no transfer at all; the contents will still gradually reach the surrounding temperature.

mcq.explanation: Being a good insulator means transferring thermal energy slowly, not blocking it completely or keeping a fixed temperature forever.

mcq.stem: Why do metals generally conduct thermal energy much better than non-metals?

options.text: Metal particles vibrate more strongly than non-metal particles even at the same temperature.
options.why_wrong: is not the reason given in this lesson; particle vibration strength depends on temperature, not on whether a material is a metal.

options.text: Metal particles are smaller than non-metal particles, so energy passes between them faster.
options.why_wrong: invents a particle-size explanation that is not part of the conduction mechanism taught in this lesson.

options.text: Metals have mobile delocalised electrons that drift quickly and carry energy along, in addition to particle-to-particle vibration.
Non-metals do not have particles that vibrate at all.
options.why_wrong: is incorrect: every solid's particles vibrate; non-metals still conduct, only more slowly, via vibration alone.

mcq.explanation: The extra mechanism unique to metals is mobile delocalised electrons, which drift quickly and carry energy, on top of the particle-to-particle vibration every solid has.

mcq.stem: A metal bench and a wooden bench, both outdoors overnight, are at exactly the same temperature in the morning. Why does the metal bench feel colder to sit on?

options.text: The metal bench is actually at a lower temperature than the wooden bench.
options.why_wrong: contradicts the question, which states both benches are at exactly the same temperature.

options.text: The metal bench contains extra stored cold that the wooden bench does not have.
options.why_wrong: treats 'cold' as a substance that can be stored; there is no such thing as stored cold, and both benches are at the same temperature — the difference is only how quickly each conducts energy away from the body.

options.text: The wooden bench absorbs body heat and stores it, while the metal bench reflects it away.
options.why_wrong: invents a reflection mechanism that is not how conduction works for either material.

options.text: The metal bench conducts thermal energy away from the body faster than the wooden bench does.

mcq.explanation: Since both benches are at the same temperature, the sensation of 'colder' comes from the metal conducting energy away from the body faster, not from an actual temperature difference.

flashcards.front: What is a thermal conductor?
flashcards.back: A material that transfers thermal energy quickly from a warmer region to a cooler region, such as most metals.

flashcards.front: What extra particle, beyond vibrating atoms, allows metals to conduct especially well?
flashcards.back: Mobile (delocalised) electrons, which drift quickly through the metal and carry energy with them.

flashcards.front: True or false: in conduction, the solid's particles themselves travel from the hot end to the cold end.
flashcards.back: False. Each particle stays near its own fixed position; it is vibration energy, passed from particle to particle, that travels along the material.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between how a non-metal and a metal conduct thermal energy?
flashcards.back: A non-metal conducts only by passing vibration energy from particle to particle; a metal does this too, but also has mobile delocalised electrons that drift quickly and carry energy along much faster.

flashcards.front: A metal object and a wooden object are at exactly the same temperature. Why does the metal feel colder to touch?
flashcards.back: The metal conducts thermal energy away from the warmer hand faster than the wood does, which feels colder, even though neither object is actually at a lower temperature than the other.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In conduction, the solid's particles themselves travel from the hot end to the cold end.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Energy visibly moves from one end of a conducting object to the other, so it is tempting to imagine something physical travelling along with it, the way water flows along a pipe.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes 'hot particles moving along the rod' or 'particles flowing' from the hot end to the cold end.
misconceptions.correct_model: In conduction, each particle stays close to its own fixed position; it is vibration energy, not the particles themselves, that is passed from one particle to its neighbour, and then on to the next, along the material.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare conduction to a row of people passing a message by tapping the next person's shoulder: the message travels along the row, but no person actually changes position.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A good insulator completely stops any thermal energy transfer.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Insulators are introduced by contrast with conductors as the materials that 'don't conduct', which is easy to overstate into 'block transfer entirely'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims an insulated container never changes temperature at all, however long it is left.
misconceptions.correct_model: An insulator conducts much more slowly than a conductor, but it still transfers some thermal energy; it reduces the rate of transfer rather than stopping it completely. A well-insulated drink still eventually reaches room temperature, just much more slowly than an uninsulated one.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would eventually happen to a hot drink in a very good insulated flask if left for a whole day, to separate 'slower' from 'never'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A metal feels warmer or conducts well because it contains stored heat, the way a sponge contains stored water.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday language talks about 'holding heat' or 'trapping heat', which can be misread as a material storing a special, hidden quantity of heat ready to be released.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner explains why metal feels cold to the touch by saying metal 'has more cold stored in it' rather than by describing how quickly it transfers energy.
misconceptions.correct_model: A metal conducts well because it transfers thermal energy away from your hand quickly, not because it stores extra energy of its own. A metal object at room temperature feels colder to the touch than a wooden object at the exact same room temperature, because the metal conducts energy away from your warmer hand much faster, not because it is actually colder.
misconceptions.remediation: Point out that a metal spoon and a wooden spoon left in the same room for hours are at the same temperature, then ask why the metal one still feels colder when touched.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing conduction as particles physically travelling from the hot end to the cold end of a solid.
common_mistakes.why: Energy visibly moves along the material, which is easy to picture as something physical flowing, like water in a pipe.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always describe conduction as vibration energy being passed from particle to particle, with each particle staying near its own fixed position.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying an insulator stops thermal energy transfer completely.
common_mistakes.why: Insulators are introduced by contrast with conductors as 'poor at transferring', which is easy to round down to 'transfers nothing at all'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Say explicitly that an insulator transfers energy much more slowly than a conductor, not that it blocks transfer entirely.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining why metal feels cold by saying it is actually colder, or that it stores extra cold.
common_mistakes.why: The strong sensation of cold feels like it should correspond to an actual temperature difference.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the two objects are stated to be at the same temperature; if so, explain the sensation using the rate of energy transfer, not a stored quantity of heat or cold.

exam_notes: When explaining conduction, always state clearly that particles stay in place and that it is vibration energy (and, in metals, electrons) that moves.
Describe an insulator as transferring energy slowly, never as blocking transfer completely.
A full explanation of why metals conduct well at this level must mention delocalised/mobile electrons, not just 'metals are good conductors' as an unexplained fact.

summary.big_idea: Conduction transfers thermal energy through a solid by particles passing vibration energy to their neighbours while staying in place, and metals conduct especially well because mobile delocalised electrons carry energy through the structure much faster than vibration alone.
key_points: A conductor transfers thermal energy quickly; an insulator transfers it only slowly, not never.
In conduction, particles stay near their fixed positions; vibration energy, not the particles, moves along the material.
Metals have mobile delocalised electrons that drift quickly and carry extra energy, in addition to particle-to-particle vibration.
An object feeling colder to touch does not necessarily mean it is at a lower temperature; it may simply conduct energy away faster.
Good design often pairs a conductor (for fast transfer) with an insulator (for slow transfer) in the same object, such as a saucepan.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Conduction moves vibration energy from particle to particle, never the particles themselves; metals conduct fastest because mobile electrons carry extra energy along; and 'feels colder' is about the rate of energy transfer, not necessarily the actual temperature.

objectives.statement: Describe convection as the transfer of thermal energy through the bulk movement of a liquid or a gas, and identify convection currents in everyday liquid and gas examples.
Explain convection in terms of heating causing a region of fluid to expand, become less dense than its surroundings, and rise, with denser surrounding fluid moving in to replace it.

prerequisites.statement: State that heating a solid, liquid or gas at constant pressure generally makes it expand, because its particles settle further apart on average.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Convection is explained entirely through a heated region of fluid expanding and becoming less dense; without the expansion idea from the previous lesson, density change has no starting cause.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate density as mass divided by volume, and compare the densities of two samples.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Explaining why a warmer region of fluid rises depends on comparing its density with the surrounding cooler fluid's density, so the density calculation and comparison skill from density and the particle model needs to already be secure.

diagnostic_items.question: (a) A sample of oil has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 300 cm³. Calculate its density, and give the unit. (b) The same sample is warmed so that it expands to a volume of 310 cm³, with none of it lost. State whether its density increases, decreases or stays the same, and give a reason.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: (a) Density $=\dfrac{m}{V}=\dfrac{240}{300}=0.80\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. (b) The density decreases, because the same mass now occupies a larger volume, so there is less mass in each cubic centimetre.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has multiplied instead of dividing, so the definition of density as mass per unit volume is not yet secure.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The density stays the same, because the mass has not changed.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is treating density as another word for mass and is not tracking the volume at all.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The density increases, because the warm oil's particles are moving faster.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is linking density to particle speed rather than to how much mass is packed into a given volume.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that density can be calculated as mass divided by volume and, more importantly, that expanding at constant mass is recognised as lowering the density. Every explanation in this lesson depends on that second step.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise two or three density calculations where the mass is held fixed and the volume is changed, saying out loud each time what has happened to the mass, to the volume and to the density, before connecting any of it to convection.

theory_blocks.title: A heated fluid starts moving
theory_blocks.body:
If a drop of food colouring is placed in a beaker of water and the beaker is then gently heated from below at one point, the colouring does not just spread evenly outward: it is swept upward above the heated spot, moves sideways near the surface, and sinks back down elsewhere, tracing out a loop.

This moving pattern is a [[blue:**convection current**]], and it only happens in liquids and gases, never in solids, because it requires a whole region of fluid to physically move from one place to another.

This is the key difference between convection and conduction. In conduction, particles stay near their fixed positions and only vibration energy passes between them.

In convection, the fluid itself — its actual particles — physically travels from one place to another, carrying its energy along with it as it moves.

theory_blocks.title: Tracing a complete convection loop

assets.caption: A complete convection loop in a container of fluid heated at one point on its base. Fluid above the heat source warms, expands and is pushed upward by denser fluid sinking around it (1-2); it then cools and sinks at the sides (3), before flowing back along the base to be heated again (4), closing the loop.
assets.purpose: Make the full four-stage convection loop explicit, rather than only showing 'warm fluid rises', directly supporting the worked-rule procedure for describing a convection current completely.

theory_blocks.title: Convection needs a fluid; solids don't convect
theory_blocks.body:
Convection depends entirely on [[blue:a region of material being able to physically flow past the material around it]], carrying its particles — and their energy — to a new place.

In a liquid or a gas, particles are free to slide past or move around one another, so this bulk flow is possible.

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and cannot move past their neighbours, so no region of a solid can physically relocate: [[red:a solid cannot convect]].

This is why a heated solid relies entirely on conduction (passing vibration energy, and in metals, mobile electrons, from particle to particle) rather than on convection,

while a heated liquid or gas can make use of both bulk fluid movement (convection) and, more slowly, particle-to-particle energy transfer within the fluid itself.

theory_blocks.title: Convection in gases: heating a room
theory_blocks.body:
Convection is not limited to liquids: it works the same way in gases. A room radiator heats the air immediately around and above it;

this air expands, becomes less dense than the surrounding room air, and is pushed upward by the denser, cooler air sinking around it.

The warm air spreads out near the ceiling, gradually cools as it loses energy to its surroundings, becomes denser, and sinks back down on the far side of the room, before flowing back across the floor toward the radiator — exactly the same four-stage loop as in a heated liquid, just with air as the fluid instead of water.

This is why a radiator placed low on a wall can still warm an entire room: the convection current it sets up circulates air throughout the space, not just immediately next to the radiator itself.

theory_blocks.title: Density, not a pulling force, explains why warm fluid rises
theory_blocks.body:
Heating a region of fluid makes it expand (as in the previous lesson), so the same mass of fluid now occupies a larger volume, which means its density — mass per unit volume — is lower than it was before, and lower than the surrounding fluid that has not been heated.

Water's density, for example, falls from about $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ near $4\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to around $960\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ near $100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: noticeably less dense when hot.

Gravity pulls every fluid downward, and it pulls more strongly, per unit volume, on the denser, cooler surrounding fluid than on the less dense, warmer fluid.

As a result, the denser cooler fluid sinks down and spreads beneath the warmer fluid, physically pushing the less dense warm fluid upward and out of the way as it does so.

The warm fluid therefore rises not because heat itself pulls it up, but because it is comparatively light for its volume and gets pushed aside by the heavier fluid sinking around it.

keywords.definition: The transfer of thermal energy through the bulk physical movement of a liquid or a gas.
A continuous looping flow of fluid, driven by density differences caused by uneven heating.
Mass per unit volume of a substance; a key quantity compared between warmer and cooler regions of fluid in convection.
The downward movement of denser, cooler fluid, which pushes less dense, warmer fluid upward as it descends.
The physical travel of a whole region of material from one place to another, as opposed to energy alone passing between fixed particles.

worked_examples.statement: **Observing a convection current.** A beaker of water has a crystal of purple dye dropped to the bottom, directly above a small heating point. Describe what is observed as the water is gently heated, and name the process responsible.
knowns: dye is released from the bottom, directly above the heat source
the water is gently and steadily heated at that point
reasoning: The water directly above the heat source warms, expands, and becomes less dense than the surrounding water.
Denser, cooler water sinks around it and pushes the warmed, dyed water upward, which then spreads out and eventually sinks again elsewhere as it cools.
worked_examples.solution: A stream of purple dye is seen rising from the heated point, spreading out near the surface, and sinking back down further away, tracing out a looping path through the water. This process is convection.
worked_examples.interpretation: The dye makes the otherwise invisible bulk movement of the water visible, directly showing that the water itself, not just energy, is travelling around the loop.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the dye as simply 'spreading out evenly' (as in diffusion), rather than following the directed, looping path that convection actually produces.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing densities.** Two $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ samples of water are taken from the same tank: a warm sample near the heater has a mass of $96\,\mathrm{g}$, and a cool sample from elsewhere in the tank has a mass of $100\,\mathrm{g}$. Calculate the density of each sample, and state which sample would tend to rise if the two were brought into contact.
reasoning: Use density $=$ mass $\div$ volume for each sample.
The less dense sample is pushed upward by the denser sample sinking around it.
worked_examples.solution:
Warm sample: $96 \div 100 = 0.96\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Cool sample: $100 \div 100 = 1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

Since the warm sample is less dense ($0.96\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} < 1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), it would be pushed upward by the denser cool sample sinking around it.
worked_examples.interpretation: This connects the density-calculation skill directly to the convection explanation: the numerical comparison, not just 'warm feels lighter', is what determines which fluid rises.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the warm sample rises simply because it is warm, without actually comparing the two calculated densities.

worked_examples.statement: **A sealed box, no gravity.** A thought experiment: a sealed box of air, with a small heater at its centre, is taken into deep space where there is effectively no gravity. The heater is switched on. Explain whether a normal convection current would be expected to form, and why.
knowns: heater at the centre of a sealed box of air
reasoning: Convection depends on denser, cooler fluid sinking and pushing less dense, warmer fluid out of the way.
Sinking specifically means being pulled down more strongly by gravity, so if there is no meaningful gravity, there is nothing to make the denser fluid sink preferentially over the less dense fluid.
worked_examples.solution:
No normal convection current would be expected to form. The heated air would still expand and become less dense locally, but without gravity to pull the denser surrounding air down more strongly than the less dense warm air,

there is no force to push the warm air in any particular direction, so a directed looping current like the ones seen on Earth would not develop.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This isolates gravity's role explicitly: density difference alone is not enough for convection;

gravity acting differently on fluid of different densities is what actually drives the motion, directly ruling out the idea that heat itself pulls fluid upward.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming warm air would still rise out of habit, without checking what rising actually depends on (gravity acting on a density difference).

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining a radiator's placement.** Room radiators are almost always fitted low down on a wall, close to the floor, rather than high up near the ceiling. Using the idea of a convection loop, explain why this placement is more effective at warming the whole room.
knowns: radiator is placed low, near the floor
the goal is to warm the whole room effectively
reasoning: Air heated by the radiator expands, becomes less dense, and is pushed upward by denser air sinking around it, starting a convection loop from low down.

If the radiator were instead placed high up, the air it directly warms would already be near the top of the room, with little denser air left above it to push it further;

much of the room below would then be heated only slowly, by conduction and by cooler air eventually sinking into contact with it.
worked_examples.interpretation: This applies the four-stage convection loop to a genuine design decision, showing why the loop's geometry, not just 'warm air rises', explains the placement choice.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the placement only as 'heat rises, so put the radiator low', without describing the density-driven loop that actually distributes the warmth around the room.

guided_exercises.statement: A beaker of water is heated at one point on its base. Describe, in order, all four stages of the convection loop that forms, starting from the fluid directly above the heated point.
hints: Start with what happens to the fluid that is actually in contact with the heat source.
Think about what must happen on the way back down, not just on the way up, for the current to be a continuous loop.
Four distinct stages are needed: warming/expanding, being pushed up, cooling/sinking, and flowing back.
guided_exercises.answer: (1) Fluid directly above the heated point warms and expands, becoming less dense. (2) Denser, cooler fluid around it sinks and pushes this less dense fluid upward. (3) As the risen fluid moves away from the heat source it cools, becomes denser again, and sinks back down. (4) The sunk fluid flows back along the base toward the heated point, where it is warmed again, completing the loop.
common_errors: Stopping after stage (2) ('warm fluid rises') without describing how the fluid cools, sinks and returns to complete the loop.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Start with what happens to the fluid that is actually in contact with the heat source.

**Step 2 — Method:** Think about what must happen on the way back down, not just on the way up, for the current to be a continuous loop.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** (1) Fluid directly above the heated point warms and expands, becoming less dense. (2) Denser, cooler fluid around it sinks and pushes this less dense fluid upward. (3) As the risen fluid moves away from the heat source it cools, becomes denser again, and sinks back down. (4) The sunk fluid flows back along the base toward the heated point, where it is warmed again, completing the loop.

**Step 4 — Check:** Four distinct stages are needed: warming/expanding, being pushed up, cooling/sinking, and flowing back.

guided_exercises.statement: Two $200\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ samples of engine coolant are compared: a warm sample has a mass of $184\,\mathrm{g}$ and a cool sample has a mass of $200\,\mathrm{g}$. Calculate the density of each sample and state which would sink if the two were mixed together in the same container.
hints: Use density $=$ mass $\div$ volume for each sample separately.
The denser sample is the one that sinks, pushing the less dense sample upward.
Compare the two calculated density values directly before answering.
guided_exercises.answer: Warm sample: $184 \div 200 = 0.92\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Cool sample: $200 \div 200 = 1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The cool sample is denser ($1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} > 0.92\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), so it would sink, pushing the warm sample upward.
common_errors: Dividing volume by mass instead of mass by volume, which inverts the density values and could lead to the wrong sample being identified as denser.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Use density $=$ mass $\div$ volume for each sample separately.

**Step 2 — Method:** The denser sample is the one that sinks, pushing the less dense sample upward.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Warm sample: $184 \div 200 = 0.92\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Cool sample: $200 \div 200 = 1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The cool sample is denser ($1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} > 0.92\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), so it would sink, pushing the warm sample upward.

**Step 4 — Check:** Compare the two calculated density values directly before answering.

exercises.statement: State whether convection can happen in (a) a liquid, (b) a gas, (c) a rigid solid, and give a one-sentence reason for your answer to (c).
exercises.answer: (a) Yes. (b) Yes. (c) No, because a solid's particles are held in fixed positions and cannot flow past one another, so no region of it can physically move to a new place.
exercises.full_solution: Convection requires bulk fluid movement, which only liquids and gases can provide; solids rely on conduction instead.

exercises.statement: A student says, 'Convection is basically the same as conduction, except it happens in liquids and gases instead of solids.' Explain what is scientifically inaccurate about this statement.
exercises.answer: The statement is inaccurate because conduction and convection are different mechanisms, not the same mechanism applied to different states of matter. In conduction, particles stay near fixed positions and only vibration energy is passed between neighbours; in convection, the fluid's particles themselves physically move in bulk from one place to another, carrying their energy with them. A liquid or a gas can actually use both mechanisms (convection, plus slower particle-to-particle transfer within the fluid), while a solid can only conduct.
exercises.full_solution: The statement is inaccurate because conduction and convection are different mechanisms, not the same mechanism applied to different states of matter. In conduction, particles stay near fixed positions and only vibration energy is passed between neighbours; in convection, the fluid's particles themselves physically move in bulk from one place to another, carrying their energy with them. A liquid or a gas can actually use both mechanisms (convection, plus slower particle-to-particle transfer within the fluid), while a solid can only conduct.

exercises.statement: A fridge's cooling element is placed near the top of its interior, rather than near the bottom. Using the idea of density-driven convection, explain why this placement helps cool the whole fridge effectively, even though it seems to contradict the usual 'heater goes low' rule for radiators.
exercises.answer: The cooling element makes the air immediately around it colder, which makes that air denser than the air below it; this denser air sinks down through the fridge, pushing the less dense, warmer air below it upward to be cooled in turn near the top. Placing the cooling element high lets this density-driven sinking circulate cold air through the whole fridge, which is the opposite placement from a radiator because a radiator makes air less dense (so it should be placed low to let the warm air rise), while a cooling element makes air denser (so it should be placed high to let the cold air sink).
exercises.full_solution: The underlying principle (denser fluid sinks, less dense fluid rises) is the same in both cases; the sensible placement simply differs because a heater and a cooling element produce opposite density changes.

exercises.statement: Coastal areas often experience a 'sea breeze' on a sunny afternoon: wind blowing from the sea toward the land. During the day, the land heats up faster than the sea, so the air above the land becomes warmer than the air above the sea. Using the idea of density-driven convection, explain why this temperature difference produces a breeze blowing from sea to land at ground level.
exercises.answer: The land heats up faster than the sea during the day, so the air above the land warms, expands and becomes less dense than the air above the cooler sea. The denser, cooler air above the sea then moves in (at ground level, as the sea breeze) to push the less dense air above the land upward, exactly as in the convection loop studied in this lesson, but on the scale of the coastline rather than a single room or beaker.
exercises.full_solution: The land heats up faster than the sea during the day, so the air above the land warms, expands and becomes less dense than the air above the cooler sea. The denser, cooler air above the sea then moves in (at ground level, as the sea breeze) to push the less dense air above the land upward, exactly as in the convection loop studied in this lesson, but on the scale of the coastline rather than a single room or beaker.

exam_questions.statement: A beaker of water is heated steadily at one point on its base. (a) Describe the complete convection loop that forms, in order. (b) Explain, in terms of density, why the heated water rises rather than staying where it is heated.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The water directly above the heated point warms and expands, becoming less dense; denser, cooler water around it sinks and pushes this less dense water upward; as the risen water moves away from the heat source it cools and becomes denser again, sinking back down; the sunk water then flows back along the base to the heated point, completing the loop. (b) The heated water expands and so becomes less dense than the surrounding cooler water; gravity pulls the denser, cooler water down more strongly per unit volume than it pulls the less dense warm water, so the cooler water sinks and physically pushes the warm water upward out of the way.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The water directly above the heated point warms and expands, becoming less dense; denser, cooler water around it sinks and pushes this less dense water upward; as the risen water moves away from the heat source it cools and becomes denser again, sinking back down; the sunk water then flows back along the base to the heated point, completing the loop. (b) The heated water expands and so becomes less dense than the surrounding cooler water; gravity pulls the denser, cooler water down more strongly per unit volume than it pulls the less dense warm water, so the cooler water sinks and physically pushes the warm water upward out of the way.
mark_scheme: States that the heated water warms, expands and becomes less dense.
States that denser, cooler water sinks and pushes the less dense water upward.
States that the risen water cools, becomes denser, and sinks elsewhere, then flows back to the heat source.
States that the warm water is less dense than the surrounding water.
Explains that gravity acting on the denser surrounding water (making it sink) is what pushes the less dense warm water upward, not heat acting as a direct upward force.
common_errors: Describing only the rising stage of the loop and omitting the cooling, sinking and return-flow stages needed for a complete answer to part (a).

exam_questions.statement: A student argues that a convection current could form inside a heated metal block, in the same way as in a heated liquid. (a) State whether the student is correct. (b) Explain your answer in terms of the particles in a solid. (c) State the mechanism that does transfer thermal energy through the metal block instead.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The student is not correct. (b) A solid's particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and vibrate about those positions, but they cannot flow or move past one another, so no region of the solid can physically travel to a new place, which convection requires. (c) Conduction, in which vibration energy (and, in a metal, mobile delocalised electrons) is passed from particle to particle while each particle stays near its fixed position.
exam_questions.full_solution: This tests the direct contrast between convection (requires bulk flow) and conduction (particles stay fixed) established earlier in this lesson.
mark_scheme: States the student is not correct.
States that a solid's particles are fixed in position and cannot flow past one another.
Links this directly to why bulk movement (required for convection) is impossible in a solid.
Names conduction as the mechanism that does operate in the solid.
common_errors: Stating correctly that the student is wrong but failing to explain why in terms of fixed particle positions, instead simply restating 'solids can't convect' as an unexplained fact.

challenge_questions.statement: A test tube is filled with water and a small piece of ice is held near the bottom by a loose metal gauze. The water near the top of the tube is heated with a flame until it boils, yet the ice at the bottom takes a long time to melt. (a) Explain why heating the water at the top does not set up a convection current that would carry energy down to the ice. (b) Explain why very little energy reaches the ice by conduction instead. (c) Predict what happens if the flame is moved to the bottom of the tube, and explain your prediction in terms of density. (d) Explain why the ice has to be held down by the gauze at all.
hints: A convection current only forms if the warmed fluid ends up below cooler, denser fluid.
Think about where the warmed, less dense water is already sitting when the flame is at the top.
In (d), compare the density of ice with the density of liquid water.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The water heated at the top expands and becomes less dense than the cooler water beneath it. Less dense fluid stays above denser fluid, so the warmed water simply remains at the top and nothing circulates downwards; there is no convection current to carry energy to the ice. (b) Water is a poor thermal conductor, and so is the glass of the tube, so conduction can only pass energy slowly down the column of water. (c) With the flame at the bottom the ice melts far more quickly. The water at the bottom is heated, expands, becomes less dense than the water above it and rises; the cooler, denser water above sinks to take its place, and this convection loop carries energy through the whole tube, including past the ice. (d) Ice is less dense than liquid water, so a loose piece would float straight to the top of the tube, which is exactly where the flame is; the gauze keeps it at the bottom so that the test is actually about how energy travels down through the water.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The whole question rests on one rule: a convection current only forms when the heated, less dense fluid has denser fluid above it to swap places with. Heating at the top leaves the less dense water already in the place it would rise to, so the fluid does not circulate and only conduction is left, which in water is very slow. Heating at the bottom gives the classic loop: warmed water rises, cooler denser water sinks, and energy is carried through the bulk of the liquid. Part (d) is a check on the same density idea in a different guise, since ice floats for exactly the reason a warmed region of water rises.
common_errors: Saying that heat 'rises', rather than that less dense warmed fluid rises; it is the fluid that moves, and only when there is denser fluid above it.
Assuming conduction through water will do the job in a reasonable time, when water is a poor conductor.
Forgetting part (d) entirely, or claiming the gauze is there to stop the ice being heated directly by the flame.

mcq.stem: Why does warm air actually rise above a radiator?

options.text: The warm air is less dense than the surrounding cooler air, which sinks and pushes the warm air upward.
Heat is a force that pulls the warm air directly upward.
options.why_wrong: treats heat as a force with its own direction, when heat is a transfer of energy, not a directional pulling force.

options.text: The warm air molecules are individually lighter than cold air molecules.
options.why_wrong: confuses the mass of individual molecules (unchanged by temperature) with the density of the air overall, which changes because of expansion, not molecule mass.

options.text: Warm air always moves toward the ceiling regardless of the air around it.
options.why_wrong: ignores the surrounding air entirely, when rising specifically depends on a density comparison with the surrounding fluid.

mcq.explanation: Rising happens because the warm, expanded air is less dense than the surrounding air, which sinks (pulled by gravity) and pushes the warm air upward as it does; nothing pulls the warm air up directly.

mcq.stem: A metal block is heated strongly at one end. Why does no convection current form inside the block?

options.text: Metal is always too cold for convection to start.
options.why_wrong: confuses temperature with the actual requirement for convection, which is about whether particles can flow, not about how hot or cold the material is.

options.text: A solid's particles are fixed in position and cannot flow past one another, so no region of it can physically move.
Metal particles are too heavy to be pushed by gravity.
options.why_wrong: misapplies the density/gravity reasoning from fluids to particles in a solid, where the real obstacle is that particles are fixed in position, not their individual weight.

options.text: Convection only happens below room temperature.
options.why_wrong: invents an unrelated temperature restriction with no basis in the actual requirement (fluid particles able to flow).

mcq.explanation: Convection requires bulk movement of material; a solid's fixed particle positions make this impossible, so solids conduct instead of convecting.

mcq.stem: Two equal-volume samples of the same liquid have different temperatures. Sample P has a mass of $94\,\mathrm{g}$ and sample Q has a mass of $100\,\mathrm{g}$, both for a volume of $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Which sample would rise if they were brought together, and why?

options.text: Sample Q, because it has the greater mass.
options.why_wrong: compares mass alone, ignoring that both samples share the same volume, so density (mass divided by volume) is what actually determines which one rises.

options.text: Sample Q, because its density ($1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) is higher, and denser fluid rises.
options.why_wrong: gets the direction backwards: the denser sample sinks and the less dense sample is pushed upward, so Q would sink, not rise.

options.text: Sample P, because its density ($0.94\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) is lower than sample Q's ($1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$).
Neither; equal volumes always rise and sink together.
options.why_wrong: ignores that equal volumes can still have different densities if their masses differ, which is exactly the case described.

mcq.explanation: Density $=$ mass $\div$ volume: sample P is $94\div100=0.94\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and sample Q is $100\div100=1.00\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$; the less dense sample (P) is pushed upward by the denser sample (Q) sinking around it.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes convection from conduction?

options.text: In convection, only energy passes between particles that stay in place; in conduction, the whole material physically moves.
options.why_wrong: swaps the two mechanisms: it is conduction where particles stay in place, and convection where the fluid physically moves.

options.text: Convection and conduction both involve the same bulk movement of material, just in different states of matter.
options.why_wrong: claims the two mechanisms are the same process in different states of matter, when they are genuinely different mechanisms (bulk flow vs vibration handover).

options.text: Convection only transfers energy, never any material; conduction transfers material as well as energy.
options.why_wrong: gets both halves backwards: convection does transfer material (the fluid itself moves), while conduction transfers no material, only vibration energy.

options.text: In convection, the fluid itself physically moves, carrying its particles and their energy; in conduction, particles stay near fixed positions and only vibration energy is passed along.

mcq.explanation: Convection is bulk movement of fluid, carrying both particles and energy; conduction is energy (vibration, and in metals, electrons) passed between particles that stay near fixed positions.

flashcards.front: What is convection?
flashcards.back: The transfer of thermal energy through the bulk physical movement of a liquid or a gas, carrying particles and their energy from one place to another.

flashcards.front: What are the four stages of a complete convection loop?
flashcards.back: (1) Fluid near a heat source warms and expands; (2) it becomes less dense and is pushed upward by denser fluid sinking around it; (3) it cools and becomes denser as it moves away; (4) it sinks and flows back to the heat source.

flashcards.front: True or false: warm air rises because heat is a force that pulls it directly upward.
flashcards.back: False. Warm air rises because it is less dense than the surrounding cooler air, which sinks under gravity and pushes the warm air upward; heat itself is not a directional pulling force.

flashcards.front: How does convection differ from conduction?
flashcards.back: Convection physically moves the fluid itself, carrying particles and energy together; conduction keeps particles near fixed positions and only passes vibration energy (and, in metals, electrons) between them.

flashcards.front: Why are room radiators placed low on a wall rather than high up?
flashcards.back: A low radiator heats air near the floor, which rises as it becomes less dense, setting up a full convection loop that circulates warm air through the whole room; a high radiator would not drive this loop as effectively.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Hot air rises because heat itself pulls it upward, like an invisible force dragging it up.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Heat is often spoken about as if it were a substance or a force with its own direction ('heat rises'), which makes an upward pull sound like the natural cause.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says 'heat pulls the air up' or 'heat makes things float upward' without mentioning density at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: Nothing pulls the warm fluid upward directly. The warm, expanded fluid is simply less dense than the cooler fluid around it, so the denser surrounding fluid sinks beneath it (pulled down by gravity more strongly, per unit volume, than the less dense warm fluid), pushing the less dense warm fluid upward as it does so. The movement is caused by a density difference acting together with gravity, not by heat acting as its own upward force.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly: what would happen to a sealed bubble of warm air if gravity did not exist at all? Without gravity pulling the denser surrounding fluid down, there would be nothing to push the warm fluid up, showing that gravity and density, not heat itself, cause the rise.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Convection happens the same way in a heated rigid solid as it does in a liquid or a gas.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Having just studied conduction in solids, it is tempting to assume the next transfer mechanism also applies to solids in the same way.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes 'convection currents' inside a heated metal bar or other solid object.
misconceptions.correct_model: Convection requires bulk movement of the heated material itself, with less dense regions physically flowing past denser regions. A rigid solid's particles are fixed in position and cannot flow past one another, so a solid cannot convect; solids transfer thermal energy by conduction instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would need to be true of a material's particles for a whole region of it to physically move to a new place, then check whether a solid's particles can do that.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In convection, only energy moves from place to place; the fluid itself stays where it is.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Conduction, studied in the previous lesson, transfers only energy while particles stay in place, so it is easy to assume every thermal transfer mechanism works the same way.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes convection as 'energy passing through the liquid' without mentioning the liquid or gas itself physically moving.
misconceptions.correct_model: Convection is different from conduction precisely because the fluid itself physically moves: warmer, less dense fluid actually travels upward, carrying its particles (and their energy) with it, while cooler, denser fluid actually travels to take its place. This bulk movement of material, not just energy passing between fixed particles, is what defines convection.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast the two mechanisms directly: in conduction, particles stay put and energy is handed along; in convection, ask what is different about a food colouring drop added to water heated at the base, which visibly travels with the current rather than staying still.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining convection as 'heat rises' without mentioning density at all.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday language treats heat as if it naturally travels upward on its own.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always explain rising in terms of a density comparison with the surrounding fluid, pushed by gravity acting on the denser fluid, not as heat acting as an upward force.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing convection currents inside a heated solid object.
common_mistakes.why: It is easy to assume every thermal transfer mechanism applies to every state of matter equally.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check first whether the material is a liquid, a gas, or a solid: only a fluid that can flow can convect; a solid conducts instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing convection as energy moving while the fluid itself stays still.
common_mistakes.why: Conduction, studied immediately before this lesson, transfers only energy between fixed particles, which can bleed into how convection is described.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that in convection the fluid's own particles physically travel to a new place, carrying their energy with them, unlike in conduction.

exam_notes: A full description of convection names all four loop stages (warm/expand, rise, cool/sink, return), not just 'warm fluid rises'.
An explanation of why warm fluid rises must refer to density and to the denser surrounding fluid sinking, never to heat as a direct upward-pulling force.
If asked whether a solid can convect, answer in terms of fixed particle positions preventing bulk flow, and name conduction as the mechanism the solid uses instead.

summary.big_idea: Convection transfers thermal energy by the bulk physical movement of a liquid or a gas: heating makes a region of fluid expand and become less dense, and denser surrounding fluid, pulled down more strongly by gravity, sinks and pushes it upward, driving a continuous four-stage loop that only a fluid, never a rigid solid, can sustain.
key_points: Convection moves the fluid itself, carrying particles and their energy, unlike conduction, which only passes energy between fixed particles.
A heated region of fluid expands, becomes less dense, and is pushed upward by denser surrounding fluid sinking under gravity.
A complete convection description has four stages: warm/expand, rise, cool/sink, return flow.
Only liquids and gases can convect; a solid's fixed particle positions prevent any bulk flow.
Convection works the same way in gases (e.g. a heated room) as in liquids (e.g. a heated beaker of water).
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Warm fluid rises because it is less dense and is pushed upward by denser cool fluid sinking under gravity, never because heat pulls it up directly, and the convection loop is only complete once the risen fluid cools, sinks and flows back.

06_Thermal_radiation_and_choosing_transf.title: Thermal radiation and choosing transfer controls
06_Thermal_radiation_and_choosing_transf.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Explain that thermal (infrared) radiation can transfer energy without a medium, and compare how dull/black and shiny/light surfaces absorb and emit radiation.
Design a fair comparison of absorbers and emitters, and use the idea of absorbed and emitted radiation to explain the Earth's overall radiation balance.
Select and justify which of conduction, convection and radiation dominates in a given everyday context, and explain how an object's design can control more than one mechanism at once.

prerequisites.statement: Describe conduction as particles passing on vibration energy while staying in fixed positions, and convection as the bulk movement of a liquid or a gas.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson's final skill is choosing between all three transfer mechanisms, so conduction and convection need to already be clearly understood and distinguishable before radiation is added as a third option.

prerequisites.statement: Use $Q=mc\Delta T$ to calculate the energy absorbed by a known mass of a substance from its temperature rise.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Comparing how much energy two different surfaces absorb from radiation is measured through the temperature rise of a known mass of water behind each surface, so this calculation skill is used directly in this lesson's experiments.

diagnostic_items.question: (a) Describe, in terms of particles, how energy is transferred from the hot end of a metal bar to its cold end by conduction. (b) Explain why convection cannot happen inside that solid bar.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: (a) The particles at the hot end vibrate more vigorously and pass energy on to their neighbours as they push against them; the particles themselves stay in their fixed positions, so only the energy moves along the bar. In a metal there are also mobile (delocalised) electrons, which move through the metal and carry energy much faster, which is why metals conduct so well. (b) Convection is energy carried by the bulk movement of the material itself, which needs particles that are free to move from place to place. In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and cannot flow, so there is nothing to carry energy that way.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The hot particles move along the bar to the cold end, taking their energy with them.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is describing convection, so conduction and convection are not yet distinguished; this lesson's final skill is choosing between the mechanisms, which needs them to be separate ideas.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The heat flows along the bar like a liquid.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is treating heat as a substance rather than as energy passed on between particles, so no particle-level reason is available for either mechanism.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Convection could happen in the bar if it were hot enough to glow.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has not tied convection to the ability of the material to flow; only melting the bar would make convection possible, and then it would no longer be a solid.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that conduction and convection are held as two distinct mechanisms, with the right particle picture for each. This lesson adds radiation as a third option and then asks students to choose between all three, which is impossible if the first two are blurred.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit the conduction and convection lessons and write one sentence for each mechanism that says what moves: in conduction the energy moves but the particles stay put; in convection the particles themselves move, carrying their energy with them.

theory_blocks.title: Radiation needs no medium at all
theory_blocks.body:
Conduction needs particles to pass vibration energy along, and convection needs particles free to flow in bulk; both are completely impossible in a true vacuum, where there are no particles at all.

Yet energy from the Sun clearly reaches the Earth, crossing the huge, essentially empty vacuum of space in between. This energy cannot be arriving by conduction or convection, since neither can operate without particles.

The transfer mechanism that explains this is [[blue:**thermal radiation**]]: energy carried as electromagnetic waves (mainly in the infrared part of the spectrum for objects at everyday temperatures), which do not need any particles or medium to travel at all.

This is the key feature that sets radiation apart from the previous two lessons' mechanisms: it is the only one of the three that works just as well through a vacuum as through air.

theory_blocks.title: Surface finish controls absorption and emission
theory_blocks.body:
How well a surface absorbs or emits thermal radiation depends strongly on its finish, independently of what the object is made of underneath.

A **dull, black** surface is a good absorber of incoming radiation (it takes in radiation rather than reflecting it away) and, separately, a good emitter of radiation (it readily radiates its own thermal energy away).

A **shiny, light-coloured** surface is a poor absorber (it reflects most incoming radiation instead of absorbing it) and a poor emitter (it radiates its own thermal energy away only slowly).

This is why a shiny kettle stays hotter for longer than an identical matte black kettle at the same starting temperature: the shiny surface emits its stored thermal energy away only slowly, while the black surface emits it quickly.

It is also why, in sunlight, a matte black object absorbs radiation and warms up faster than an identical shiny object, even though the shiny surface might look as if it is 'catching' more light.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing the dominant transfer mechanism
theory_blocks.body:
To decide which thermal transfer mechanism dominates in a given situation, check these questions in order: **Is a vacuum involved, or could the transfer happen even with no particles present at all?** If yes, radiation must be involved, since it is the only mechanism that needs no medium.

**Is the material a fluid (a liquid or a gas) that is free to flow in bulk?** If yes, convection is likely to dominate, since it is usually much faster than conduction alone within a fluid.

**Is the material a solid, or is bulk flow prevented?** If yes, conduction is the mechanism available, carried by particle vibration (and, in a metal, mobile electrons).

Many real objects are designed to control more than one mechanism at once, each with a different design feature.

A vacuum flask is a clear example: the vacuum gap between its inner and outer walls prevents both conduction and convection (both need particles, and the vacuum has none), while a shiny coating on the inner wall reduces radiation (a shiny surface is a poor emitter and a poor absorber).

No single feature controls all three mechanisms; each needs its own targeted design choice.

theory_blocks.title: Designing a fair absorber/emitter comparison

assets.caption: A fair test of absorption: two cans of the same size and shape, each holding the same mass of water at the same starting temperature and fitted with a thermometer, placed the same distance $d$ from the same radiant heater, so that only the outer surface finish differs. After the same length of time, the can whose water shows the larger temperature rise is the one with the better absorbing surface.
assets.purpose: Show a paired surface experiment with every controlled variable made explicit: the equal heater-to-can distances are marked along the two sight lines themselves, and each can carries the thermometer that the temperature rise is read from, so the fair-comparison requirement for radiation experiments is clear.

theory_blocks.title: The Earth's radiation balance
theory_blocks.body:
The Earth receives radiation from the Sun (mostly visible light and some infrared and ultraviolet) and, like every object, also emits its own thermal radiation outward (mostly infrared, since the Earth is far cooler than the Sun).

The Earth's average temperature stays roughly steady over long periods because, on average, the rate at which it absorbs radiation from the Sun roughly balances the rate at which it emits radiation back out into space.

Not all incoming solar radiation is absorbed: some is reflected straight back into space by clouds, ice, snow and other light-coloured or reflective surfaces, just as a white or shiny surface reflects more radiation than a dull black one.

If the balance between absorbed and emitted radiation shifts — for example, if more radiation is absorbed than is emitted,

or if emitted radiation is increasingly trapped rather than escaping to space — the Earth's average temperature changes until a new balance is reached.

keywords.definition: The transfer of thermal energy as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared), which needs no particles or medium and can cross a vacuum.
A surface that takes in incoming radiation; dull, black surfaces are good absorbers, while shiny surfaces are poor absorbers.
A surface that radiates its own thermal energy away; dull, black surfaces are good emitters, while shiny surfaces are poor emitters.
The condition in which a body's rate of absorbing radiation roughly equals its rate of emitting radiation, keeping its average temperature roughly steady.
A test of two surfaces' absorption or emission that keeps every variable the same except the surface finish being investigated.

worked_examples.statement: **Which surface absorbs better?** A matte black metal plate and a shiny silver metal plate of identical size are placed in the same sunlight for the same length of time. State which plate is expected to reach the higher temperature, and why.
knowns: identical size and material, except surface finish
unknowns: which plate reaches a higher temperature
reasoning: A dull, black surface is a good absorber of radiation; a shiny surface is a poor absorber, reflecting most radiation away instead.
The plate that absorbs more radiation energy in the same time will warm up more.
worked_examples.solution: The matte black plate is expected to reach the higher temperature, because its surface absorbs incoming solar radiation well, while the shiny silver plate reflects most of the radiation away instead of absorbing it.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the most direct application of the absorber/emitter surface rule: identical objects, differing only in finish, responding differently to the same radiation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Predicting the shiny plate warms up more because it 'reflects more light toward itself' or looks more actively involved with the light, confusing visible glare with absorption.

worked_examples.statement: **Measuring absorbed energy.** Two identical cans, A (matte black) and B (shiny silver), each contain $0.200\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water starting at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Both are placed the same distance from the same radiant heater for the same time. Can A's water reaches $32\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; can B's water reaches $23\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Take the specific heat capacity of water as $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$. Calculate the energy absorbed by the water in each can, and state how many times more energy can A absorbed than can B.
reasoning: Use $Q=mc\Delta T$ separately for each can, since the mass and specific heat capacity are the same but the temperature rise differs.
Divide the two results to find how many times greater can A's absorbed energy is.
worked_examples.solution: $Q_A = 0.200 \times 4200 \times 12 = 10\,080\,\mathrm{J}$. $Q_B = 0.200 \times 4200 \times 3 = 2520\,\mathrm{J}$. Ratio: $10\,080 \div 2520 = 4$, so can A (matte black) absorbed exactly $4$ times as much energy as can B (shiny silver).
worked_examples.interpretation:
This turns the qualitative absorber/emitter rule into a precise, fair, numerical comparison, exactly as the fair-test design requires: the only difference between the cans was surface finish,

so the $4\times$ difference in absorbed energy is attributed entirely to that.
worked_examples.common_mistake:
Comparing the two final temperatures directly ($32\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ vs $23\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) as if that ratio describes the energy absorbed,

rather than first finding the temperature rise ($\Delta T$) from the same starting temperature and only then calculating $Q$.

worked_examples.statement: **How a vacuum flask controls all three mechanisms.** A vacuum flask has a narrow vacuum gap between its inner and outer walls, and the inner wall facing the gap is coated with a shiny, reflective layer. Explain how this single design controls conduction, convection and radiation together.
knowns: vacuum gap between inner and outer walls
shiny reflective coating on the inner wall
reasoning: Both conduction and convection require particles; a vacuum contains essentially no particles.
Radiation does not require particles, so a vacuum alone cannot block it; a separate feature is needed.
worked_examples.solution:
The vacuum gap prevents both conduction (no particles are present to pass vibration energy across the gap) and convection (no fluid is present in the gap to form a bulk current).

Radiation, however, can cross a vacuum, so the vacuum gap alone does nothing to stop it; the shiny reflective coating on the inner wall addresses this separately, since a shiny surface is a poor absorber and a poor emitter, greatly reducing the radiation transferred across the gap.

Together, the two features target all three mechanisms, each with its own specific design choice.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a direct worked application of the idea that one design can control multiple mechanisms, but only through separate, mechanism-specific features, never through one single feature doing everything.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the vacuum alone is enough to keep the flask's contents hot, forgetting that radiation does not need a medium and so passes through a vacuum freely unless separately reduced.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing materials for a solar water heater.** A simple solar water heater consists of a metal pipe carrying water, painted matte black, mounted inside a glass-fronted box with a reflective (shiny) backing sheet and insulating foam around the back and sides. (a) Explain why the pipe is painted matte black rather than left shiny. (b) Explain why a reflective backing sheet is placed behind the pipe. (c) Explain why insulating foam, rather than a good thermal conductor, is used around the back and sides of the box.
reasoning: The pipe's job is to absorb as much radiation as possible to heat the water inside it.
The backing sheet's job is to reflect radiation that missed the pipe back toward it, rather than letting that radiation be absorbed by the back of the box or escape.
The foam's job is to reduce energy loss from the box to the surroundings, rather than to absorb or emit radiation.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Matte black is a good absorber of radiation, so painting the pipe black maximises how much of the incoming solar radiation the pipe absorbs and converts into thermal energy for the water inside.

(b) A shiny backing sheet reflects any solar radiation that passes by the pipe without being absorbed, redirecting it back toward the black pipe for a second chance at absorption, rather than letting it reflect away or be absorbed uselessly elsewhere.

(c) Insulating foam is a poor thermal conductor, so it reduces the rate of conduction (and, by trapping air, convection) of thermal energy out of the back and sides of the box to the cooler surroundings,

keeping the absorbed energy inside the box rather than letting it escape.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This question requires choosing a different mechanism-specific reason for each material: absorption (pipe), redirection of radiation (backing sheet), and reduced conduction/convection loss (foam),

rather than one generic 'keeps it warm' answer for all three.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Giving the same generic reason ('it keeps the heat in') for all three materials, rather than identifying the specific mechanism each one is designed to control.

guided_exercises.statement: A student wants to compare how well two identical mugs, one white and one dark green, emit thermal radiation. State at least three variables that must be kept the same between the two mugs for this to be a fair test, other than their colour.
hints: Think about what could affect how quickly a mug cools down, besides its colour.
Consider both the mug itself (size, material, starting condition) and its surroundings during the test.
A fair test changes only the one variable being investigated.
guided_exercises.answer: Any three of: the mugs' size and shape, the material they are made from, the mass/volume of liquid they contain, their starting temperature, the surrounding (room) temperature during the test, and their distance from any other heat sources or draughts.
common_errors: Naming the colour itself as something that must be kept the same, when colour is specifically the variable being tested, not controlled.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Think about what could affect how quickly a mug cools down, besides its colour.

**Step 2 — Method:** Consider both the mug itself (size, material, starting condition) and its surroundings during the test.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Any three of: the mugs' size and shape, the material they are made from, the mass/volume of liquid they contain, their starting temperature, the surrounding (room) temperature during the test, and their distance from any other heat sources or draughts.

**Step 4 — Check:** A fair test changes only the one variable being investigated.

guided_exercises.statement: A spacecraft orbiting the Earth has one side facing the Sun and one side facing away, with empty space (a vacuum) all around it. Explain how the sunward side can still become very hot and the shaded side very cold, even though there is no air at all around the spacecraft to transfer energy by conduction or convection.
hints: Identify which transfer mechanism, of the three studied in this unit, does not need any particles at all.
Think about what reaches the sunward side directly from the Sun across the vacuum of space.
Consider what the shaded side is not receiving, and what it may still be losing.
guided_exercises.answer: The sunward side heats up because it absorbs thermal radiation arriving directly from the Sun, and radiation can cross the vacuum of space with no particles needed at all, unlike conduction or convection. The shaded side receives no direct solar radiation (it faces away from the Sun) but can still emit its own thermal radiation out into space, so without a matching input of radiation to balance that loss, it can become very cold.
common_errors: Assuming no thermal transfer at all can happen in space, because conduction and convection are ruled out, without considering that radiation is still possible.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which transfer mechanism, of the three studied in this unit, does not need any particles at all.

**Step 2 — Method:** Think about what reaches the sunward side directly from the Sun across the vacuum of space.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The sunward side heats up because it absorbs thermal radiation arriving directly from the Sun, and radiation can cross the vacuum of space with no particles needed at all, unlike conduction or convection. The shaded side receives no direct solar radiation (it faces away from the Sun) but can still emit its own thermal radiation out into space, so without a matching input of radiation to balance that loss, it can become very cold.

**Step 4 — Check:** Consider what the shaded side is not receiving, and what it may still be losing.
