exercises.statement: State, for each pair, which surface is the better absorber of thermal radiation: (a) dull black or shiny silver, (b) matte dark green or polished chrome.
exercises.answer: (a) Dull black. (b) Matte dark green.
exercises.full_solution: In both pairs, the dull/dark, non-reflective surface is the better absorber; the shiny/polished surface reflects more radiation instead of absorbing it.

exercises.statement: A camping kettle is sold in both a matte black version and a shiny silver version, at the same price. Recommend which version a camper should buy if their main goal is to keep boiled water hot for as long as possible after taking it off the stove, and justify your answer.
exercises.answer: The camper should buy the shiny silver kettle, because a shiny surface is a poor emitter of thermal radiation, so it loses thermal energy to its surroundings by radiation more slowly than an identical matte black kettle would, keeping the water hot for longer.
exercises.full_solution: This reverses the usual 'black absorbs better' framing to the emission side: for keeping something hot, a poor emitter (shiny) is actually the better choice, not the better absorber (black).

exercises.statement: A cavity wall in a house has an air gap between its inner and outer brick layers, which is sometimes filled with foam insulation. Explain which thermal transfer mechanism the foam mainly targets, and why simply having an air gap (without foam) is less effective at reducing energy loss than a foam-filled gap.
exercises.answer: The foam mainly targets convection (and, to a lesser extent, conduction through the air). An open air gap still allows the air inside it to form convection currents, circulating warmth across the gap; foam insulation breaks the air up into many tiny trapped pockets, preventing it from flowing in bulk and so greatly reducing convection, while the foam material itself is also usually a poor conductor.
exercises.full_solution: The foam mainly targets convection (and, to a lesser extent, conduction through the air). An open air gap still allows the air inside it to form convection currents, circulating warmth across the gap; foam insulation breaks the air up into many tiny trapped pockets, preventing it from flowing in bulk and so greatly reducing convection, while the foam material itself is also usually a poor conductor.

exercises.statement: Firefighters' protective suits are often made with an outer layer that is light-coloured or has a reflective, metallic-looking finish, rather than being dark or black. Using what you know about surfaces and radiation, suggest why this design choice makes sense for a suit that must be worn near intense heat and flame.
exercises.answer: A light-coloured or reflective outer layer is a poor absorber of thermal radiation, so it reflects much of the intense radiant heat from flames and hot surfaces away from the firefighter, rather than absorbing it; a dark or black outer layer would absorb far more of that radiation, transferring more thermal energy toward the wearer and making the suit less protective.
exercises.full_solution: A light-coloured or reflective outer layer is a poor absorber of thermal radiation, so it reflects much of the intense radiant heat from flames and hot surfaces away from the firefighter, rather than absorbing it; a dark or black outer layer would absorb far more of that radiation, transferring more thermal energy toward the wearer and making the suit less protective.

exam_questions.statement: Two identical metal cans, X (painted matte black) and Y (painted shiny silver), each contain $0.150\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water starting at $18\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Both are placed the same distance from the same radiant heater for ten minutes. Can X's water reaches $38\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; can Y's water reaches $22\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Take the specific heat capacity of water as $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$. (a) Calculate the energy absorbed by the water in each can. (b) State which can absorbed more radiation, and explain why, in terms of surface finish.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Can X: $Q = 0.150\times4200\times(38-18) = 0.150\times4200\times20 = 12\,600\,\mathrm{J}$. Can Y: $Q = 0.150\times4200\times(22-18) = 0.150\times4200\times4 = 2520\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) Can X (matte black) absorbed more radiation, because a dull black surface is a good absorber of thermal radiation, while can Y's shiny silver surface reflects most of the radiation away instead of absorbing it.
exam_questions.full_solution: Each can's $\Delta T$ must be found from its own starting and final temperature before $Q=mc\Delta T$ is applied; the two $Q$ values are then compared to justify part (b).
mark_scheme: Calculates can X's temperature rise as $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and energy as $12\,600\,\mathrm{J}$.
Calculates can Y's temperature rise as $4\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and energy as $2520\,\mathrm{J}$.
States can X absorbed more radiation.
Explains using surface finish: the dull black surface is a good absorber of thermal radiation (1 mark); the shiny silver surface is a poor absorber / reflects most of the radiation (1 mark).
common_errors: Using $38\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $22\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ directly as $\Delta T$ instead of first subtracting the shared starting temperature of $18\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

exam_questions.statement: A homeowner is deciding how to reduce energy loss from their house. They are considering: (i) filling the cavity wall with foam insulation, (ii) fitting double-glazed windows with a trapped air/gas layer, and (iii) adding reflective foil behind radiators on external walls. For each measure, state the thermal transfer mechanism it is mainly designed to reduce, with a brief reason.
exam_questions.answer: (i) Cavity wall foam mainly reduces convection (and conduction through the air), by trapping air so it cannot circulate in bulk across the cavity. (ii) Double glazing mainly reduces conduction (and convection) through the window, since the trapped air/gas layer is a poor conductor and too thin/restricted to convect strongly. (iii) Reflective foil behind a radiator mainly reduces radiation loss through the wall, by reflecting radiant energy from the radiator back into the room instead of letting the wall absorb and conduct it outward.
exam_questions.full_solution: Each measure targets a different mechanism, directly testing the idea that no single feature controls every mechanism at once; a good answer names a different mechanism for each of the three measures.
mark_scheme: States cavity wall foam mainly targets convection (accept conduction as a secondary effect).
Gives a correct reason involving trapped air preventing bulk flow.
States double glazing mainly targets conduction (accept convection as a secondary effect) through the trapped layer.
States reflective foil mainly targets radiation, with a correct reason involving reflection back into the room.
Uses a different primary mechanism for each of the three measures, rather than repeating one mechanism for all three.
common_errors: Giving 'insulation' as a single undifferentiated reason for all three measures, without naming which specific mechanism each one targets.

challenge_questions.statement: In a hot desert, the ground becomes extremely hot during the day, but on a clear night the temperature can fall close to freezing. When the sky is cloudy, the same desert night stays much warmer. (a) Explain, in terms of emission and absorption of thermal radiation, why a clear desert night gets so cold. (b) Explain why cloud makes such a difference. (c) People living in such places often wear loose, light-coloured robes that cover most of the skin, rather than as little clothing as possible. Explain how this choice works on two different energy-transfer mechanisms at once. (d) A student says the robes 'must be hotter, because they stop the body losing heat'. Explain what this argument misses.
hints: Everything emits thermal radiation, and a hot surface emits a great deal of it. Where does the ground's radiation go on a clear night?
Clouds are not transparent to infrared radiation: think about what they do with the radiation that reaches them from below.
In (c), one mechanism is about the surface of the cloth and the Sun's radiation; the other is about the air between the cloth and the skin.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) During the day the ground absorbs a great deal of radiation from the Sun and becomes very hot. At night it goes on emitting thermal (infrared) radiation, and on a clear night that radiation travels straight out through the dry, cloudless air into space, with nothing sending any of it back. The ground emits far more energy than it receives, so its temperature falls sharply. (b) Cloud absorbs the infrared radiation emitted by the ground and re-emits radiation in all directions, so a large share of it is returned to the ground. The ground therefore receives much more radiation back than it does under a clear sky, the net loss is far smaller and the night stays warmer. (c) First, a light-coloured surface is a poor absorber and a good reflector of the Sun's radiation, so much less of it is absorbed than by dark cloth or bare skin, and covering the skin also keeps direct solar radiation off it. Second, the looseness lets air circulate between the cloth and the skin, so warm, moist air is carried away by convection and replaced, which also allows sweat to evaporate and cool the skin. (d) The argument treats the robe purely as an insulator between a warm body and cooler surroundings. In a desert at midday the surroundings are hotter than the body, so energy is arriving at the skin rather than leaving it, and the robe's job is to reduce what arrives by radiation while still allowing convection and evaporation to remove energy from the skin.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) and (b) are the same balance read twice: the ground's temperature falls when the radiation it emits exceeds the radiation it absorbs. A clear sky returns almost none of the emitted infrared, so the loss is large; cloud absorbs and re-emits it, returning much of it, so the net loss is small. (c) asks for two mechanisms rather than one: surface colour acts on radiation, and the loose fit acts on convection (and on evaporation from the skin). (d) is a check on direction: insulation reduces transfer both ways, so whether that helps or hurts depends on which way the energy is flowing, and in bright desert sun it is flowing towards the body.
common_errors: Saying the clear night is cold because 'there is no Sun', which does not explain why a cloudy night at the same place is warmer.
Describing cloud as 'trapping heat' without saying that it absorbs the infrared emitted by the ground and re-emits some of it downwards.
Answering (c) with surface colour only, and never mentioning the air circulating under the loose cloth.

mcq.stem: Why can thermal radiation from the Sun reach the Earth, crossing the vacuum of space, when conduction and convection could not?

options.text: Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves, which do not need particles or a medium to travel.
Space actually contains enough particles for conduction and convection to work slowly.
options.why_wrong: incorrectly claims space is not really a vacuum, when the near-total absence of particles in space is exactly why conduction and convection cannot work there.

options.text: The Sun is simply too large for a lack of medium to matter.
options.why_wrong: invents a size-based exemption with no physical basis for why a vacuum would stop mattering.

options.text: Radiation is a much weaker effect that only matters over huge distances like that from the Sun.
options.why_wrong: misdescribes radiation as a 'weak, long-distance-only' effect, when it is simply the only one of the three mechanisms that works without a medium, at any distance.

mcq.explanation: Thermal radiation is carried by electromagnetic waves, which need no particles at all, unlike conduction and convection, both of which require a medium.

mcq.stem: A matte black surface and a shiny silver surface, both at the same temperature, are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The shiny surface absorbs radiation better, because it visibly interacts more with light.
options.why_wrong: confuses visible glare (a sign of reflection) with absorption, which is the opposite effect.

options.text: The matte black surface is both a better absorber and a better emitter of thermal radiation than the shiny surface.
Both surfaces absorb and emit radiation equally well, since surface colour does not affect radiation.
options.why_wrong: denies that surface finish matters at all, contradicting the central rule of this lesson.

options.text: The shiny surface is a better emitter, but the matte black surface is a better absorber.
options.why_wrong: splits the two properties incorrectly; a good absorber is also a good emitter, and a poor absorber (shiny) is also a poor emitter, not the reverse pairing given here.

mcq.explanation: A dull, black surface is both a good absorber and a good emitter of thermal radiation; a shiny surface is poor at both, not split between the two.

mcq.stem: Two identical cans of water, one matte black and one shiny silver, both start at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and are placed the same distance from the same heater for the same time. The black can's water reaches $30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; the shiny can's water reaches $25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Both cans contain $0.100\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water (specific heat capacity $4200\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,^{\circ}C)}$). How many times more energy did the black can's water absorb than the shiny can's water?

options.text: $1.2$ times, found by comparing the final temperatures ($30\div25$).
options.why_wrong: incorrectly compares the final temperatures directly instead of the temperature rises from the shared starting temperature.

options.text: $4$ times, found by squaring the ratio of the temperature rises ($(10\div5)^2$).
options.why_wrong: invents a squaring step with no basis in $Q=mc\Delta T$, which is a direct proportionality, not a squared relationship.

options.text: $2$ times, found by comparing the correctly calculated temperature rises.
The two cans absorbed equal energy, since they are the same size.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the temperature rises (and so the absorbed energies) are clearly different, despite the cans being identical in size.

mcq.explanation: Black can: $\Delta T=10\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $Q=0.100\times4200\times10=4200\,\mathrm{J}$. Shiny can: $\Delta T=5\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $Q=0.100\times4200\times5=2100\,\mathrm{J}$. Ratio: $4200\div2100=2$.

mcq.stem: A vacuum flask keeps a drink hot using a vacuum gap and a shiny inner coating. Which statement correctly explains why both features are needed?

options.text: The vacuum gap alone would be enough, since it blocks all three transfer mechanisms.
options.why_wrong: incorrectly claims a vacuum blocks radiation too, when radiation needs no medium and can cross a vacuum freely.

options.text: The shiny coating blocks conduction and convection; the vacuum gap is needed separately to reduce radiation.
options.why_wrong: swaps the two features' roles; it is the vacuum that blocks conduction/convection, and the shiny coating that targets radiation, not the reverse.

options.text: Both features do the same job, so either one alone would be just as effective.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the two features target different mechanisms, so removing either one would leave that mechanism uncontrolled.

options.text: The vacuum gap blocks conduction and convection (both need particles); the shiny coating is needed separately to reduce radiation, which a vacuum cannot block.

mcq.explanation: A vacuum removes the particles conduction and convection both require, but radiation needs no particles and so is unaffected by a vacuum; the shiny coating is needed specifically to reduce radiation, since a shiny surface absorbs and emits it poorly.

flashcards.front: What is thermal radiation, and what makes it different from conduction and convection?
flashcards.back: Energy transferred as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared); unlike conduction and convection, it needs no particles or medium at all, so it can cross a vacuum.

flashcards.front: How do dull black and shiny surfaces compare as absorbers and emitters of thermal radiation?
flashcards.back: A dull black surface is a good absorber and a good emitter; a shiny surface is a poor absorber and a poor emitter, reflecting most radiation instead.

flashcards.front: True or false: a single insulating feature, like a vacuum gap, can control conduction, convection and radiation all at once.
flashcards.back: False. A vacuum gap blocks conduction and convection (both need particles) but not radiation, which needs no medium; a separate feature, such as a shiny coating, is needed to reduce radiation.

flashcards.front: What three questions help you choose the dominant thermal transfer mechanism in a situation?
flashcards.back: Is a vacuum involved (then radiation)? Is the material a fluid free to flow in bulk (then convection likely dominates)? Is it a solid, or is bulk flow prevented (then conduction)?

flashcards.front: Why is a solar water heater's pipe painted matte black, with a shiny sheet behind it?
flashcards.back: The matte black pipe absorbs incoming solar radiation well, converting it to thermal energy in the water; the shiny backing sheet reflects any radiation that misses the pipe back toward it, for a second chance at absorption.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Thermal radiation needs air (or some other medium) to travel through, like conduction and convection do.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Conduction and convection, studied in the previous two lessons, both need particles (a solid, liquid or gas) to work at all, so it is a reasonable-looking pattern to extend to radiation too.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims the Sun could not warm the Earth if space were a true vacuum, or that radiation 'needs something to carry it' the way sound needs air.
misconceptions.correct_model: Thermal (infrared) radiation is transferred as electromagnetic waves, which do not need any particles at all to travel; this is exactly why sunlight can cross the vacuum of space between the Sun and the Earth, unlike conduction and convection, which both require particles and cannot happen in a vacuum.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly how sunlight reaches Earth across empty space if radiation needed a medium, since space between the Sun and the Earth contains essentially no particles.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A shiny surface absorbs thermal radiation better than a dull black surface, because it 'catches more light'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Shiny surfaces visibly interact strongly with light (producing bright glare and reflections), which can be mistaken for absorbing more rather than reflecting more.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a shiny kettle will heat up faster in sunlight than a matte black one, or says shiny surfaces 'soak up' more radiation.
misconceptions.correct_model: A dull, black surface is a good absorber (and a good emitter) of thermal radiation; a shiny, light surface mostly reflects radiation instead of absorbing it, and is a poor emitter. The glare from a shiny surface is a sign of reflection, which is the opposite of absorption, not evidence of better absorption.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast what happens to incoming radiation at each surface directly: a dull black surface lets radiation in and converts it to internal energy (absorption); a shiny surface bounces radiation straight back off (reflection), which is why it stays cooler.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A single piece of insulation (such as a wall cavity or a flask's design) can only control one thermal transfer mechanism at a time.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Conduction, convection and radiation are taught and practised separately, lesson by lesson, which can leave the impression that controlling them also has to happen separately, in separate objects.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a vacuum flask or a cavity wall as working against only one mechanism, missing that its design features each target a different mechanism simultaneously.
misconceptions.correct_model: A single well-designed object can control multiple transfer mechanisms at once, with different features of its design each targeting a different mechanism. A vacuum flask, for example, uses a vacuum gap to prevent conduction and convection (since both need particles, and there are none in a vacuum) and a shiny inner surface to reduce radiation (since a shiny surface absorbs and emits radiation poorly), tackling all three mechanisms together in one design.
misconceptions.remediation: Take a real insulated design (a vacuum flask, a house wall) and ask, feature by feature, which specific mechanism each feature is aimed at, to show that several different features are needed for several different mechanisms.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming thermal radiation needs air or another medium to travel, like conduction and convection do.
common_mistakes.why: The two previous lessons' mechanisms both strictly require particles, making it a tempting (but incorrect) pattern to extend to radiation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that sunlight crossing the vacuum of space to reach Earth is direct evidence that radiation needs no medium at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting that a shiny surface absorbs radiation better because it 'catches more light'.
common_mistakes.why: Shiny surfaces visibly interact strongly with light through glare and reflection, which can be mistaken for strong absorption.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Separate reflection (what a shiny surface does) from absorption (what a dull black surface does); strong reflection is the opposite of strong absorption, not evidence for it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining an insulated design, like a vacuum flask, as if one single feature controls all three transfer mechanisms.
common_mistakes.why: Conduction, convection and radiation are easy to think of as one combined 'heat loss', rather than as three mechanisms needing three separate design responses.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: For any insulated design, identify a separate feature for each mechanism being controlled, and check that no mechanism has been left unaddressed.

exam_notes: If a question involves a vacuum, radiation is the only transfer mechanism that can still operate; say so explicitly.
Always pair 'good absorber' with 'good emitter' (dull black) and 'poor absorber' with 'poor emitter' (shiny); never split the two properties between the two surface types.
When asked to explain an insulated design with multiple features, identify a different mechanism for each feature rather than giving one generic 'keeps heat in' answer for all of them.

summary.big_idea: Thermal radiation is the only transfer mechanism that needs no medium at all, since it travels as electromagnetic waves; a surface's finish, not what it is made of, controls how well it absorbs and emits that radiation, and real designs must target conduction, convection and radiation separately, since no single feature controls all three at once.
key_points: Radiation needs no particles and can cross a vacuum, unlike conduction and convection.
Dull, black surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters; shiny surfaces are poor at both, reflecting radiation instead.
A fair comparison of surfaces controls every variable except the finish being tested, and can be measured numerically using $Q=mc\Delta T$.
The Earth's average temperature depends on a rough balance between absorbed solar radiation and emitted thermal radiation.
Controlling all three transfer mechanisms in one design (such as a vacuum flask) needs a separate, targeted feature for each mechanism.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Radiation is the only mechanism that crosses a vacuum; dull black absorbs and emits well, shiny does neither well; and a good insulated design always has a separate feature for each of conduction, convection and radiation, never just one feature for all three.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from thermal physics accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Which one of the following statements is not true? A The molecules in a solid vibrate about a fixed position. B The molecules in a liquid are arranged in a regular pattern. C The molecules in a gas exert negligibly small forces on each other, except during collisions. D The densities of most liquids are about 1000 times greater than those of gases because liquid molecules are much closer together than gas molecules. E The molecules of a gas occupy all the space available.
exercises.answer: Statement B is not true.
exercises.full_solution: Checking each statement against the simple kinetic (particle) model: in a solid the particles vibrate about fixed lattice positions (A is true). In a gas, particles are far apart and essentially only interact during collisions, so intermolecular forces are negligible between collisions (C is true). Because gas particles are spaced roughly ten times further apart in each direction than liquid particles, a liquid's density works out to be of the order of 1000 times a gas's density (D is true, and a quick check confirms it: water ≈ 1000 kg/m³ versus air ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ gives a ratio of about 800, i.e. 'about 1000 times' as a rough statement). A gas expands to completely fill any container because its particles move freely and randomly with no fixed arrangement (E is true). Statement B, however, is false: it is solids, not liquids, whose particles are held in a regular, ordered pattern. In a liquid the particles are close together (similar spacing to a solid) but are free to slide past one another with no long-range regular arrangement, which is exactly why liquids can flow and take the shape of their container while solids cannot. So the statement that is NOT true is B.

exercises.statement: Using what you know about the compressibility (squeezability) of the different states of matter, explain why (a) air is used to inflate tyres (b) steel is used to make railway lines.
exercises.answer: (a) Air is a gas and gases are easily compressed, so the air in a tyre acts like a cushion/spring that absorbs shocks and gives a comfortable ride. (b) Steel is a solid and solids are essentially incompressible, so railway lines keep a fixed, rigid shape and do not squash or deform under the weight of a train.
exercises.full_solution: In a gas the particles are far apart with large, easily reduced gaps between them, so a gas is easily squeezed into a smaller volume (highly compressible). (a) Because the air trapped inside a tyre can be compressed, it behaves like a spring: when the wheel hits a bump the air compresses slightly and then pushes back, absorbing the shock and giving a smoother, more comfortable ride than a solid wheel would. In a solid, the particles are already packed tightly together in a rigid structure with very little space between them, so a solid strongly resists being squeezed (virtually incompressible). (b) Because steel cannot be compressed under the loads involved, railway lines keep an exact, unchanging shape and spacing (gauge) even under the very large weight of a passing train, which is essential for the wheels to run safely and smoothly along the track.

exercises.statement: Some water is stored in a bag of porous material, such as canvas, which is hung where it is exposed to a draught of air. Explain why the temperature of the water is lower than that of the air.
exercises.answer: Water seeps through the porous bag and evaporates from its outer surface; the draught of air sweeps the water vapour away as fast as it forms, keeping evaporation fast, and since the most energetic (fastest-moving) water molecules are the ones that escape, the average kinetic energy — and so the temperature — of the water left behind falls below that of the surrounding air.
exercises.full_solution: Water molecules in the liquid have a wide spread of speeds (kinetic energies). Evaporation happens when the fastest-moving molecules near the surface have enough kinetic energy to break free of the attractive forces holding them in the liquid and escape as vapour. Because it is specifically the highest-energy molecules that leave, the molecules remaining in the liquid have a lower average kinetic energy than before, and since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, the liquid's temperature drops — this is evaporative cooling. The porous canvas constantly lets a thin film of water seep to the outside surface, giving a large exposed area for evaporation, and the draught of air continuously carries away the water vapour that forms, preventing the air next to the bag from becoming saturated (which would slow evaporation down). With evaporation kept rapid in this way, the water inside the bag is cooled continuously and settles at a temperature noticeably below that of the surrounding (warmer) air — the same principle used in old-fashioned unglazed-pot or canvas water coolers.

exercises.statement: Explain why a bottle of milk keeps better when it stands in water in a porous pot in a draught.
exercises.answer: Water evaporating from the wet, porous pot in the draught cools the pot and the water inside it by evaporative cooling, which in turn keeps the milk bottle standing in that water colder than the surrounding air; the lower temperature slows down the growth of bacteria in the milk, so it stays fresh for longer.
exercises.full_solution: This uses the same evaporative-cooling idea as Question 3. Water soaks through the walls of the porous pot and evaporates from its outer surface; the draught carries the resulting water vapour away, keeping the rate of evaporation high. Since evaporation removes the most energetic molecules from the water, the remaining water (and the pot itself) cools below the air temperature. The milk bottle, standing in this cooled water, is kept at a lower temperature than it would be simply sitting in the room. Because the rate at which bacteria multiply in milk increases sharply with temperature, keeping the milk cooler by this simple evaporative method slows bacterial growth and souring, so the milk stays fresh (keeps better) for longer, even without a refrigerator.

exercises.statement: If the temperature of a fixed mass of gas rises, and its volume remains constant, does the pressure (a) increase (b) stay the same (c) decrease?
exercises.answer: (a) The pressure increases.
exercises.full_solution: Raising the temperature of a gas increases the average kinetic energy, and so the average speed, of its particles. If the volume (and therefore the space available) is kept fixed, the faster-moving particles hit the container walls both more often and with greater force on each impact. Since pressure is simply the total force exerted on the walls divided by their area, these more frequent and more violent collisions mean the pressure must increase. (Beyond what this syllabus requires, this is summarised by the pressure law, p/T = constant at fixed volume, where T must be the temperature in kelvin, not °C.)

exercises.statement: If the volume of a fixed mass of gas is doubled, and the temperature remains constant, is the pressure (a) doubled (b) unchanged (c) halved?
exercises.answer: (c) The pressure is halved.
exercises.full_solution: This is a direct application of Boyle's law, which states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pV = constant, so p is inversely proportional to V. A quick check: if p1 = 100 (arbitrary units) and V1 = 1, then p1V1 = 100. Doubling the volume gives V2 = 2, and since p2V2 must still equal 100, p2 = 100/2 = 50 — exactly half of p1. Physically, doubling the volume means the same number of gas particles are now spread through twice the space, so there are only half as many particles per unit volume near the walls; with half as many collisions per second on each unit of wall area, the pressure is halved.

exercises.statement: Explain why (a) the metal lid on a glass jam jar can be unscrewed easily if the jar is inverted for a few seconds with the lid in very hot water (b) furniture may creak at night after a warm day (c) concrete roads are laid in sections with pitch between them.
exercises.answer: (a) The metal lid expands more than the glass jar for the same temperature rise, loosening its grip so it unscrews more easily. (b) As the temperature falls overnight, different parts and joints of the furniture (often different materials or different wood grain directions) contract by different amounts, creating stresses that are released as creaking sounds. (c) The gaps of pitch allow the concrete sections to expand in hot weather without buckling, cracking or pushing against each other.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Different materials expand by different amounts for the same rise in temperature, and metals generally have a much larger expansivity than glass. When the inverted jar is dipped so the lid sits in very hot water, the metal lid heats up and expands considerably, while the glass jar (especially its inner neck, which is not directly in the hot water and heats more slowly/less) expands much less. This difference opens up the fit between lid and jar very slightly, reducing the grip of the lid on the glass thread, so the lid can be twisted off with far less force. (b) During a warm day, the wood and joints/fixings of furniture are warmer and slightly more expanded; as night falls and the temperature drops, these parts contract again, but not always at exactly the same rate (different materials, or wood fibres along versus across the grain, contract by different amounts). The resulting small relative movements between joints create friction and sudden releases of stress, which are heard as creaking. (c) Concrete expands when it heats up in warm/sunny weather. If a road were laid as one continuous slab, this expansion would have nowhere to go and the slab would buckle, crack or lift. Laying the road in separate sections with a flexible pitch (bitumen) filler between them leaves room: each section can expand slightly into the soft pitch-filled gap in hot weather (and the gap reopens as it contracts in cold weather) without the sections being forced against each other and cracking.

exercises.statement: A bimetallic strip is made from aluminium and copper. When heated it bends in the direction shown in the supplied diagram (the strip, straight at room temperature with aluminium on top and copper on the bottom, curves downward on heating so that the aluminium layer is on the outside/convex side of the curve). (a) Which metal expands more for the same rise in temperature, aluminium or copper? (b) Draw a diagram to show how the bimetallic strip would appear if it were cooled to below room temperature.
exercises.answer: (a) Aluminium expands more than copper for the same temperature rise. (b) Cooling below room temperature bends the strip the opposite way to heating: it curves with the copper layer now on the outside (convex side) of the bend and the aluminium on the inside (concave) side — i.e. the strip curls in the opposite sense to the supplied diagram, roughly a mirror image of the heated shape.
exercises.full_solution: In a bimetallic strip, when the two riveted metals are heated, the metal that expands more for a given temperature rise becomes longer than the other, and since the two strips are fixed together and cannot slide apart, the whole strip must bend so that the metal which has got longer forms the outside (larger-radius, convex) curve, while the metal that expanded less forms the inside (smaller-radius, concave) curve. In the supplied diagram the strip bends, when heated, with aluminium on the outside of the curve, so aluminium must be the metal that has expanded more; this agrees with the real physical property that aluminium has a larger coefficient of thermal expansion than copper. (b) Cooling has the opposite effect to heating: instead of expanding, both metals contract, and again aluminium (the metal with the greater expansivity) contracts more than copper for the same fall in temperature. This means the aluminium side becomes relatively shorter than the copper side, so the strip bends the opposite way to the heated case — now curving so that copper is on the outside (convex) of the bend and aluminium is on the inside (concave), i.e. a mirror image, roughly, of the bent shape shown for heating in the supplied diagram.

exercises.statement: From the list of temperatures 1530 °C, 120 °C, 55 °C, 37 °C, 19 °C, 0 °C, −12 °C, −50 °C, choose the most likely value for each of the following: (a) the melting point of iron (b) the temperature of a room that is comfortably warm (c) the melting point of pure ice at normal pressure (d) the lowest outdoor temperature recorded in London in winter (e) the normal body temperature of a healthy person.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Iron is a metal with a very high melting point — of the values given, only 1530 °C is in the right range for a metal's melting point (the accepted value is close to 1535–1538 °C, so 1530 °C is clearly the intended match, with 120 °C and 55 °C far too low for a metal). (b) A 'comfortably warm' room is typically around 18–20 °C; of the remaining values, 19 °C fits this, while 37 °C is body temperature (too warm for a room) and 55 °C/120 °C are far too hot. (c) By definition, pure ice at normal (standard) atmospheric pressure melts at exactly 0 °C. (d) London's winters are cold but rarely extreme; a reading around −12 °C is a plausible 'coldest on record' figure for London, whereas −50 °C is an unrealistically extreme value for a UK city (more typical of polar regions), so −12 °C is the sensible choice. (e) The normal (healthy, resting) human body temperature is 37 °C. This leaves 120 °C and −50 °C unused, since they are included as unrealistic distractors for these five everyday contexts.

exercises.statement:
**Extension (beyond this course).** Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences (GCSE) covers thermal expansion and its everyday applications (P2.2.1), but not the design of thermometers, so this item is not examined. Try it for interest once you have worked through the on-syllabus items.

(a) How must a property behave to measure temperature? (b) Name three properties that qualify. (c) Name a suitable thermometer for measuring (i) a steady temperature of 1000 °C (ii) the changing temperature of a small object (iii) a winter temperature at the North Pole.
exercises.answer: (a) It must be a physical property that changes continuously, smoothly and in a known (ideally linear), repeatable way with temperature over the range to be measured, so that each temperature corresponds to one specific value of the property. (b) Examples: the volume/length of a liquid (e.g. mercury or alcohol) in a capillary tube; the electrical resistance of a metal wire (or a thermistor); the e.m.f. produced at a thermocouple junction (a gas's pressure at constant volume is another valid example). (c) (i) a resistance thermometer (platinum); (ii) a thermocouple thermometer; (iii) an alcohol (ethanol)-in-glass thermometer.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A property used as the basis of a thermometer (a 'thermometric property') must vary continuously and reproducibly with temperature over the whole range being measured, with a one-to-one correspondence between temperature and the value of the property (ideally a straightforward, close-to-linear relationship), and it must be something that can be measured conveniently and accurately. (b) Properties commonly used include: the volume (length of a column) of a liquid such as mercury or alcohol in a capillary tube; the electrical resistance of a metal wire such as platinum, or of a thermistor; and the e.m.f. generated at the junction between two different metals (a thermocouple). The pressure of a fixed volume of gas is a further example used in constant-volume gas thermometers. (c)(i) For a steady high temperature of 1000 °C, a platinum resistance thermometer is suitable: the text states it accurately covers roughly −200 °C to 1200 °C, comfortably including 1000 °C, and it is 'bulky and best used for steady temperatures', matching this case. (ii) For the rapidly changing temperature of a small object, a thermocouple thermometer is best: its junction can be made very small and has low thermal mass/inertia, so it responds quickly to changes and can be inserted into or placed against a small object. (iii) For a North Pole winter, an alcohol (ethanol)-in-glass thermometer is appropriate rather than mercury: mercury freezes at about −39 °C and would solidify and stop working in extreme polar cold, whereas alcohol/ethanol has a much lower freezing point (around −115 °C), so it stays liquid and usable at the very low temperatures found at the North Pole.

exercises.statement:
**Extension (beyond this course).** Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences (GCSE) covers thermal expansion and its everyday applications (P2.2.1), but not the design of thermometers, so this item is not examined. Try it for interest once you have worked through the on-syllabus items.

In order to make a mercury thermometer that will measure small changes in temperature accurately, would you A decrease the volume of the mercury bulb B put the degree markings further apart C decrease the diameter of the capillary tube D put the degree markings closer together E leave the capillary tube open to the air?
exercises.answer: C — decrease the diameter of the capillary tube.
exercises.full_solution: To detect small temperature changes accurately, a thermometer needs to be as sensitive as possible: a small change in temperature should produce as large and as clearly visible a change as possible in the reading. When mercury in the bulb expands, the small extra volume of mercury is pushed up the capillary tube. If the capillary tube has a smaller diameter (smaller cross-sectional area), the same small increase in volume has to travel further up the narrower tube to be accommodated, so it produces a longer movement of the mercury thread for the same temperature change — this makes the thermometer more sensitive to small changes. Option A (a smaller bulb) would do the opposite: less mercury means less expansion for a given temperature rise, which would reduce sensitivity. Options B and D, simply spacing the printed degree markings differently, do not change the actual physical amount the mercury thread moves for a given temperature change, so they cannot by themselves make the measurement more accurate or sensitive — they only relabel the same movement. Option E, leaving the capillary open to the air, is not a sensitivity improvement at all and is poor design (mercury thermometers are normally sealed, often with an inert gas or vacuum above the mercury, to prevent oxidation and loss of mercury). So the correct choice is C.

exercises.statement:
**Extension (beyond this course).** Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences (GCSE) covers thermal expansion and its everyday applications (P2.2.1), but not the design of thermometers, so this item is not examined. Try it for interest once you have worked through the on-syllabus items.

Describe the main features of a clinical thermometer.
exercises.answer: A clinical thermometer has: a short, narrow range (about 35 °C to 42 °C) spread over a long scale for high sensitivity; a thin-walled, small bulb for quick response to body heat; a very fine (narrow-bore) capillary tube, often with a lens-shaped (magnifying) cross-section, to make the thin mercury thread easy to read; and a narrow constriction in the tube just above the bulb, which lets mercury expand past it into the stem when heated but stops it flowing back into the bulb once removed from the patient, so the reading can be taken at leisure (and the mercury must be shaken back down before reuse).
exercises.full_solution: A clinical thermometer is designed specifically to measure human body temperature quickly, safely and precisely. Its key features are: (1) a short temperature range, typically about 35 °C to 42 °C, centred on normal body temperature (37 °C) — because the range needed is small, the same length of scale can be spread over fewer degrees, giving high sensitivity (a big movement of the mercury thread per degree) so that small, medically significant changes in temperature can be read accurately. (2) A thin-walled bulb containing only a small amount of mercury, which lets heat from the body reach the mercury quickly, so the thermometer responds and settles to the correct reading rapidly. (3) A very narrow (fine-bore) capillary tube — often given a lens-like (roughly triangular) cross-section — so the small volume change of mercury produces a long, clearly visible, and magnified thread that is easy to read precisely. (4) A constriction (a narrowed kink) in the capillary just above the bulb: as the mercury warms and expands it is pushed past this constriction into the main stem, but when the thermometer is removed from the patient and the mercury in the bulb starts to cool and contract, the thread of mercury breaks at the constriction rather than flowing back into the bulb. This leaves the reading in the stem fixed at the highest temperature reached, giving the doctor or nurse time to read it accurately after removing it from the patient; the thermometer must then be given a sharp shake to force the mercury back down past the constriction before it can be reused.

exercises.statement: Explain why (a) newspaper wrapping keeps hot things hot, e.g. fish and chips, and cold things cold, e.g. ice cream (b) fur coats would keep their owners warmer if they were worn inside out (c) a string vest helps to keep a person warm even though it is a collection of holes bounded by string.
exercises.answer: (a) Newspaper (and the air trapped within its crumpled layers) is a poor conductor of heat, so it greatly slows heat flow either out of a hot item or into a cold item, keeping each at its original temperature for longer. (b) Fur insulates by trapping a layer of still air; worn the normal way round, wind can get into the fur from outside and disturb (blow away) this trapped air by convection, but worn inside out the smooth outer skin shields the fur and its trapped air from the wind, keeping the insulating air layer intact. (c) The string vest traps a thin layer of still air in its mesh and between the vest and the skin/next garment; this trapped air is a poor conductor and, held in place by the strings, cannot easily circulate away, so it insulates the body in the same way as a layer of air trapped in any other clothing.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Newspaper is a poor conductor of heat, and crumpled/layered newspaper also traps many small pockets of air, which is an even poorer conductor. Wrapped around a hot item such as fish and chips, this insulation sharply slows the rate at which heat can conduct away from the food to the cooler surroundings, so the food stays hot for longer. Wrapped around a cold item such as ice cream, the same poor conductivity slows the rate at which heat from the warmer surroundings can conduct into the ice cream, so it stays cold (and melts more slowly) for longer. In both cases the newspaper is not 'adding' or 'removing' heat — it is simply slowing down the transfer of heat in whichever direction it would naturally flow. (b) Fur keeps an animal (or a person wearing it) warm mainly by trapping a layer of still air among the hairs, since air is a poor conductor of heat and an insulating layer of it next to the skin reduces heat loss by conduction. However, if the furry side faces outward (the normal way to wear it), wind can blow into the fur and disturb or sweep away this trapped air, replacing it with cooler moving air (forced convection), which increases heat loss. If the coat is worn inside out, the smoother outer (skin/leather) side faces the wind and shields the fur, so the layer of warm trapped air next to the body is protected from being disturbed by wind, and insulation — and so warmth — is improved. (c) Although a string vest is mostly holes, the string mesh is very good at trapping a thin layer of air both within its mesh and between the vest and the skin or the next layer of clothing. Because air is a poor thermal conductor, this trapped layer resists the conduction of heat away from the body; and because the air is held in place by the mesh rather than being free to circulate, convective heat loss is also reduced. It is this trapped, still layer of air — not the string itself — that provides the insulation, which is why a vest made almost entirely of holes can still help keep a person warm.

exercises.statement: What is the advantage of placing an electric immersion heater (a) near the top (b) near the bottom of a tank of water?
exercises.answer: (a) Near the top: it quickly heats only the water above it, giving a small amount of hot water economically and rapidly (e.g. for washing a few dishes) without wasting energy heating the whole tank. (b) Near the bottom: it sets up convection currents that circulate and heat the entire volume of water in the tank, so eventually the whole tank becomes hot — needed when a large supply of hot water is required.
exercises.full_solution: Water heated by an immersion heater becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser water sinks to take its place, setting up a convection current — but only the water above the level of the heater is carried upward and heated by this circulation; water below the heater is left largely undisturbed and stays cool because convection does not carry heat downward. (a) If the heater is placed near the top of the tank, only the relatively small volume of water above it is heated and circulated, so a small quantity of hot water can be produced quickly and without the cost/energy of heating the full tank — useful for jobs needing just a little hot water, such as washing a few dishes or hands. (b) If the heater is placed near the bottom of the tank, essentially the whole volume of water above it is drawn into the convection current, is heated in turn, and circulates, so that eventually the entire tank of water becomes hot. This is what is needed when a full tank's worth of hot water is required, such as for baths or multiple uses throughout a household.

exercises.statement: Explain why on a cold day the metal handlebars of a bicycle feel colder than the rubber grips.
exercises.answer: Although both the metal and the rubber are at the same (cold) temperature, metal is a good conductor of heat, so it conducts heat away from your hand quickly, cooling your skin fast and feeling very cold; rubber is a poor conductor, so it conducts heat away from your hand much more slowly, and so feels less cold even though it is at the same actual temperature.
exercises.full_solution: On a cold day, both the bare metal handlebars and the rubber grips are at the same surrounding (low) temperature — neither is 'colder' than the other in terms of actual temperature. What we sense as 'how cold something feels', though, depends on how quickly heat is conducted away from our skin, not just on the object's temperature. Metal is an excellent conductor of heat, so when your warm hand touches it, heat flows out of your skin into the metal very rapidly; this fast loss of heat cools the skin's surface quickly, which your nerve endings register as feeling very cold. Rubber, by contrast, is a poor conductor of heat (an insulator), so even though it is at the same low temperature as the metal, heat leaves your hand through the rubber much more slowly; your skin does not cool nearly as fast, so the rubber grips feel noticeably less cold, even though a thermometer would show both surfaces to be at the same temperature.

exercises.statement: The door canopy in the supplied diagram shows in a striking way the difference between white and black surfaces when radiation falls on them (the photo shows a striped black-and-white canopy covered in snow, with the snow melted away and icicles dripping from the black stripes while snow remains intact on the white stripes). Explain why.
exercises.answer: Black (dull/dark) surfaces are much better absorbers of radiation than white (light/shiny) surfaces. The black stripes of the canopy absorb more of the incoming radiation, so they warm up and melt the snow sitting on them (the meltwater then refreezes as dripping icicles), while the white stripes reflect most of the radiation instead of absorbing it, so they stay cold and keep their covering of snow.
exercises.full_solution: When radiation (such as sunlight, which includes both visible and infrared/thermal components) falls on a surface, how much of it is absorbed versus reflected depends strongly on the colour and texture of that surface. Dull, black surfaces are good absorbers of radiation: most of the radiant energy that hits them is absorbed and converted into internal (thermal) energy, warming the surface up. Light-coloured, white surfaces are good reflectors (and so poor absorbers) of radiation: most of the radiant energy that strikes them bounces off rather than being absorbed, so they warm up far less. On the striped door canopy, the black stripes absorb much more of the radiation falling on them than the white stripes do, so the black stripes become noticeably warmer. This extra warmth is enough to melt the layer of snow sitting directly on the black stripes, and the resulting meltwater runs to the edge and refreezes into icicles, which is exactly what the photograph shows. The white stripes, absorbing far less radiation, stay much colder, so the snow on them does not melt and remains in place. This striking visual difference nicely demonstrates the general rule (stated in the question) that dark, dull surfaces are both better absorbers and better emitters of radiation than light, shiny surfaces.
